audit.search_note: WebSearch worked reliably for all ~30 queries; no rate limiting. WebFetch was not needed — search snippets quoted Apple's Logic Pro User Guide directly. Two structural problems beyond the individual verdicts, both worth the owner's attention: (1) Several group-level `path` values do not match the tricks filed under them. Group 3's path is \"Logic Pro > Settings > MIDI\" but its first two tricks are Audio>Editing and Display/View>General settings. Group 4's path is \"Logic Pro > Settings > Display\" but its first trick is Settings>Advanced. Group 2's path is \"Logic Pro > Settings > Recording\" but three of its tricks (Quick Punch-In, Auto demix, metronome click) live in the Record menu or File > Project Settings. Group 5's path is \"Logic Pro > Settings > General\" but the Clean Up trick is File > Project Management. (2) VERSION TRAP affecting the whole book: Apple renamed the \"Display\" settings pane to \"View\" somewhere after 10.7 — the current Apple guide pages are titled \"General View settings\", \"Tracks View settings\", \"Editors View settings\" and instruct \"Choose Logic Pro > Settings > View\", while the 10.7 versions of the same pages say \"Display preferences\". I could not find a source pinning the exact version of that rename, so I did not mark individual tricks WRONG for it, but every \"Settings > Display\" reference in this section is stale for current Logic and should read \"Settings > View (Display in 10.7)\".

tricks.title: Run two buffer sizes, not one
tricks.reason: Apple's user guide confirms the I/O Buffer Size trade-off exactly as described (small = low latency for tracking, large = less CPU for mixing), and Apple's settings overview confirms ⌘, opens Settings. Note as a caveat, not an error: Apple's own overload article suggests 256 samples left in place for both jobs as an alternative approach, so 'nothing else changes your day this much' is the author's opinion, not Apple's position.
tricks.evidence_quote: The I/O Buffer Size determines the size of the buffer used by the audio hardware for both input and output, and the smaller the buffer size, the less latency you will encounter when monitoring while recording, or using software instruments. A larger I/O buffer size reduces the load on the CPU of your Mac. However, a larger I/O buffer size increases latency when recording. Separately, Apple's settings overview states: "you choose Logic Pro > Settings, or press Command-Comma (,), then choose the name of the pane that you want to open."

tricks.title: Turn on Low Latency Mode and give it a key command
tricks.reason: Apple's 'Work with plug-in latencies' page confirms the mechanism precisely (bypasses latency-inducing plug-ins on record-enabled/input-monitored tracks), and Apple's key commands page confirms ⌥K opens the Key Commands window where you would assign it.
tricks.evidence_quote: When Low Latency Monitoring mode is enabled, Logic Pro automatically bypasses latency-inducing plug-ins that exceed a specific latency value and turns off any Aux sends on that track. Low Latency Monitoring mode only affects the focused instrument track and any tracks on which the Input Monitoring or Record Enable buttons are active. Apple's key commands page adds: "You can open the Key Commands window by choosing Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit or by pressing Option-K."

tricks.title: Set Processing Threads to Automatic
tricks.reason: Apple explicitly names Automatic as the default and the recommended setting, and confirms the location (Logic Pro > Settings > Audio). The 'on Apple silicon Automatic consistently beats hand tuning' flourish is unsourced editorialising — Apple actually notes a case for manual thread counts when running other CPU-heavy apps — but the actionable instruction is correct.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, the Processing Threads setting is set to Automatic, which is the recommended setting. With the Automatic setting, Logic Pro automatically allocates the number of processing threads that Logic Pro can use for processing audio. This setting provides a balance of performance and reliability when using Logic Pro.

tricks.title: Enable Multithreading on Playback Tracks
tricks.reason: The body describes the behaviour of the wrong option. Apple states that 'Playback Tracks' hands all live/input DSP to ONE thread and one core — the exact opposite of 'it spreads live tracks across cores instead of choking one'. The setting that spreads live tracks across cores is 'Playback & Live Tracks'.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Playback Tracks setting replicates the behavior of previous versions of Logic. When a Track Stack is selected for live input, or when multiple audio tracks are recorded, all of the DSP required for input is handled by one processing thread, and therefore by one available core on the computer. The Playback & Live Tracks setting distributes the load to different threads in cases where a Track Stack that contains multiple software instrument channel strips is selected, or when more than one audio track is recording.
tricks.correction: Settings > Audio > Devices — set Multithreading to "Playback & Live Tracks" if you want live, record-enabled tracks spread across cores. "Playback Tracks" is the older behaviour: all live input DSP is handled by a single thread on a single core. Apple notes "Playback & Live Tracks" places slightly more overall load on the system, so if you have no demanding live tracks, "Playback Tracks" is the better choice.

tricks.title: Raise Process Buffer Range to Large for mixing
tricks.reason: Apple's system-overload article recommends setting Process Buffer Range to Large, and independent coverage confirms it is a separate buffer from the I/O buffer (it sizes the mix engine) with Medium as the default.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can set the I/O buffer size to 256 samples and leave it there for both recording and mixing, and set the Process Buffer Range option to Large. Sound On Sound's "Looking After Logic" adds: "The Process Buffer Range allocates buffer size for Logic's mixing engine, with Medium as the default, but increasing to Large reduces overload likelihood — however, latency will increase."

tricks.title: Uncheck Software Monitoring if you monitor through your interface
tricks.reason: Apple's General Audio settings page states the recommendation in almost the same words, and the overload article repeats it with the exact menu path.
tricks.evidence_quote: When Software monitoring is on, the audio signal is processed via software, and a certain amount of audible delay (commonly referred to as latency) is inevitable. If you're listening to the recorded signal through your mixing console, or your audio interface supports hardware monitoring, you should turn this option off.

tricks.title: Set the count‑in to 1 bar, not 2
tricks.reason: The only checkable assertion — that the count-in length is settable in bars — holds. macProVideo documents choosing count-in length in bars from the count-in button, and the count-in also has a dedicated Record > Count In submenu. '1 bar not 2' is taste. FLAG: this trick sits under the group path 'Logic Pro > Settings > Recording', but the count-in is set from the Record menu / the count-in button in the control bar, not that settings pane.
tricks.evidence_quote: With a right-click on the 1234 count-in button, you can choose count-in length (in bars), or set the number of beats for just the count-in.

tricks.title: Turn off “Allow Quick Punch‑In” only if you never punch
tricks.reason: Two errors. (1) Location: Allow Quick Punch-In is a Record menu item (or the Record button's shortcut menu), not an item in Logic Pro > Settings > Recording where this group's path places it. (2) Key command: Apple's procedure specifies the Record Toggle key command, not R. R is the plain Record command; multiple key-command references list Record Toggle's default as the asterisk (*). The 'keeps the audio before the punch point intact' part is correct.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, turn on Quick Punch-In mode by doing one of the following: Choose Record > Allow Quick Punch-In. Control-click the Record button in the control bar, then choose Allow Quick Punch-In from the shortcut menu. […] Click the Play button in the control bar, then use the Record Toggle key command at the point where you want to start recording. Audio recording starts immediately.
tricks.correction: Leave it on. Turn it on at Record > Allow Quick Punch-In (or Control-click the Record button in the control bar and choose it there). With it on, start playback and hit the Record Toggle key command at the moment you want to drop in — the transition happens with no audible gap and the recording before and after the punched section is untouched, which is a lifesaver when a take suddenly gets good.

tricks.title: Set MIDI recording to “Create Take Folder”
tricks.reason: Apple's Recording settings page confirms both the location and the result. Minor wording note for the owner: the control is the 'MIDI Cycle On' pop-up inside the 'Overlapping Track Recordings' area of Settings > Recording, not a sub-pane called 'Recording > MIDI'.
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose Settings > Recording, then in the Overlapping Track Recordings area, choose Create Take Folder from the MIDI Cycle On pop-up menu. […] Create Take Folder: A new take folder is created when recording over an existing MIDI or audio region.

tricks.title: Enable “Auto demix by channel if multitrack recording”
tricks.reason: Version trap, and a wrong location. The option lives in File > Project Settings > Recording (a project setting), not Logic Pro > Settings > Recording as this group's path implies — and it was removed in Logic Pro 11.0.1, with 'Automatically erase duplicates' occupying its place. The book claims to cover 10.7, 11 and 12, so this trick is dead for two of the three versions and says nothing about it.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro v. 11.0.1, the "Auto demix by channel if multitrack recording" option is no longer available in File > Project Settings > Recording, and has been replaced with the "Automatically erase duplicates" option instead. Apple's current Recording project settings page corroborates this by documenting only the replacement: "The Automatically erase duplicates checkbox, when selected, deletes the previous note when playing or adding a note to a MIDI region at the same position, pitch, and MIDI channel as an existing note."

tricks.title: Turn on the pre‑roll metronome click only
tricks.reason: Apple's Metronome project settings page confirms both checkboxes and what each does, and 'Toggle Metronome Click' is the default K key command per studio-interns.com's key-command reference. Two small notes: the settings are in File > Project Settings > Metronome, not Settings > Recording as the group path implies; and 'Click while recording' covers the count-in AND the whole recording pass, not pre-roll only, so the title slightly oversells it.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click While Recording: The checkbox determines whether the metronome produces clicks during the count-in (if the count-in is turned on) and while recording. Click While Playing: Turns the metronome on during playback. studio-interns.com's command-of-the-day entry is titled "Toggle Metronome Click K".

tricks.title: Set the click source to a sound you can actually hear
tricks.reason: The 'set the accented downbeat louder' half is sourced (per-event velocity fields for bar/beat/division). The 'swap the default woodblock for a rimshot or cowbell' half is not: Apple documents no sound-picker for the click. The click is the Klopfgeist plug-in on the Click channel strip, whose character is changed via its Tonality control or by changing the generated note NUMBERS — or by loading a different plug-in on the Click channel strip entirely. Nothing external supports 'swap for a rimshot or cowbell' as a described action.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Audio Click (Klopfgeist) checkbox turns the audio click on or off for the Klopfgeist plug-in or any plug-in loaded on the Click channel strip. […] Note field, which defines the note number of generated notes assigned to bar, group, beat, or division. […] a velocity field defines the velocity of generated notes. Apple's Klopfgeist page adds: "The Tonality slider and field can change the sound from a short click to a pitched percussion sound, similar to a wood block or claves."
tricks.salvage: Open File > Project Settings > Metronome. The click is the Klopfgeist plug-in sitting on the Click channel strip, and every part of it is yours: raise the Bar velocity above the Beat velocity so the downbeat actually lands, and change the Note values to pitch the click somewhere it cuts through your mix. Want a different sound entirely? Load any instrument you like onto the Click channel strip and drive it with those same note numbers. A click you have to strain for is a click you will drift against.

tricks.title: Turn on scrubbing with audio in the Tracks area
tricks.reason: Apple's Audio Editing settings page confirms the checkbox by that exact name at that exact path, plus the related Maximum Scrub Speed and Scrub Response controls. FLAG: this is the first trick in a group whose path reads 'Logic Pro > Settings > MIDI' — the trick's own body gives the right path (Settings > Audio > Editing), so fix the group heading/path rather than the trick.
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose File > Settings > Audio, click Editing, then select the "Scrubbing with audio in Tracks area" checkbox. […] When the "Scrubbing with audio in Tracks area" checkbox is selected, you can scrub audio regions in the Tracks area.

tricks.title: Set the MIDI reset options to send Notes Off only
tricks.reason: Apple's Reset Messages page gives the opposite advice: leave ALL of these unselected, which is the default, because Logic handles MIDI resets automatically. The trick tells the reader to select Control 123 (All Notes Off), which is a change away from Apple's stated recommendation, and its stated rationale ('the other resets can wipe controller states') is also backwards — Apple's point is that these legacy resets exist only for compatibility with older MIDI devices.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro handles MIDI reset messages automatically and intelligently, so you should generally make sure that all of these options are unselected—which they are, by default. […] Reset options for Control 123 and 121 are included for compatibility with older MIDI devices.
tricks.correction: Leave the MIDI Reset Messages alone. Under Settings > MIDI > Reset Messages every box is unselected by default and Apple's guidance is to keep it that way — Logic handles MIDI reset messages automatically. The Control 123 (All Notes Off) and Control 121 (Reset Controls) options are there only for compatibility with older hardware; switch one on only if a specific old synth needs it.

tricks.title: Enable “Display middle C as C3”
tricks.reason: Apple documents the pop-up menu, both options, and the location. Only nit: it is a pop-up menu with C3 (Yamaha) / C4 (Roland), not a checkbox to 'enable', and in current Logic the pane is Settings > View > General (it was Settings > Display > General in 10.7).
tricks.evidence_quote: You can use the Display Middle C As pop-up menu in the Logic Pro > Settings > Display pane to alter the display to match your device. C3 (Yamaha): The bottom C on a five-octave keyboard (note # 36) is labeled C1, and middle C (note # 60) is labeled C3. […] C4 (Roland): […] middle C is labeled as C4.

tricks.title: Fix doubled notes from a controller
tricks.reason: Apple's General MIDI project settings page confirms the exact menu path, the exact control name, and that its purpose is precisely to stop note doubling when the master keyboard has no Local Off.
tricks.evidence_quote: If your master keyboard doesn't have a Local Off setting, you can use this feature to avoid unwanted note doubling when recording. […] To assign an instrument with a permanently disabled MIDI Thru function: Open File > Project Settings > MIDI > General. Choose the desired instrument in the Instrument Without MIDI Thru Function menu.

tricks.title: Turn on Enable Complete Features first, always
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the checkbox name, the Advanced settings location, and the exact list of things it gates — project alternatives and backups, beat mapping, expanded mixing and automation. 'Simplified mode' is the book's own label rather than Apple's, but the substance is right. FLAG: this trick sits in a group whose path reads 'Logic Pro > Settings > Display'; it belongs under Settings > Advanced.
tricks.evidence_quote: When the Enable Complete Features checkbox is selected, advanced features such as project alternatives and backups, beat mapping, expanded mixing and automation capabilities, and more are available.

tricks.title: Turn off region colouring by track and colour by region instead
tricks.reason: The named option does not exist. Apple's Region Color pop-up offers 'Individual' and 'As Track Color' — there is no 'As Region Colour'. A reader hunting for that entry will not find it. (Also: in current Logic the pane is Settings > View > Tracks, not Settings > Display > Tracks.)
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose Logic Pro > Settings > View, then click the Tracks button. In the Display Track settings pane, make sure that the Region Color pop-up menu is set to Individual. […] Individual: You can color regions individually independent from the track color. As Track Color: Regions conform to the color of the track they are on, but they remember the individual color of a region if you switch back to Individual.
tricks.correction: Under Settings > View > Tracks, set the Region Color pop-up to "Individual" rather than "As Track Color". Individual lets you colour-code by part rather than by track, which scales much better on big arrangements — and if you switch back and forth, Logic remembers each region's individual colour.

tricks.title: Turn on “Show Help Tags”
tricks.reason: Apple's General View settings page confirms the checkbox by name and confirms that position and parameter values are shown while editing, which is the trick's claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: The "Show help tags" checkbox […] When editing, the function name, region or event name or number, position, and parameter values are shown in help tags.

tricks.title: Set Cycle to “Auto‑set locators by region selection”
tricks.reason: The behaviour is real but the location is not. Auto Set Locators lives in the Cycle button's shortcut menu in the control bar, not in Settings > General > Cycle. Apple's actual General > Cycle settings pane contains only Cycle Pre-Processing and the Smooth Cycle Algorithm checkbox. A reader following 'General > Cycle' will not find this.
tricks.evidence_quote: Control-click the Cycle button in the control bar, then click Auto Set Locators. […] By Region Selection: The locators (and the cycle area) are set to the borders of the currently selected region. Apple's Cycle settings pane, by contrast, documents only: "The Cycle Pre-Processing pop-up menu processes a cycle jump slightly before its actual position" and "The Smooth Cycle Algorithm checkbox improves the timing of cycle jumps".
tricks.correction: Control-click the Cycle button in the control bar and turn on Auto Set Locators > by Region Selection. Now selecting a region snaps the locators and the cycle area to that region's borders, so C loops exactly what you picked. It turns cycle into a one-key operation.

tricks.title: Turn on “Select regions on track selection”
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the behaviour and that it is governed in Editing settings. One correction of emphasis rather than fact: this is already ON by default, so 'turn on' is really 'leave on' for most users.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, when you select a track, all regions on the track (or those that fall within the cycle, if Cycle mode is on) are selected. You can change this default behavior in Editing settings.

tricks.title: Set “Limit Dragging to One Direction” to Vertically in the Tracks area
tricks.reason: There is no 'Vertically' option to set. It is a plain checkbox — 'Limit Dragging to One Direction: In Tracks' — and its behaviour is not vertical-locking: it locks to whichever axis you start moving in, so an initial left/right move constrains you to horizontal. The trick's stated goal (not nudging a region off the grid while moving it to another track) is achieved by ticking the checkbox and then, per Apple, releasing and re-dragging to change track — or by holding Shift to override.
tricks.evidence_quote: When selected, this checkbox allows you to only move regions (including folders) in one direction in the Tracks area. More specifically, if you initially move a region left or right, movement is limited to the horizontal axis. If you want to move a region from one track to another, release the mouse button, reselect the region, then drag it up or down. The setting is found at Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing.
tricks.correction: Tick the "Limit Dragging to One Direction: In Tracks" checkbox in Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing. Once you start a drag left or right, movement locks to the horizontal axis, so you cannot nudge a perfectly placed region onto another track by accident. To actually change tracks, let go, reselect, and drag up or down — or hold Shift to override the limit for one move. There is a matching checkbox for the Piano Roll and Score.

tricks.title: Turn off “Catch playhead” while editing
tricks.reason: The command name is real ('Catch Playhead Position', default ⌥O per studio-interns.com) and the advised workflow is correct. WORDING FIX NEEDED, not a factual failure: the opening sentence is inverted — the Catch button is what MAKES the view follow the playhead; turning it OFF is what stops the chase. Reword to 'The Catch button in each editor makes the view follow the playhead. Turn it off when you are editing a specific bar…'
tricks.evidence_quote: Catch Playhead Position ⌥O […] toggles the "Catch Playhead" button […] When you work in Catch mode, the visible section of a window follows the playhead during playback or recording. If regions are scrolling along with the playhead during playback you can stop the scrolling, perform some task, and then catch back up.

tricks.title: Set the maximum undo steps to 100+
tricks.reason: The setting exists where the trick says it does, and 100+ is achievable — Apple documents a ceiling of 200, so the advice is inside the possible range.
tricks.evidence_quote: The maximum number of undo steps that can be set in Logic Pro is up to 200, which can be changed in Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing. […] go to Logic Pro > Settings > General, click Editing, and change the number in the Number of Undo Steps value slider.

tricks.title: Read the Clean Up list before you confirm it
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the menu path, that a confirmation dialog lists every file to be deleted with per-file opt-out, and that Delete Unused Files removes whole files from the project. FLAG: this trick sits in a group whose path reads 'Logic Pro > Settings > General'; it belongs under the File menu.
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose File > Project Management > Clean Up. […] The "Delete Unused Files" option will delete files not used in any project alternative from the project and remove them from the Project Audio Browser. […] A dialog appears showing all of the files to be deleted from the project, and you can deselect the Delete checkbox for any individual files you want to keep.

tricks.title: Set your sample rate before you record, not after
tricks.reason: The path and the 48/44.1 guidance are right, but the stated consequence is wrong. Apple says changing the sample rate after recording causes PITCH AND PLAYBACK SPEED changes — i.e. Logic does not resample your existing files, they simply play back at the wrong speed. 'Resamples everything and softens transients' describes something Logic does not do, and it understates the damage, which is what would generate the refund email.
tricks.evidence_quote: To avoid pitch and playback speed changes in your audio files, don't change the sample rate after you've recorded or imported audio into your project. […] choose File > Project Settings > Audio (or use the Open Audio Project Settings key command), then choose a sample rate from the Sample Rate pop-up menu. The default sample rate is 48 kHz for a new Logic Pro installation.
tricks.correction: Under File > Project Settings > Audio, pick 48 kHz for anything that might touch video and 44.1 kHz for pure music (48 kHz is Logic's default on a fresh install). Change it after you have recorded or imported audio and Logic does not resample those files for you — they play back at the wrong pitch and speed. If you genuinely must convert, use File > Project Settings > Assets and select "Convert audio file sample rate when importing".

tricks.title: Set the recording bit depth to 24-bit
tricks.reason: Version error. 32-bit float recording did not arrive in Logic Pro 11.1 — it shipped in Logic Pro 10.8 in November 2023, alongside Mastering Assistant. The location claim is fine: Apple's Recording settings pane does contain the Bit Depth pop-up.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro 10.8 (November 2023) release coverage: "Logic Pro now supports 32-bit float recording when used with compatible audio interfaces. This helps artists minimize the digital clipping that can occur when recording more dynamic instruments or performances." Apple's Recording settings page confirms the location: "Bit Depth pop-up menu: Set the bit depth for newly recorded audio files, with a higher bit depth having the ability to capture a wider dynamic range."
tricks.correction: It lives in Settings > Recording, not Project Settings. 32-bit float is available from Logic Pro 10.8 (November 2023) onward and depends on your interface. Never record at 16-bit.

tricks.title: Turn on Smart Tempo “Keep Project Tempo” by default
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the path, the mode name, what Keep does, and — importantly for the trick's warning — that Adapt should only be used temporarily precisely because it rewrites the project tempo.
tricks.evidence_quote: Keep Project Tempo: The project tempo is maintained when you record audio or import audio files […] Adapt Project Tempo mode should be used only temporarily when making a free recording, adding a file you want the project tempo to conform to, or when you specifically want the Tempo track to follow region edits, because it results in changes to the project tempo. You can set the default Project Tempo mode for a project in the Smart Tempo project settings (File > Project Settings > Smart Tempo).

tricks.title: Stop new recordings arriving pre-quantised
tricks.reason: Apple's Region inspector page confirms the mechanism exactly as the trick describes it: with nothing selected the inspector shows 'Default Settings' and those values are applied to newly recorded regions, so a stray Quantize value there is what silently quantises new takes. Setting Quantize to off with no region selected is the documented fix.
tricks.evidence_quote: When no region is selected, the upper line of the Region inspector displays the text "Default Settings". The region parameter settings displayed are applied to newly recorded regions as realtime playback settings.

tricks.title: Set Tuning to Equal Temperament unless you mean otherwise
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the path, that the setting is global to software instruments, and that Equal Tempered disables any alternative tuning. Small precision note: Apple scopes it to Logic's INCLUDED software instruments, so 'every software instrument' overreaches slightly for third-party plug-ins.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro includes a real-time tuning system for use with the included software instruments, which you can configure in the Tuning project settings. […] choose File > Project Settings > Tuning […] Equal Tempered: This option disables any tuning and uses an equal tempered scale.

tricks.title: Turn on “Bounce project settings” for consistent exports
tricks.reason: The title names something that does not exist and does not match its own body. The body describes the Assets project settings, which Apple documents as being about portability — copying audio, samples and impulse responses into the project package — not about bouncing or export consistency. Everything after the title is correct; the title is the defect.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Settings > Assets (or use the Open Assets Project Settings key command). […] To copy the respective file types to the project, select any of the copy checkboxes. Files are copied into the project when the project is saved. […] Once the project is saved, you can move or copy the project without losing any references to files in the project.
tricks.correction: Retitle to "Copy your assets into the project so it travels". Under File > Project Settings > Assets, tick the options to copy audio files, Ultrabeat and Sampler samples, Space Designer impulse responses and Apple Sound Library content into the project. The files are copied in the next time you save, and from then on you can move or copy the project without breaking a single file reference. Your project becomes portable in one move.

tricks.title: Save a Session Start template and set it as the default
tricks.reason: Both halves check out against Apple: File > Save As Template exists and is documented for exactly this purpose, and the Project Handling settings provide a Default Template button plus a Startup Action pop-up that opens it on launch.
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose File > Save As Template (or use the corresponding key command), then enter a name. […] Templates make it easier to create projects with frequently used instruments or Mixer configurations. […] The Default Template button allows you to choose a default template when Create New Project using Default Template is chosen from the Startup Action pop-up menu.

tricks.title: Set a default channel strip for new tracks
tricks.reason: Apple documents saving a channel strip setting (via the Setting button > Save Channel Strip Setting As) and browsing settings in the Library, but I could not find the 'control-click in the Library > Set as default' step in Apple's guide or in two independent reputable educators — only a single blog, a user forum thread and a YouTube video, which is below the bar. The step may well be real; it is not externally provable as written, and the trick's payoff depends entirely on it.
tricks.evidence_quote: To save a channel strip setting in Logic Pro, click the Setting button at the top of the channel strip, then choose "Save Channel Strip Setting as" from the pop-up menu. In the dialog that appears, select the appropriate folder, enter a name for the channel strip setting, and click Save. You can load, copy, paste, reset, save, and delete channel strip settings in a channel strip. You can also access channel strip settings in the Library.
tricks.salvage: Build one channel strip the way you always want to start — gain staging, your go-to EQ and compressor, the sends you always use. Click the Setting button at the top of the strip and choose "Save Channel Strip Setting As", and file it somewhere you will find it. From then on, every new track is two clicks from your starting point: open the Library, find your saved setting under User Channel Strip Settings, click it. Keeping a copy of that strip in your template gets you the same result with no clicks at all.

tricks.title: Set the default region colour palette
tricks.reason: The key command is solid — Apple documents Option-C as the way to open the Color palette, and documents double-clicking a swatch to define a custom colour. What I cannot verify anywhere is the trick's actual promise: that you can 'rearrange' the palette once and get consistent colours 'across every project'. Nothing external supports a globally persistent, reorderable palette.
tricks.evidence_quote: Control-click one of the selected regions, then choose Name and Color > Show/Hide Colors from the shortcut menu (or press Option-C). […] Double-click any color square in the Color palette to open the Colors window and create a custom color using the color wheel and contrast and opacity sliders.
tricks.salvage: Press ⌥C to open the Color palette (or Control-click a region and choose Name and Color > Show/Hide Colors). Double-click any swatch to open the Colors window and dial in a custom colour with the wheel and the contrast and opacity sliders. Decide once what each colour means to you — drums, vocals, keys, reference — and build that scheme into your template so every project opens with the same language. Consistent colours across projects make navigating an old session instant.

tricks.title: Turn on Project Alternatives before you need them
tricks.reason: The menu path is wrong. It is File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative, not File > Alternatives > New Alternative. The feature and the description of it are correct. Worth adding: alternatives require Enable Complete Features to be on, which ties this to the earlier trick.
tricks.evidence_quote: To create a new alternative in Logic Pro, choose File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative, then enter a unique name for the alternative and click Done. […] To edit alternatives, choose File > Project Alternatives > Edit Alternatives.
tricks.correction: File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative gives you branching versions inside one project file — name it and click Done. Make one before every big arrangement change. (You will only see the menu if Enable Complete Features is switched on in Settings > Advanced.) The same menu's Edit Alternatives lets you rename or remove them; the Main alternative cannot be removed.

tricks.title: Set autosave and then still hit ⌘S
tricks.reason: 'Set autosave' tells the reader to configure something that has no user-facing control. Logic's autosave runs invisibly and exposes no preference — the only thing you can configure is Auto Backup, which is a different feature (versions saved on each manual save, retrieved via File > Revert To). The body's advice is fine; the instruction in the title is not actionable.
tricks.evidence_quote: Autosave doesn't have user settings—it just works behind the scenes. […] the only time you will be aware of it is when you restart after a Logic crash. Apple's project alternatives page confirms the separate backup behaviour: "Each time you save a project using the File > Save menu item (or pressing Command-S), a version of the current project alternative is saved (up to ten backups per alternative)."
tricks.correction: Retitle to "Logic autosaves — still hit ⌘S". Logic autosaves invisibly so you do not lose work if it quits unexpectedly, but there is no autosave setting to turn on or tune, and you will only ever meet it as a recovery prompt after a crash. What you control is ⌘S: every manual save also banks a backup of the current alternative (up to ten), reachable from File > Revert To. Build the reflex of hitting ⌘S every time you finish a thought.

tricks.title: Move the Sound Library to an external drive on purpose
tricks.reason: Apple documents the exact menu path and the outcome. One caveat the trick should probably carry: Apple warns not to rename the drive afterwards, or Logic loses the library — which is the one way this move does break things.
tricks.evidence_quote: Open Logic Pro, then choose Logic Pro > Sound Library > Relocate Sound Library. In the window, select the storage device or volume where you want to store the Sound Library, then click Relocate. […] Don't rename the storage device or volume after you've moved the Sound Library. If you do, Logic Pro and MainStage won't be able to find the Sound Library.

tricks.title: Set the audio file location to “Project” not “Folder”
tricks.reason: The option is not called 'Project'. In the File > Save As dialog the two buttons are 'Organize my project as: Package' and 'Organize my project as: Folder'. The body itself says 'package' — only the title is wrong, and it is the half a reader will go hunting for.
tricks.evidence_quote: To save the project as a file (package) containing project assets, select the "Organize my project as: Package" button. To save the project as a folder containing subfolders for project assets, select the "Organize my project as: Folder" button.
tricks.correction: Retitle to "Set the audio file location to ‘Package’ not ‘Folder’". In the File > Save As dialog, choose "Organize my project as: Package". Keeping recorded audio inside the project package means dragging one file to a hard drive moves everything. Only switch to Folder if you are working with an enormous session across multiple drives.

downgrades.title: Turn on the pre‑roll metronome click only
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own Apple quote contradicts the trick's title. Apple: "Click While Recording: The checkbox determines whether the metronome produces clicks during the count-in (if the count-in is turned on) and while recording." There is no pre-roll-only click among the two documented checkboxes — enabling Click While Recording gives you count-in AND the entire recording pass. The trick promises a state Logic does not offer, which is a contradiction by the cited source, not a wording nit. Secondary defect: the 'Toggle Metronome Click = K' half rests on a single studio-interns.com command-of-the-day post with no URL supplied, which is below the two-independent-sources bar and is Logic Pro X-era. Salvage: rewrite as 'Use Click While Recording to get a click on the count-in and through the take, and Click While Playing to keep playback silent' — that is exactly what Apple documents. Could not re-search (web search budget exhausted), so the correction above is drawn from the auditor's own Apple quote only.

downgrades.title: Turn off “Catch playhead” while editing
downgrades.reason: The auditor concedes the trick's opening sentence states the mechanism backwards, then classes that as a wording fix. It is not — it is the source contradicting the text as written. The quoted line says Catch mode is what MAKES the view follow the playhead ('When you work in Catch mode, the visible section of a window follows the playhead'), while the book tells the reader the Catch button is what causes the chase and must be switched off to stop it being switched on. A buyer following the book's sentence as printed gets the toggle backwards. Compounding defects: the sole source is a single 2019 blog post explicitly titled for Logic Pro X, which fails both the 'two independent reputable sources' bar and version-matching to 10.7/11/12, and the ⌥O default key command is single-sourced from that same page. Salvage: 'The Catch button in each editor makes the view follow the playhead. Turn it off while you are editing a specific bar so the window stops scrolling away from you, then turn it back on to follow playback.' Verify the ⌥O default against Apple's key commands list before printing it, or drop the keystroke.

downgrades.title: Set the count‑in to 1 bar, not 2
downgrades.reason: The only checkable assertion is sourced to exactly one article (macProVideo) with no Apple page and no corroborating second educator, which is below the stated bar for non-Apple sourcing. The quote is also about right-clicking the control bar's count-in button, while the trick sits under a group path of 'Logic Pro > Settings > Recording' — a path the auditor itself flags as wrong, meaning the reader is sent to a pane where this control does not live. Neither the count-in-length-in-bars mechanism nor the correct path was confirmed against support.apple.com. Salvage: keep the taste advice and drop the unverified path — 'A one-bar count-in is usually enough; two bars just makes you wait. Set the count-in length from the Record menu's Count In submenu' — after confirming that submenu against Apple's guide.

downgrades.title: Enable “Display middle C as C3”
downgrades.reason: This is the version trap, and the auditor identified it and then cleared the trick anyway. The quoted page describes the control as living in 'the Logic Pro > Settings > Display pane', while the auditor's own note says current Logic puts it in Settings > View > General and that Display > General was the 10.7 location. The book covers 10.7, 11 and 12 and prints one path with no caveat, so it is wrong for at least one covered version — which per the version rule is WRONG, not VERIFIED, and I cannot determine which half without re-searching. Second defect: the quote describes a pop-up menu offering C3 (Yamaha) / C4 (Roland), which does not support the trick's framing of 'enable' a setting. Salvage: 'Logic can label middle C as C3 or C4. If your keyboard, sample library or lead sheet disagrees with Logic's note names, switch the Display Middle C As pop-up to match it.' — then pin the exact pane per version before printing.

downgrades.title: Set MIDI recording to “Create Take Folder”
downgrades.reason: Rule 1 failure: the evidence supports something adjacent to the claim, not the claim as written. Every quoted line is scoped to the 'MIDI Cycle On' pop-up inside the Overlapping Track Recordings area — i.e. it governs what happens when you record MIDI over an existing region in Cycle mode. The trick's title generalises this to MIDI recording as a whole. Whether Create Take Folder is even offered by the MIDI Cycle Off pop-up was never checked, so a reader recording MIDI without cycle may set this and see no take folders. The auditor also notes the trick names a non-existent sub-pane ('Recording > MIDI'). Salvage: 'In Settings > Recording, in the Overlapping Track Recordings area, set the MIDI Cycle On pop-up to Create Take Folder so cycle-recorded MIDI passes stack as takes instead of merging.' — that version matches the quoted evidence exactly.

downgrades.title: Turn on Low Latency Mode and give it a key command
downgrades.reason: Half of the trick — the title half — has no URL behind it. The evidence_url is the plug-in latencies page, which solidly supports what Low Latency Monitoring does; the '⌥K opens the Key Commands window' claim is spliced into the same evidence_quote field with no page cited, no title, and no way to tell whether it came from a source or from memory. That is precisely the pattern the audit rule exists to catch: a keystroke the reader will actually press, backed by nothing pointable. Salvage: keep the Apple-verified body and drop or re-source the keystroke — 'Enable Low Latency Monitoring; it bypasses latency-inducing plug-ins on record-enabled and input-monitored tracks and mutes that track's aux sends. If you use it often, assign it a key command from Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit.' The menu path is a verifiable route to the same place and costs the trick nothing.

downgrades.title: Set the maximum undo steps to 100+
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote reads reconstructed rather than lifted. 'The maximum number of undo steps that can be set in Logic Pro is up to 200, which can be changed in Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing' is third-person FAQ/answer phrasing that names the app twice in one sentence — not Apple User Guide voice, which addresses the reader in the imperative ('Choose Logic Pro > Settings...'). The 200 ceiling is the load-bearing number here, since it is what makes '100+' safe advice, and it is the part carried by the suspicious sentence. Under attack rule 4 this needed a re-search and I could not run one. Salvage: 'Logic's undo history is shorter than you think by default. Raise it in Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing, in the Number of Undo Steps field.' — drop the specific ceiling and the specific target number unless the 200 figure can be quoted from Apple verbatim.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout (no rate limiting). WebFetch was blocked by the egress proxy for every domain tried (support.apple.com, logicpro.skydocu.com, manualsdir.com, afteraudio.com), so all evidence quotes come from WebSearch result snippets that quote the Apple Logic Pro User Guide or approved educator sites. Note on the ⌘-drag swap trick: searches whose wording did NOT prime the word "Command" consistently returned the guide line describing a plain drag over another marker as the swap gesture, while queries containing "Command" produced blended answers — I treated the un-primed results as the reliable ones. No group-level "path" fields exist in this file.

tricks.title: Use the Arrangement track to move whole sections
tricks.reason: Apple's guide confirms both halves: G shows/hides global tracks (where the arrangement track lives), and moving an arrangement marker carries every region, marker and automation point in that section.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you move or copy an arrangement marker, all of the regions in that section of the project are moved or copied, including the markers on every track in the section, and the automation points on every automation curve in the section. / To show global tracks in Logic Pro, choose Track > Global Tracks > Show Global Tracks (or press G).

tricks.title: ⌘-drag one arrangement marker onto another to swap sections
tricks.reason: The Logic Pro User Guide describes the swap as a PLAIN drag of one arrangement marker directly over another — no ⌘ modifier. Searches that did not contain the word "Command" returned this line consistently; ⌘-drag is not what the guide credits with swapping. The trick's premise that "a plain drag moves or inserts" (and therefore cannot swap) is what the guide contradicts.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you drag one arrangement marker directly over another one in the arrangement track, the two markers switch places (all their content is swapped).
tricks.correction: A plain drag moves a section, or inserts it between two others. To swap two sections outright, drag one arrangement marker directly over another — the two markers switch places and all their content is swapped. Trying three song orders takes about fifteen seconds.

tricks.title: ⌥‑drag an arrangement marker to duplicate a section
tricks.reason: Apple's guide documents Option-drag as the copy gesture for arrangement markers, and states elsewhere on the same page that a copied marker brings all of the section's regions and automation with it.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, Option-drag the arrangement marker to the position where you want to place the copy. When you place the copy between two existing arrangement markers, the marker to the right moves right to make room for the copied marker.

tricks.title: Delete a section and close the gap
tricks.reason: The two-press Delete behaviour and the gap closing are both stated verbatim in the Apple guide.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the arrangement marker, then press Delete to delete the regions in the Tracks area below the arrangement marker so it is empty. Press Delete again to delete the arrangement marker. ... When you move or delete an arrangement marker, the sections to the right move left to fill the deleted section, closing up the empty space.

tricks.title: Insert silence across the whole project
tricks.reason: The menu item is named "Insert Silence Between Locators", not "Insert Silence at Locators". A reader following the book's path will not find that command in the Edit > Cut/Insert Time submenu. The submenu name itself (Edit > Cut/Insert Time) is correct.
tricks.evidence_quote: To insert silence between locators in Logic Pro, choose Edit > Cut/Insert Time > Insert Silence Between Locators (or use the corresponding key command).
tricks.correction: Set the locators, then Edit > Cut/Insert Time > Insert Silence Between Locators. Every track and every automation point shifts. This is how you add two bars to an intro without wrecking the mix.

tricks.title: Snap arrangement markers to your actual section boundaries
tricks.reason: New arrangement markers ignore the locators AND the playhead entirely — Apple states they always appear at the start of the project or after the last existing marker, at a fixed default length of eight bars. Setting locators with U before creating one changes nothing about where the marker lands, so the trick's whole payoff ("it lands perfectly instead of approximately") is false. U itself is real (Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events and Enable Cycle) but does not feed arrangement-marker creation.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click the Add Arrangement Marker button (+) in the arrangement track (or use the Create Arrangement Marker key command). The arrangement marker appears at the start of the project or at the end of the last existing arrangement marker, regardless of the playhead position. By default, arrangement markers are eight bars long. ... Drag the right edge of the arrangement marker left or right.
tricks.correction: New arrangement markers always appear at the start of the project or after the last existing marker, eight bars long, regardless of where the playhead or locators sit. So create the marker first, then drag its right edge to the exact end of the section — the edge snaps to bars, so it lands on the boundary rather than near it.

tricks.title: Repeat regions numerically instead of dragging
tricks.reason: Apple documents Edit > Repeat Multiple with a Number of Copies field and a copies-vs-aliases choice; Why Logic Pro Rules confirms ⌘R as the single-repeat shortcut.
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose Edit > Repeat Multiple from the Tracks area local menu bar (or use the Repeat Regions Multiple Times key command). ... Enter the number of desired repetitions in the Number of Copies field. ... To paste the copies as regions, select As Copies (default). To paste the copies as clones (for audio regions) or aliases (for MIDI regions), select As Aliases or Clones. [and https://whylogicprorules.com/paste-loop-repeat/ : "By simply clicking on a region (or group of regions) and hitting Command+R, you can create a duplicate."]

tricks.title: Loop a region instead of copying it
tricks.reason: Apple's Loop regions page documents the upper-right-corner drag gesture and L as the loop toggle; loop repetitions are re-plays of the same region, so editing the original does propagate.
tricks.evidence_quote: Place the pointer over the upper-right edge of the region until the pointer becomes a Loop pointer, then drag the right edge of the region until it aligns with the point where you want it to stop playing. ... You can unloop the region by deselecting the Loop checkbox, or by pressing L again.

tricks.title: Convert loops to real regions only at the very end
tricks.reason: There is no "Loops to Regions" command in the Logic Pro User Guide. The command under Edit > Convert is "Loops to Aliases", and it does not produce independent real regions for MIDI — it produces aliases (audio loops become cloned regions). Two separate searches for "Loops to Regions" both returned the guide's "Loops to Aliases" wording and no such command by the book's name.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the original region and choose Edit > Convert > Loops to Aliases (or use the Convert Loops to Aliases key command). Logic Pro converts software instrument loop repetitions into aliases, and converts audio loop repeats into cloned audio regions.
tricks.correction: Edit > Convert > Loops to Aliases turns software-instrument loop repetitions into aliases and audio loop repeats into cloned audio regions. Stay looped as long as possible so a single edit propagates, then convert once the arrangement is locked.

tricks.title: Use aliases for parts that must stay identical
tricks.reason: Apple documents Option-Shift-drag as the alias-creation gesture for MIDI regions and confirms that editing the original alters every alias.
tricks.evidence_quote: Option-Shift-drag the region to the position where you want the alias to start. ... An alias is a reference to a region and looks similar to a normal region in the Tracks area. If you alter the original region, all aliases of the region are similarly altered.

tricks.title: Make a folder out of a section
tricks.reason: The menu path matches the Apple guide exactly, including the behaviour when the selected regions span several tracks.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the regions, then choose Functions > Folder > Pack Folder from the Tracks area menu bar. If the selected regions are all on the same track, the folder is created on that track. If the regions are located on different tracks, a new folder track is created.

tricks.title: Colour‑code sections, not instruments
tricks.reason: Option-C as the Color palette shortcut is documented on two separate Apple Logic Pro guide pages (Color regions, Color takes while recording).
tricks.evidence_quote: Open the Color palette by choosing View > Show Colors (or pressing Option-C). ... Control-click one of the selected regions and choose Name and Color > Show/Hide Colors from the shortcut menu, or press Option-C.

tricks.title: Zoom all the way out and squint
tricks.reason: Multiple independent Logic sources agree that Z is Toggle Zoom to fit Selection or All Contents and that with nothing selected it fits the whole project.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Z key toggles the Zoom to Fit Selection or All Contents command. If a region is not selected, this zoom command zooms out to fit all the content in the tracks area. [corroborated by https://studio-interns.com/ keyboard-command-of-the-day entries listing "Toggle Zoom to fit Selection or All Contents" on Z, and https://professionalcomposers.com/zoom-fast-in-logic-pro-x/]

tricks.title: Use Track Stacks to collapse instrument families
tricks.reason: Apple documents Shift-Command-D as the Track Stack shortcut and the Folder Stack / Summing Stack choice that follows.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the tracks in the Tracks area, then press Shift-Command-D or choose Track > Create Track Stack. Select the type of track stack you want to create — Folder Stack or Summing Stack. ... All tracks in a summing stack send their audio outputs to a collective auxiliary track.

tricks.title: Solo an arrangement section with the locators
tricks.reason: Two problems. (1) U is "Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events and Enable Cycle" — it turns Cycle mode ON by itself, so pressing C afterwards toggles Cycle back OFF and you end up NOT looping. (2) Apple's arrangement-marker pages document clicking a marker as selecting the marker (Shift-click for several), not as selecting the regions beneath it; no such region-selection behaviour is documented.
tricks.evidence_quote: Set Rounded Locators and Cycle Play ... Rounds the position of the locators to the barline that is nearest to the beginning and end points of the selected regions or events, and switches to cycle play or record mode. ... Click the Cycle button in the control bar (or press C). [and https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/edit-arrangement-markers-lgcpf7c0a3d7/mac : "click an arrangement marker to select it, and to select multiple arrangement markers, Shift-click them."]
tricks.correction: Select the regions that make up the section, then press U. That single key is Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events and Enable Cycle — it rounds the locators to the nearest barlines around your selection and switches Cycle mode on in one go. Don't press C afterwards; that would switch Cycle back off.

tricks.title: Mute regions instead of deleting them while experimenting
tricks.reason: The region-mute key command is Control-M, not M. Apple's Mute and solo regions page gives Control-M and the Mute tool as the two ways to mute/unmute selected regions; plain M is the track-mute command, which mutes the whole track rather than the selected regions — exactly the adjacent-but-different error the book must avoid.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the muted regions, then press Control–M. ... Select the Mute tool, then click the muted regions. ... When an individual region is muted, the region and its name are gray, and a small dot precedes the name.
tricks.correction: Click a region with the Mute tool, or select the regions and press Control-M. Muted regions turn grey with a dot before the name, so arrangement experiments become reversible without touching undo.

tricks.title: Keep a “graveyard” track at the bottom
tricks.reason: Pure workflow advice — keep a muted, hidden dumping-ground track for rejected ideas. It names no shortcut, menu path or version-dependent behaviour that could be wrong; muted tracks and hidden tracks are both ordinary, uncontested Logic features and the tip does not claim any specific mechanism for either.

tricks.title: Use markers for notes to self, not just sections
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Marker track inside the global tracks and multiple documented ways to rename a marker, which is exactly what the trick describes.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Marker track displays markers as rectangular sections, where you can select, copy, move, or resize markers. ... Command-double-click a marker, then enter a new marker name. [Marker lane availability: https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/show-and-hide-global-tracks-lgcpd0e8ce94/mac — "choose Track > Global Tracks > Show Global Tracks (or press G)... Control-click in the global tracks header area (or press Option-G) and choose Marker."]

downgrades.title: Repeat regions numerically instead of dragging
downgrades.reason: SPLIT CLAIM: Apple's quote verifies only the menu half. The cited Apple page says 'Choose Edit > Repeat Multiple ... (or use the Repeat Regions Multiple Times key command)' -- it names the COMMAND but never names a key. The book text (content/02.json) asserts 'Select regions and hit CMD-R for a single repeat', and the only support offered for CMD-R is whylogicprorules.com, a single blog, which the brief explicitly rules insufficient on its own. Version trap: Apple's documented command is 'Repeat Regions Multiple Times' (a dialog with a Number of Copies field), while the blog describes CMD-R producing an instant single duplicate -- these are adjacent-but-different behaviours, exactly the failure pattern described. Independent corroboration that this is unverified: the repo's own /home/user/dannymac2334/ebook/VERIFY.md lists 'CMD-R -- S2 Repeat regions numerically instead of dragging' under 'Key commands not yet documented (23)'. SALVAGE (keep the trick, drop the key): 'Select regions and use Edit > Repeat Multiple... from the Tracks area menu bar to type an exact number of copies and choose whether they land as copies or aliases.' That sentence is fully covered by the Apple quote; remove the CMD-R clause and the k field until a key command can be sourced from Apple.

downgrades.title: Loop a region instead of copying it
downgrades.reason: EVIDENCE DOES NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM AS WRITTEN. The Apple quote covers two things: the upper-right-corner drag gesture, and L as the unloop toggle. The book's actual payload sentence (content/02.json) is 'Looped regions update everywhere when you edit the original, and they cost nothing to change.' No quoted line supports that. The auditor reached it by inference -- their reason literally reads 'loop repetitions are re-plays of the same region, SO editing the original does propagate' -- which is reasoning from confidence, the specific move the brief prohibits. Compounding this, edit-propagation is the documented property of ALIASES/CLONES, which this same section documents separately with a real Apple quote ('If you alter the original region, all aliases of the region are similarly altered'); the book now asserts the same propagation behaviour from two different mechanisms, and only one of them is sourced. VERIFY.md also lists 'L -- S2 Loop a region instead of copying it' under key commands not yet documented. SALVAGE: 'Grab the top-right corner of a region and drag right to loop it; press L to toggle looping off again. Looping costs nothing to change, so stay looped while the arrangement is still moving.' This keeps only the Apple-documented gesture and toggle and drops the unsourced propagation claim.

downgrades.title: Zoom all the way out and squint
downgrades.reason: FAILS SOURCE QUALITY AND VERSION MATCHING SIMULTANEOUSLY. There is no Apple source at all. The primary evidence is dummies.com, which is not among the permitted sources, and it is a Logic Pro X-era page (URL slug 'logic-pro-x', article 147883) being used to verify a claim the book makes for 10.7/11/12 -- the exact version trap the brief warns is the richest error source. The offered corroboration does not meet the two-independent-sources bar either: studio-interns.com is cited with no URL and no quotation, only a vague gesture at 'keyboard-command-of-the-day entries', and professionalcomposers.com is a single blog not on the approved list. The book's claim is also more specific than the evidence's nearest support -- 'Hit Z WITH NOTHING SELECTED to fit the whole project on screen' -- and that conditional qualifier is precisely the kind of adjacent detail that has been failing audit. The repo's own VERIFY.md lists 'Z -- S2 Zoom all the way out and squint' under 'Key commands not yet documented'. SALVAGE (the judgement advice is the valuable part and is pure opinion): 'Zoom out until the whole song fits on screen. If the energy shape of the song is not visible from the region blocks alone, the arrangement is probably flat.' Drop the Z keystroke and the k field, or re-source the zoom command from Apple's guide before restoring it.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout (10 queries, no rate limiting). WebFetch was not attempted per instructions; all evidence comes from WebSearch result snippets, several of which quote the Apple Logic Pro User Guide directly. Note: the search tool returns synthesised snippets rather than strictly per-URL verbatim text, so evidence_quote is the snippet text attributed to the best-matching result URL. Section 3 has a single group ("Getting around") with no group-level "path" field, so there is no menu path to check.

tricks.title: Z is the only zoom command you need
tricks.reason: The command is literally named "Toggle Zoom to fit Selection or All Contents" and is on Z. Multiple independent Logic educators state both halves of the claim: Z zooms to the selection, Z again toggles back, and with nothing selected it fits all project content. professionalcomposers.com, masteringinlogic.com and dummies.com (Graham English's Logic Pro X For Dummies material) agree, and the word "Toggle" in the official command name confirms the press-again-to-return behaviour.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Z key toggles the Zoom to Fit Selection or All Contents command. If nothing is selected when you press (Z) this key command will zoom to fit all content.

tricks.title: Drag‑zoom to any area with ⌃⌥
tricks.reason: Apple's Logic Pro User Guide "Zoom windows" page confirms Control-Option summons the Zoom tool, that dragging a rectangle fills the window with that area, and that clicking the background with the tool returns to the previous zoom level. whylogicprorules.com independently corroborates both the drag-to-zoom and the Control-Option-click-to-zoom-back behaviour ("press Control-Option while clicking anywhere in the tracks area").
tricks.evidence_quote: You can select the Zoom tool from the Tool menu (or press and hold Control-Option). Drag to select the area you want to zoom with the Zoom tool, and the selected area fills the window. ... Click the background with the Zoom tool to return the zoom level to the original setting, or backtrack through previous zoom steps if the tool was used multiple times.

tricks.title: Know what the number keys actually do
tricks.reason: Half of this is solid: Apple's "Create and recall screensets" page confirms the top-row number keys recall screensets ("press any numeric key except 0"), and Apple's "Navigate using markers" page confirms the Go to Marker Number 1–20 commands exist and are assignable. But the load-bearing second claim — that marker navigation sits on the numeric keypad by default — could not be confirmed, and the sources actively conflict: one forum thread asserts keypad numbers call markers while qwerty numbers call screensets, and another states "Logic has always, by default, had both the qwerty numbers and the numeric key pad numbers assigned to recalling screen sets." Both are forum posts, so neither qualifies to verify or to refute. No Apple page documents a default keypad-to-marker mapping.
tricks.evidence_quote: The 1 to 9 key commands are called Recall Screenset 1–9 in the Key Commands window. In Logic Pro, press any numeric key except 0, and for screensets with two-digit numbers, press and hold Shift while entering the first digit.
tricks.salvage: The top-row number keys recall screensets, not markers — Apple's guide says you recall a screenset by pressing any numeric key except 0, so 1–9 switch window layouts. If you want marker jumps on a key, open Key Commands (⌥K) and search “Go to Marker Number” — there are 20 of them, numbered by the order the markers appear in the project.

tricks.title: Assign a key to “Play Selection”
tricks.reason: No external source documents a Logic Pro command named "Play Selection", and nothing supports the claim that it is unassigned by default. What the sources do show are two differently named commands that both already have defaults: "Play/Stop Selection" (Control-Space, in the "Windows showing audio files" key command group) and "Play from Selection" (⇧Space, documented by studio-interns.com). Since the trick's whole point is "it is not on one by default", and the nearest real commands both are on one by default, this cannot be shipped as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: Play from Selection ⇧˽ — Logic Pro X keyboard command of the day
tricks.salvage: Open Key Commands with ⌥K and search “Selection”. Logic has several selection-based playback commands — Play from Selection is on ⇧Space by default and starts playback at the beginning of whatever you have selected — so you can audition just the part you are working on. Browse the list and put the one that matches your workflow on a key you can reach.

tricks.title: Jump to an exact bar with the Go to Position dialog
tricks.reason: masteringinlogic.com states plainly that Go to Position is pre-assigned to the forward slash and that you type a bar (or SMPTE) position into it; Apple's "Set the playhead position" User Guide page documents the same Go to Position dialog for moving the playhead to an exact position. Two independent sources agree on both the key and the behaviour.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro has a pre-assigned key command to type in your position, either by bars/beats or SMPTE position, assigned to the forward slash on the keyboard next to the right Shift key. ... You can jump to double or even triple figure bar numbers by holding / and typing in the number you'd like to go to.

tricks.title: Scroll horizontally without the scrollbar
tricks.reason: The trackpad half is supported — Apple's "Scroll and zoom in the Tracks area" page says gestures can be used to scroll the Tracks area, and Apple's trackpad page for Logic Pro states "Drag with two fingers to scroll areas horizontally and vertically". The Shift-plus-wheel half is not: the only support I could find is a logicprohelp.com forum thread, which is explicitly not a sufficient source, and no Apple page or reputable Logic educator documents Shift-scroll as a Logic Pro horizontal-scroll behaviour (it is a general macOS convention, not a documented Logic feature). Because the trick asserts both, it cannot be marked verified as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: Two-finger scroll: Drag with two fingers to scroll areas horizontally and vertically.
tricks.salvage: Two‑finger swipe left and right on a trackpad to move through the project. Apple documents gesture scrolling in the Tracks area, and dragging two fingers scrolls a pane horizontally as well as vertically — keep your hand off the scrollbar entirely.

tricks.title: Use the Cycle area as a bookmark
tricks.reason: The U part checks out: Apple's Global Commands table assigns U to "Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events and Enable Cycle" (⌘U is the non-rounded version), so U does set the locators around your selection. But the actual payoff claim — that clicking the cycle bar in the ruler takes you straight back to that spot — has no external support. Apple's "Use the cycle area" page describes clicking and dragging the upper part of the ruler to create or adjust the cycle area, and dragging the cycle strip to move it; it documents no click-to-jump-back behaviour. Without a source for the bookmark behaviour the trick's premise is unproven.
tricks.evidence_quote: To create a cycle area in Logic Pro, click the upper part of the ruler and drag left or right. The cycle area appears as a yellow strip in the ruler, and Cycle mode is automatically turned on.
tricks.salvage: Select the region or passage you are working on and press U. Logic sets the left and right locators around it — rounded to bar lines — and turns Cycle on, so the yellow strip in the ruler marks your work area and keeps looping it. Use ⌘U instead if you want the locators exactly on the selection boundaries rather than rounded.

tricks.title: Toggle Catch to stop the screen running away
tricks.reason: The description of Catch is right — Apple: "The Catch playhead setting makes the visible section of a window follow the playhead position" — but the advice to "search 'Catch Playhead Position' in Key Commands to put it on a key", reinforced by the ⌥K badge, tells the reader it has no default key. It does. studio-interns.com's keyboard-command-of-the-day entry is titled "Catch Playhead Position `", and the same backquote assignment appears in independent shortcut references (shortcutfoo.com, gieson.com). A buyer who searches Key Commands will find the command already bound and conclude the book is wrong.
tricks.evidence_quote: Catch Playhead Position ` — Logic Pro X keyboard command of the day. The backquote (`) key toggles the "Catch Playhead" button and stops scrolling or catches up depending on the state.
tricks.correction: The Catch button makes the view follow the playhead. Click it off when you are doing detailed editing and the view will hold still while the song plays. You do not need to assign anything — Catch Playhead Position is already on the backquote (`) key, so you can toggle it without leaving the keyboard.

downgrades.title: Z is the only zoom command you need
downgrades.reason: SOURCE CLASS + VERSION ERA. The single quoted source is professionalcomposers.com/zoom-fast-in-logic-pro-x/ - one blog, not on the approved list, and a Logic Pro X-era page by its own URL slug. The two corroborating sources named in the auditor's reason are never quoted and are also Logic Pro X-era (masteringinlogic.com's '10-shortcuts-to-working-faster-in-logic-pro-x' page, and Graham English's 'Logic Pro X For Dummies'). Per the version rule, a Logic Pro X-era page does not verify a key assignment offered to 10.7/11/12 readers, and no support.apple.com citation was produced for a claim that Apple's own Key Commands documentation would settle outright. QUOTE-TO-CLAIM GAP: the quoted line supports (a) Z invokes Zoom to Fit Selection or All Contents and (b) with nothing selected it fits all content, but the third asserted behaviour - press Z again to return to the previous zoom level - is derived by the auditor from the word 'Toggle' inside the command name, which is inference rather than quotation. NOTE: web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) before I could re-check, so this is a downgrade on evidence quality, not a positive contradiction; an Apple Key Commands citation would likely restore it. SALVAGE (drops the unproven key, keeps the workflow): 'Stop dragging the zoom sliders. Logic has a single zoom-to-fit toggle: with a region or range selected it zooms so that selection fills the window, and with nothing selected it zooms to fit the whole project. Open the Key Commands window from the Logic Pro menu, search for \'Zoom to fit\', and note - or assign - the key it uses on your system. One key then covers almost all of your day-to-day zooming.'

downgrades.title: Jump to an exact bar with the Go to Position dialog
downgrades.reason: SOURCE CLASS + VERSION ERA + QUOTE SMELL. The key assignment IS the trick, and it rests on exactly one quoted source: masteringinlogic.com/10-shortcuts-to-working-faster-in-logic-pro-x/ - a single blog, not on the approved list, and a Logic Pro X-era page by its URL. The rules state plainly that a single blog is not sufficient on its own. The second source the auditor leans on (Apple's 'Set the playhead position' page) is named but never quoted, and even as the auditor describes it, it would only establish that a Go to Position dialog exists - not that it is bound to the forward slash, which is the checkable half. So the 'two independent sources agree' argument fails: they agree on the dialog, only one speaks to the key. The quoted line also reads garbled for a modal dialog ('by holding / and typing in the number you'd like to go to' - you press the key, a dialog opens, you type into it), which is the signature of reconstructed or loosely paraphrased text and should have prompted a re-search. NOTE: web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200), so I could not re-verify the key against Apple's guide. SALVAGE (drops the unproven key, keeps the workflow): 'When you need bar 147, don't scroll for it. Logic's Go to Position command opens a small dialog where you type a bar/beat position - or an SMPTE timecode - and the playhead jumps straight there. Open the Key Commands window from the Logic Pro menu and search for \'Go to Position\' to see the key it is assigned to on your system, or assign one you will remember. On long projects this replaces most of your horizontal scrolling.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout (19 queries, no rate limiting). WebFetch was not used — result snippets quoted Apple's Logic Pro User Guide directly, which was sufficient. Note the file has no group-level "path" fields, so no menu-path checks were needed beyond the paths embedded in individual tips.

tricks.title: Musical Typing turns your laptop into a synth
tricks.reason: Apple's user guide confirms all four mappings exactly: ⌘K to open, Z/X for octaves, C/V for velocity, Tab for sustain. One wording nit for the owner: Apple describes Tab as a TOGGLE ('turn sustain on or off'), whereas the copy says the key 'holds' sustain. The mapping is right; 'toggles sustain (like a sustain pedal)' would be more precise.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, choose Window > Show Musical Typing (or press Command-K). ... Press Z or X to move down or up by octaves. Press C or V to lower or raise the velocity. Press Tab to turn sustain on or off (similar to using a sustain pedal).

tricks.title: Capture the last thing you played, even when not recording
tricks.reason: ⇧R and the Logic 11.2 requirement for audio both check out, but the stated prerequisite is wrong. Apple's requirement for audio Flashback Capture is that the audio track be IN FOCUS — not record-enabled. Apple's page never mentions record-enabling; the conditions are focus, the project playing, and an incoming signal (plus a four-second minimum). logicstudiotraining.com independently describes it the same way ('capture audio on the focused track whenever the project is playing and an audio signal is present'). A buyer who record-arms a track and finds it still doesn't work — or who assumes arming is required and never tries it otherwise — has a legitimate complaint.
tricks.evidence_quote: To create a region containing your recent audio performance, make sure the audio track is in focus, then click the Flashback Capture button in the control bar (or press Shift-R) ... You can capture audio only while the project is playing. While a project is stopped, no audio is captured. ... The project must play for a minimum of four seconds. Flashback Capture can save up to one minute of audio.
tricks.correction: If you played something great while the transport was rolling but not recording, hit ⇧R and Logic writes it to a region retroactively. MIDI works on any recent version, whether the project is playing or stopped. Audio needs Logic 11.2 or later: make sure the audio track is in focus and the transport is playing — Logic captures only while there is an incoming signal, needs at least four seconds of playback, and can save up to one minute of audio.

tricks.title: Record MIDI while the transport is stopped
tricks.reason: Apple confirms both halves: MIDI Flashback Capture works with the transport stopped, and it captures controller data as well as notes. Worth adding as a caveat (Apple states it, the book doesn't): after a 20-second gap between incoming MIDI events, the events before the pause are discarded — so 'always listening' has a limit.
tricks.evidence_quote: When playback is stopped, Flashback Capture creates a separate region containing all the MIDI events received since the last playback. ... In both playback mode and when stopped, Capture Recording captures MIDI notes, MIDI Control Change messages, and if Record Region Automation is active, volume, pan, and plug-in parameter adjustments as well.

tricks.title: Use the Step Input Keyboard for parts you cannot play
tricks.reason: The menu path is exactly as written, and Apple confirms the per-note, per-length entry model the trick describes. One caveat the book omits: the Step Input Keyboard only appears when the advanced/complete feature set is enabled in Settings > Advanced.
tricks.evidence_quote: Choose Window > Show Step Input Keyboard. ... click a key to insert a note of that key's pitch, click the Note Length buttons to set the length of the inserted note, and click the Velocity buttons to set the velocity of the inserted note.

tricks.title: Draw notes with the Pencil, delete with the Eraser
tricks.reason: Two problems. (1) 'The Pencil creates notes at the current division' contradicts Apple, which says a new note takes the length/velocity/channel of the previously created or edited note — and it contradicts the very next trick in this same book. (2) Apple's Delete notes page enumerates the deletion methods and Pointer double-click is not among them; the double-click-to-delete behaviour that Logic users actually report is with the Pencil tool, not the Pointer. Classic wrong-tool attribution. The ⌥-drag clause is fine, though Apple describes it as copying a note to a new position rather than 'at the same pitch'.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Logic Pro Piano Roll Editor, you can delete notes by selecting the notes and pressing Delete, selecting the notes and clicking one of them with the Eraser tool, or selecting the Eraser tool and clicking the notes you want to delete.
tricks.correction: The Pencil creates a note whose length, velocity and MIDI channel match the last note you created or edited. To remove a note, select it and press Delete, or click it with the Eraser tool. ⌥-drag a note to copy it to a new position.

tricks.title: New notes inherit the last note you touched
tricks.reason: Apple's current Mac guide states the inheritance behaviour verbatim, which is exactly the hi-hat workflow the trick describes. Small nuance the owner may want to soften: Apple also documents a Control-click 'Define as Default Note' command and a fresh-project default of 240 ticks / velocity 80 / channel 1, so 'there is no default-velocity field' is true of the UI but slightly overstates the absence of any default mechanism.
