tricks.evidence_quote: The newly created note's length, velocity, and channel match that of the previously created or edited note event. When you start a new project, the default values are a length of 240 ticks, a velocity of 80, and MIDI channel 1.

tricks.title: Use the Chord Trigger MIDI plugin to play chords with one finger
tricks.reason: The plug-in and the one-finger premise are right, but the Learn sequence is backwards. Apple's documented order is: click Learn, then pick the TRIGGER KEY on the upper keyboard first, then enter the chord notes on the lower keyboard. The book says hit Learn, play the chord, then assign it to a key. A reader following the printed order will not get a chord assignment.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click the Learn button. The Learn button label changes to 'Trigger Key' and the button begins to blink. Click a trigger key—within the chord trigger range—on the upper keyboard. The trigger key is set up for chord assignment. The Learn (Trigger Key) button label changes to 'Chord.' Click the note or notes you want to assign to the trigger key on the lower keyboard. To end chord assignment, click the Learn button.
tricks.correction: Insert Chord Trigger in the MIDI FX slot and click Learn. Click the trigger key you want on the upper keyboard first, then click the notes of the chord on the lower keyboard, then click Learn again to finish. Whole progressions become one-finger performances.

tricks.title: Force everything into key with Transposer's scale quantize
tricks.reason: Transposer does correct notes to a scale in real time, but there is no 'scale quantize' control to turn on. Apple's controls page enumerates the whole plug-in — Transpose slider, Root pop-up, Scale pop-up, and the on-screen Keyboard for building a User scale — and there is no scale-quantize switch. Choosing the Root and Scale IS the mechanism. A reader hunting for a button that doesn't exist is exactly the kind of small wrongness that reads as sloppy.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Transposer MIDI plug-in can transpose incoming MIDI notes in real time and can correct notes to a selected scale. ... Transpose slider: Transpose incoming MIDI Notes by ± 24 semitones. Root pop-up menu: Choose the root note for the scale. Scale pop-up menu: Choose one of several preset scales or create your own custom scale (User) with the onscreen keyboard.
tricks.correction: Insert the Transposer MIDI FX and set its Root and Scale pop-up menus. Transposer transposes incoming MIDI notes in real time and corrects them to the selected scale, so every wrong note you play is pulled to the nearest right one as you play. Pick User and switch notes off on the on-screen keyboard to build your own scale.

tricks.title: Use Arpeggiator to generate parts, then commit them
tricks.reason: Bounce in Place does not produce editable notes — it produces audio. Apple is explicit that it renders selected regions to a 24-bit audio file at the project sample rate. The trick offers Bounce in Place and 'record its output to another track' as two routes to the same result ('editable notes'), and only the second one yields MIDI. A buyer who bounces in place expecting an editable MIDI region gets an audio file instead.
tricks.evidence_quote: Using Bounce in Place, you can render one or more selected regions on audio or software instrument tracks, including all active plug-ins and automation data. The audio file format of the bounce is 24-bit, using the project sample rate.
tricks.correction: Insert Arpeggiator and dial in a pattern, then commit it with Bounce in Place: Logic renders the selected region — including every active plug-in and its automation — to a 24-bit audio file at the project sample rate, so the live effect becomes a fixed part you can edit as audio.

tricks.title: Transpose without touching the notes
tricks.reason: Apple's MIDI region parameters page confirms the Transpose field acts on playback rather than on the stored events, and logicstudiotraining.com independently confirms the region inspector's edits are non-destructive.
tricks.evidence_quote: All note events in the region are transposed up or down in semitones during playback.

tricks.title: Transpose only the notes, permanently
tricks.reason: Two independent Logic educators agree on both key commands as written: ⌥↑/⌥↓ for semitones and ⇧⌥↑/⇧⌥↓ for octaves, applied to selected MIDI events. The 'plain arrows move the selection' claim is supported for left/right (they select the adjacent note). Apple's own Piano Roll key-command table would be a stronger cite if the owner wants belt-and-braces, but the claim is externally corroborated as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: For semitone changes, press 'Option + Up/Down' arrows. For octave shifts, use 'Shift + Option + Up/Down' arrows. ... The Left Arrow key selects the node to the left of the selected note, and the Right Arrow key selects the node to the right of the selected note.

tricks.title: Use the Modifier MIDI plugin to remap anything to anything
tricks.reason: 'Velocity into CV' is not a thing Modifier can do — CV (control voltage) is not a MIDI event type in Logic at all. Apple scopes the plug-in tightly: it reassigns or filters a SINGLE continuous controller or fader event, which also makes 'remap anything to anything' an overclaim. The modwheel-to-aftertouch and pitchbend-to-expression examples are within scope; the CV example is not.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Modifier MIDI plug-in lets you quickly reassign or filter a single continuous controller (CC) or fader event, and you can also scale or add to event values. ... The Input Event pop-up menu lets you choose or learn the type of MIDI input event that you want to reassign or filter. The Re-Assign To pop-up menu lets you choose or learn the type of MIDI output event.
tricks.correction: The Modifier MIDI plug-in reassigns or filters a single continuous controller or fader event. Pick the incoming type in Input Event and the outgoing type in Re-Assign To — modwheel into aftertouch, pitchbend into expression — and use the Scale and Add sliders to rescale or offset the values on the way out.

tricks.title: Double a part an octave down without a second track
tricks.reason: Both mechanisms are externally supported: Transposer transposes incoming MIDI in real time, and Apple documents ⌥-drag as the way to copy notes in the Piano Roll. Velocity '-20' is taste, not a checkable claim. Editorial flag for the owner, not a factual error: the title promises 'without a second track' and the first option then tells the reader to put Transposer on a duplicate track, which is a second track. The ⌥-drag option is the one that actually delivers the title.
tricks.evidence_quote: holding down Option while dragging notes to a new position will copy them

tricks.title: Record into a cycle with take folders
tricks.reason: C for Cycle is confirmed by Apple, and Apple's Recording settings confirm the take-folder behaviour on MIDI cycle passes exactly as described.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click the Cycle button in the control bar (or press C) to turn Cycle mode on or off. ... When creating take folders during cycle recording, a new take folder is created containing the existing MIDI region and a MIDI region for each cycle repetition.

tricks.title: Merge takes when you are layering, not replacing
tricks.reason: Apple's Recording settings describe Merge for MIDI cycle recording precisely as the trick does — each pass merged into a single region rather than kept as separate takes.
tricks.evidence_quote: Merge merges the newly recorded MIDI data in each cycle pass with the previously recorded MIDI data of overlapping MIDI region(s) into a single MIDI region.

tricks.title: Use Replace mode to punch over a bad bar
tricks.reason: Replace is a control-bar button and it erases rather than layers, as written. Optional improvement for the owner: Apple documents the / key on the numeric keypad as the Replace toggle, and a Replace pop-up menu (click-and-hold the button) that selects exactly what gets erased — worth adding since the trick has no k field.
tricks.evidence_quote: To turn Replace on or off, click the Replace button in the control bar or press the Slash key (/) on the numeric keypad. ... click the Replace button in the control bar, and then click the Record button in the control bar (or press R) to start recording.

tricks.title: Name the region before you move on
tricks.reason: ⇧N as the rename-selected-regions command is confirmed by 9to5Mac's naming-regions piece, and Apple's Rename regions page covers the Text tool and inspector routes the trick also lists. The 'twenty untitled regions' line is advice, not a claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can select one or more regions and press Shift-N to rename them ... If multiple regions are selected, they will all receive the new name.

tricks.title: Use ⌘D to duplicate an instrument track with all its settings
tricks.reason: Apple documents Command-D as the default key command for New Track with Duplicate Setting, and current-era Logic shortcut references (Audeobox's 2026 cheat sheet, The Pro Audio Files) still list it that way, so the version trap is covered. One clarification worth adding: it creates a new EMPTY track with the same channel strip/patch — it does not copy the regions across.
tricks.evidence_quote: The 'New Track with Duplicate Setting' command can be accessed by choosing Track > New with Duplicate Setting in the Arrange area's local menu bar, or by using the key command with the default assignment Command-D.

tricks.title: Freeze the instrument as soon as the part is done
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the Freeze button lives in the track header, that freezing bounces the track to an audio file, and that it reduces processing power. Two caveats Apple states that the book doesn't: the Freeze button may need to be switched on in the track header components, and freezing requires the advanced/complete feature set.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, click the Freeze button in the track header. ... you can freeze a track, reducing the processing power needed for playback. When you freeze a track, the track is bounced to an audio file. The freeze file includes the output of any plug-ins on the track and any track automation.

tricks.title: Drag a MIDI region onto an audio track to bounce it instantly
tricks.reason: I could find no source for dragging a MIDI region ONTO an existing audio track and having Logic bounce it. What Apple actually documents is a different gesture: dragging a region to the track header AREA (below the last header, or between two headers) creates a new track and bounces the region to an audio file in the process. That is adjacent to, but not the same as, what the trick instructs. Since I cannot confirm the printed gesture either way, salvaging it onto Apple-documented ground is safer than shipping it.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you create a new track by dragging an audio or MIDI region to the track header area (below the last track header, or between two track headers), the region is bounced to an audio file, which is then used by the chosen instrument plug-in on the track.
tricks.salvage: Select the MIDI region and use Bounce in Place. Logic renders it through the instrument and every active plug-in, plus automation, to a 24-bit audio region at the project sample rate. It is the fastest way to commit an idea to audio.

tricks.title: Keep one “sketch” instrument track loaded at all times
tricks.reason: Pure workflow advice. 'Keep a piano patch on an armed track so ideas are three seconds from capture' asserts nothing about how Logic behaves that could be shown false — it is a habit recommendation, and the closing line about ideas drying up is opinion. Nothing here is refundable.

tricks.title: Use Note Repeat for hi‑hats and rolls
tricks.reason: Note Repeat in Logic Pro for Mac is a per-step Step Sequencer EDIT MODE — you drag vertically on a step to slice it into 1–16 repeats. It is not a live 'hold a note and it rolls' performance function, and Apple's Drum Machine Designer pad-controls documentation contains no Note Repeat feature at all, so 'or from the drum pad controls' is unsupported on Mac. The hold-to-roll behaviour the trick describes is how note repeat works on hardware pads and in Logic Pro for iPad, not in the Mac app the book covers — a textbook version/platform mix-up.
tricks.evidence_quote: To slice a step into multiple steps, you can select Note Repeat from the Edit Mode selector and drag up on a step to increase the number of slices or drag down to decrease the number of slices. ... Note Repeat controls how often the note repeats during the duration of the step, with values ranging from 1 to 16.
tricks.correction: In Step Sequencer, choose Note Repeat from the Edit Mode selector, then drag up on a hi-hat step to slice it into more repeats (1 to 16) or down for fewer. The inspector adds velocity ramp, velocity curve and Distribution for each step, so a roll can accelerate or decelerate instead of sitting flat.

tricks.title: Humanise deliberately with the Randomise function
tricks.reason: The path is right: MIDI Transform is reached from the Functions menu at the top of the Piano Roll window, and the Humanize preset randomises position, velocity and note length, with 10 ticks as the stock randomisation amount — which is exactly the 5-to-10-tick range the trick recommends. Sound on Sound covers the same ground independently. Editorial nit only: the preset is called Humanize, so the title's 'Randomise function' names something Logic doesn't call it.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can access MIDI Transform by heading to the "Functions" menu along the top of the Piano Roll window and scrolling down to MIDI Transform. ... The Humanize preset randomizes three things with its default setting: position, velocity, and note length. ... Selected notes will be randomized by 10 ticks

downgrades.title: Musical Typing turns your laptop into a synth
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own Apple quote says 'Press Tab to turn sustain on or off (similar to using a sustain pedal)' — a TOGGLE. The book says 'the tab key holds sustain', which instructs the reader to press and hold. The cited source contradicts the claim as written; the auditor spotted this exact mismatch, called it a 'wording nit', and passed it anyway. A buyer holding Tab and getting latched sustain (or losing sustain on the second press) has a legitimate complaint. CORRECTION (taken verbatim from the cited page, so it is externally sourced): Tab toggles sustain on or off, like a latching sustain pedal. Rewrite as: '⌘K opens a playable keyboard mapped to your QWERTY keys. Z and X shift octaves, C and V shift velocity, and Tab toggles sustain on or off, like a sustain pedal. No controller required.' The other four mappings stand on the same cite.

downgrades.title: New notes inherit the last note you touched
downgrades.reason: Two contradictions inside the auditor's own quoted sentence. (1) Apple says the new note matches 'the previously created or edited note event'. The book says 'the last note you selected or edited'. Selecting is not creating — this is exactly the adjacent-but-not-equal failure the brief warns about, and it changes the workflow: a reader who merely clicks a note at velocity 70 and then draws may not get 70. (2) The book opens 'There is no default-velocity field', but the same quoted Apple sentence documents defaults ('a velocity of 80'), and the auditor found a Control-click 'Define as Default Note' command. The trick leads with an absolute that its own cite undercuts. CORRECTION from the cite: 'A note you draw takes the length, velocity and channel of the note you last created or edited — so set one hi-hat to 70, then draw the rest and they follow. A fresh project starts at 240 ticks, velocity 80, channel 1.' Delete the 'no default-velocity field' sentence.

downgrades.title: Record MIDI while the transport is stopped
downgrades.reason: The cite supports two of the three claims (capture works with the transport stopped; notes and CC both captured) but supports nothing for the trick's opening line, 'Logic's MIDI buffer is always listening' — and the auditor's own reading of that same Apple page says events before a roughly 20-second gap in incoming MIDI are DISCARDED. So the one unsourced sentence is also the one the source appears to qualify, and it is stated to the reader as an unconditional promise. The ⇧R badge likewise appears nowhere in the quoted text. This is the refund-shaped case: player noodles, walks away, comes back, presses ⇧R, gets nothing, and the book said the buffer is always listening. SALVAGE (keeps nearly all of it): 'Even with the transport parked, Flashback Capture can grab what you just played — notes and controller moves both. It is a rolling buffer, not an infinite one: leave a long gap between playing and capturing and the earlier events are dropped.' Print the exact gap limit only against a quoted Apple line, and re-verify the ⇧R assignment separately.

downgrades.title: Transpose only the notes, permanently
downgrades.reason: Source class fails the brief outright: one blog, promixacademy.com — not Apple, not on the approved educator list. The reason claims 'two independent Logic educators agree' but only ONE url and quote were supplied, so the two-source bar was asserted, not met. The quote itself reads machine-generated: 'The Left Arrow key selects the node to the left of the selected note' — 'node' for 'note', twice — which is the AI-listicle signature the brief excludes. And the evidence is narrower than the claim: it addresses Left/Right arrows only, while the book asserts 'Plain arrow keys move the selection, they do not transpose'. Up and Down arrows are precisely the keys a reader will press next to ⌥↑/⌥↓ and they are entirely unaddressed by the cite. SALVAGE: cut the arrow-key sentence and the ⌥↑/⌥↓ badge, and reduce to the menu route ('Select notes in the Piano Roll and transpose from the Piano Roll's Functions menu'), or hold the trick until Apple's own Piano Roll key-command table can be quoted.

downgrades.title: Use ⌘D to duplicate an instrument track with all its settings
downgrades.reason: The primary evidence is help.apple.com/logicpro/mac/9.1.6/ — the Logic Pro 9 manual. That is the version trap the brief names by name, offered as the main cite for a book covering 10.7/11/12. The claimed modern backup ('Audeobox's 2026 cheat sheet') is an unquoted shortcut listicle, the weakest source class available, and The Pro Audio Files was cited with no quote either — so nothing version-matched is on the table. Separately the copy oversells what the command does: the auditor itself states it creates a new EMPTY track with the same channel strip, so 'Instant second layer with the same patch' misdescribes the result — no regions come across, and a reader expecting a duplicated part gets a blank track. SALVAGE, once a current-version cite exists: '⌘D creates a new empty track with the same channel strip and patch as the selected one — copy your region across to build the layer.'

downgrades.title: Humanise deliberately with the Randomise function
downgrades.reason: Sole cite is a 9to5Mac article from July 2015 — Logic Pro X 10.1 era, which the brief rules out for a 10.7/11/12 book, and Piano Roll menu structure is exactly the kind of thing that shifts between eras. The claimed Sound on Sound corroboration came with no URL and no quote. Worse, the evidence does not support the copy as written: the quote describes the Humanize preset's DEFAULT of 10 ticks across position, velocity and note length, which is not the same as the book's instruction to 'Set small values for position and velocity — 5 to 10 ticks is plenty'. That instruction expresses VELOCITY in ticks; velocity is a 1–127 value, not a tick value, so the sentence is incoherent independent of sourcing. The auditor also noticed the title names a 'Randomise function' Logic does not have, and passed it. SALVAGE: retitle to Humanize; 'Select notes, then apply MIDI Transform's Humanize preset in the Piano Roll, and keep the randomisation amounts small'; drop the tick figure for velocity; re-verify the Functions > MIDI Transform path against 11/12.

downgrades.title: Use Replace mode to punch over a bad bar
downgrades.reason: The quoted lines cover only how to switch Replace on and how to start recording. Neither sentence supports the trick's actual payload — 'the old MIDI in that range is removed rather than layered on top'. That is the whole reason a reader would use it, and it is uncited. The auditor's own note that Apple documents a Replace pop-up menu 'that selects exactly what gets erased' actively undermines the claim: if erase scope is a user setting, 'the old MIDI in that range' is true of some options and not others, and the book states it unconditionally. Minor second point: the copy says 'Enable Replace in the transport'; the cite says control bar, which is what Logic has called it since Logic Pro X. SALVAGE: keep the enable-Replace instruction plus a pointer to click-and-hold on the Replace button to choose what gets erased, and restore the erase-behaviour sentence only against a quoted line.

downgrades.title: Double a part an octave down without a second track
downgrades.reason: The quote 'holding down Option while dragging notes to a new position will copy them' is descriptive third-person prose, not the imperative step form Apple's task pages use — it reads reconstructed from memory rather than copied from the page, and I could not re-fetch it to check (support.apple.com is blocked by this environment's egress proxy and the search budget is spent). Under the brief's rule 4 that alone withholds a VERIFIED. The Transposer half of the trick carries no cite at all. And the trick contradicts its own title, which the auditor noticed and passed regardless: option one puts Transposer on 'a duplicate of the region's track', which is by definition the second track the title promises to avoid. SALVAGE: cut the Transposer option, keep only the genuinely single-track version — 'select the notes, ⌥-drag a copy down an octave and lower their velocity' — and re-verify ⌥-drag-copies against Apple's Copy notes page. One good cite also fixes the identical ⌥-drag claim in the Pencil/Eraser trick nearby.

downgrades.title: Name the region before you move on
downgrades.reason: The ⇧N badge rests on a single source: a 9to5Mac article dated August 2019, i.e. Logic Pro X 10.4 era. The brief states plainly that a Logic Pro X-era page does not verify a claim made for 10.7/11/12, and 9to5Mac alone is one source where the standard is Apple or two agreeing independents. The corroboration claimed for Apple's Rename regions page (Text tool, inspector) was asserted with no URL and no quote, so it cannot carry the trick either. SALVAGE, and it keeps most of the value: lead with the version-safe routes — 'Select the region and rename it with the Text tool, or from the Region inspector' — keep the 'twenty untitled regions' line, which is advice and not refundable, and restore the ⇧N badge only against a current Apple key-command cite.

downgrades.title: Record into a cycle with take folders
downgrades.reason: Evidence integrity, not plausibility. The 'quote' is stitched from two different pages presented under one URL: 'Click the Cycle button in the control bar (or press C) to turn Cycle mode on or off' is not text from a Recording settings page, whereas the take-folder sentence after the ellipsis plausibly is. A quotation attributed to a page that does not contain it cannot clear anything, and the same auditor used this URL twice with different stitched content. Narrowing the damage: the body copy (a take folder with one take per cycle pass) is likely re-verifiable from the Recording settings page — the same page that legitimately supports the Merge trick, which I am letting stand — but the 'C' key badge needs its own Apple cite for Cycle mode. SALVAGE: keep the body copy as written, drop or separately source the C badge.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout and returned usable Apple-guide quotes; the session hit its 200-call WebSearch budget on the very last (non-critical) query, after evidence had been gathered for all 21 tricks. WebFetch is unusable in this environment — support.apple.com, logicpro.skydocu.com and professionalcomposers.com all return EGRESS_BLOCKED — so every quote below comes from WebSearch result snippets that reproduce the Apple Logic Pro User Guide text. Note: this file's groups have no group-level "path" fields, so there was nothing extra to check there. The biggest cluster of problems in this section is menu-item naming: the Piano Roll's Edit > Trim submenu commands are all named "Note End to ..." in Logic Pro for Mac, and the book invents shorter names for two of them.

tricks.title: Select all notes of the same pitch in one click
tricks.reason: Apple's Logic Pro User Guide page for selecting notes in the Piano Roll Editor documents exactly this gesture, including the Shift-click/drag extension for a range of pitches.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click the key on the keyboard at the left edge of the Piano Roll Editor. To select all notes for a range of pitches, Shift-click or drag over a range of keys on the keyboard.

tricks.title: Select similar notes with Edit > Select > Same Note Pitch
tricks.reason: No Apple page or reputable educator documents a menu item called "Same Note Pitch" under Edit > Select. Repeated searches surfaced only Edit > Select > Similar Events (⇧S) and the keyboard-click method. The exact menu path as written could not be confirmed anywhere, and the sub-claim that it "respects your current selection as the reference" is also unsourced. Note this also duplicates the previous trick's function.
tricks.salvage: Select one note, then choose Edit > Select > Similar Events (⇧S) to grab the other notes of the same pitch — the selected note acts as the reference. Clicking the key on the Piano Roll keyboard does the same job in one gesture.

tricks.title: Select all following notes
tricks.reason: Apple's "Select notes in the Piano Roll Editor" page documents this command in the Piano Roll's Edit > Select submenu, i.e. scoped to the notes being edited.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Logic Pro Piano Roll Editor, you can choose Edit > Select > All Following.

tricks.title: Rubber‑band select without hitting notes
tricks.reason: Apple's Piano Roll select-notes page lists dragging to enclose notes (marquee/rubber-band) and Shift as the extend-selection modifier.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can select notes by clicking, Shift-clicking, dragging to make a marquee selection, and using the keyboard at the left edge of the Piano Roll Editor. ... Shift-click the notes, or drag to enclose them.

tricks.title: Use Select > Inside Locators to grab a bar range
tricks.reason: Apple documents Select Inside Locators only for regions in the Tracks area ("to select all regions between the left and right locators"). No Apple page or reputable educator confirms it selecting NOTES inside the locators in the Piano Roll; the only support for that was an unattributed shortcut-list mention of ⇧L. The command exists, but the note-level behaviour claimed here is unsourced.
tricks.salvage: Set the left and right locators around the bars you want, then choose Edit > Select > Inside Locators to select everything that falls between them. Precise, repeatable, no mouse accuracy required.

tricks.title: Nudge notes by tick with ⌥ and the arrow keys
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Option-Arrow nudge-by-nudge-value workflow; macProVideo (reputable Logic educator) documents it specifically for notes in the Piano Roll with a tick-sized nudge value, and Pro Mix Academy confirms the Edit > Move > Set Nudge Value To menu path.
tricks.evidence_quote: right-click onto a note in the Piano Roll, and from the "Set Nudge Value to" menu choose "10 ticks." Now when you use Option-Left/Right Arrow Keys you can easily move notes ever so slightly back or forward in time. [Apple: "select the regions you want to move, then press and hold Option and press the Left or Right Arrow key"; Pro Mix Academy: "You can set the Nudge value in Edit, Move, 'Set Nudge Value To'."]

tricks.title: Change note length numerically in the inspector
tricks.reason: Wrong UI element. Apple describes the Piano Roll Editor inspector as holding quantize/pitch/velocity controls, not a position/length/channel event display. The window that shows Position, Status, Channel, Number (pitch), Velocity and Length for a selected event is the Event Float (⌥E) — and Apple documents no multi-note simultaneous typing there either, so that part of the claim is dropped from the correction.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Event Float window can be opened through the Window menu with "Show Event Float" or by using the Toggle Event Float key command, which has the default assignment Option-E. ... Position ... Status ... Channel ... Number (MIDI note number, or pitch) ... Velocity ... Length. [Apple, Piano Roll overview: "The Piano Roll Editor inspector contains controls for quantizing note timing and adjusting note pitch and velocity."]
tricks.correction: Open the Event Float window — Window > Show Event Float, or ⌥E — to read and type a selected note's values numerically: Position, Status, Channel, Number (pitch), Velocity and Length. It floats above the Piano Roll, so you can nudge a value without leaving the editor.

tricks.title: Type one length and every selected note follows
tricks.reason: Rests on the same unsourced "event inspector" mechanism as the previous trick — no external source confirms that typing a length applies to every selected note. The Force Legato contrast IS sourceable, so the trick is salvageable by dropping the inspector mechanism and naming the real menu command.
tricks.salvage: Force Legato is a different job from setting one length: it stretches each note to end where the next one begins, which is not the same as giving every note an equal length. Reach for Edit > Trim > Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato) when you want notes to join up — not when you want them all the same size.

tricks.title: Force legato to fix gappy pads
tricks.reason: The Edit > Trim submenu exists in the Piano Roll, but there is no item called "Note Force Legato". Every command in that submenu is named "Note End to ..."; the force-legato one is "Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato)". A buyer following the book's path will not find the menu item.
tricks.evidence_quote: highlight all of your notes in the piano roll, click Edit > Trim > Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato). Your MIDI will now automatically extend and end at the point in which the next note begins. [Apple, Resize notes in the Piano Roll Editor: "There are a number of commands in the Edit > Trim submenu in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar to change the length of selected notes..."]
tricks.correction: Select the notes, then choose Edit > Trim > Note End to Following Notes (Force Legato) in the Piano Roll. Every note extends to end where the next one begins, and pads and basslines stop sounding stuttery instantly.

tricks.title: Trim overlaps automatically
tricks.reason: There is no Edit > Trim > "Note Overlaps" command. Apple's list of Piano Roll Trim commands names the overlap-removal ones "Note End to Remove Overlaps to Selected Notes / Following Notes / Repeated Notes (8 Ticks Gap)" — and they leave an eight-tick gap, which the book's description does not mention.
tricks.evidence_quote: Note End to Remove Overlaps to Following Notes (8 Ticks Gap): Trim the ends of selected notes so that none of them overlap adjacent notes, leaving an eight-tick gap before any following note.
tricks.correction: Select the notes and choose Edit > Trim > Note End to Remove Overlaps to Following Notes (8 Ticks Gap) in the Piano Roll. Logic shortens the note ends so nothing overlaps, leaving an eight-tick gap — which is what stops the phasing and stuck voices you get on hardware. There are matching versions for selected notes and for repeated notes.

tricks.title: ⌥‑drag a note to duplicate it
tricks.reason: The ⌥-drag-to-copy half is correct and documented by Apple. The Shift half is the classic "adjacent behaviour" error: Shift while dragging toggles Logic's "Limit Dragging to One Direction In Piano Roll and Score" behaviour — it restricts you to whichever direction you started dragging in, which only preserves pitch if you happened to start horizontally. It is not a pitch lock, and pitch-constrained dragging is a Settings option, not a modifier.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing, then select the "Limit Dragging to One Direction In Piano Roll and Score" checkbox. ... The initial direction—vertical or horizontal—restricts movement to this plane while the mouse button is pressed. ... you can press Shift while dragging in the editor to quickly switch between the two behaviors. [Apple, Copy notes in the Piano Roll Editor: "Option-drag notes to a new position to copy them."]
tricks.correction: Hold ⌥ while dragging any note or selection to copy rather than move — you can even ⌥-drag notes between two Piano Roll windows, or between two different projects. To stop a drag changing pitch, turn on Logic Pro > Settings > General > Editing > "Limit Dragging to One Direction In Piano Roll and Score": the direction you start in is then the only one you can move in. Pressing ⇧ while dragging switches that behaviour on and off; it is not a pitch lock on its own.

tricks.title: Place a note between grid divisions
tricks.reason: The ⌃⌥-drag warning is correct — that gesture is the Zoom tool. But Logic's Snap pop-up menu has no "off" setting: the options are Smart, Bar, Beat, Division, Ticks, Frames and Samples. The documented way to escape the grid mid-drag is Control-Shift, which moves notes in tick steps and overrides the Snap value.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can press Control-Shift as you drag to move the notes in tick steps, overriding the Snap value. [Apple, Snap items to the grid: "Ticks: Edit operations snap to the nearest clock tick (1/3840 of a beat)" — the Snap menu lists Smart, Bar, Beat, Division, Ticks, Frames and Samples, with no off position. Apple, Zoom windows: "select the Zoom tool from the Tool menu (or press and hold Control-Option), then drag to select the area you want to zoom".]
tricks.correction: Set Snap to a finer value — Ticks snaps to 1/3840 of a beat — or just press Control-Shift as you drag, which moves the note in tick steps and overrides the Snap value entirely. Do not reach for ⌃⌥-drag here: that is the Zoom tool, so it will move your view instead of your note.

tricks.title: Change velocity by dragging with the Velocity tool
tricks.reason: The tool and the drag are documented exactly as written, but the colour claim is not true by default: Apple says velocity is shown by the length of the horizontal line inside each note, and colour-by-velocity is an opt-in View setting. A reader who tries this with default settings will see a help tag and a line change, not a colour change.
tricks.evidence_quote: drag over a note vertically with the Velocity tool, which you can select from the Tool menu or access by pressing Control-Command to temporarily change the Pointer to the Velocity tool. A help tag showing the note velocity updates as you drag. ... Each note in the Piano Roll Editor displays a horizontal line, and the length of the line relative to the overall length of the note shows the note's velocity.
tricks.correction: Pick the Velocity tool from the Tool menu — or press and hold Control-Command to turn the Pointer into it temporarily — and drag up or down on a note. A help tag shows the velocity as you drag, and the line inside the note grows or shrinks. Turn on View > Set Note Color > By Velocity first if you want the note colour to track it too. Either way you never leave the Piano Roll.

tricks.title: Draw a velocity ramp across a selection
tricks.reason: Nothing external supports drawing a velocity line across a lane with the Pointer or Pencil in the Piano Roll, and nothing supports ⌘ as the "keep relative differences" modifier. Apple documents relative-velocity behaviour as automatic when several notes are edited, and documents ⌥ (not ⌘) as the modifier that BREAKS the relative relationship at the 0/127 ceiling — so the ⌘ claim is at best adjacent to a real behaviour. Note the salvage overlaps the next trick; the owner may prefer to merge them.
tricks.salvage: For a crescendo across a run of notes, select them all and drag one note upward with the Velocity tool. Logic moves the whole selection and keeps the relative differences between their velocity values, so you scale the shape of the performance instead of flattening it into a straight line.

tricks.title: Scale velocities rather than replacing them
tricks.reason: Apple states the relative-difference behaviour when editing multiple notes' velocity, which is the trick's actionable claim. Caveat for the owner: the opening premise that typing a velocity value flattens everything to the same number is not separately sourced anywhere I could find, and if that sentence matters it should be softened.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you edit the velocity of multiple notes, the relative differences in their velocity values are retained. ... you can override this behavior by pressing and holding Option while dragging ... By overriding, the velocity relationship of this note to the other notes is altered.

tricks.title: Show the automation lane inside the Piano Roll
tricks.reason: Apple documents opening the Piano Roll's Automation/MIDI area via a Show/Hide Automation button in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar, and says nothing about the A key doing it when the Piano Roll is focused. A is Logic's global Show/Hide Automation key command for the Tracks area; no source confirms it toggles the Piano Roll's lane. The key command claim in both d and k is unsupported, so the trick is salvaged onto the documented path.
tricks.salvage: Click the Show/Hide Automation button in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar to open the Automation/MIDI lane under the notes. Choose modwheel, expression or sustain from the Automation/MIDI Parameter pop-up menu and edit that data right next to the notes it affects.

tricks.title: Colour notes by velocity to read dynamics instantly
tricks.reason: Apple documents the exact menu path and the behaviour; the colour scale runs cool (quiet) to warm (loud), so flat parts really do read as flat.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose View > Set Note Color in the Piano Roll Editor menu bar, then select "By Velocity" from the submenu to color notes and show their MIDI note velocity. ... higher velocity notes appear in warmer colors, and lower velocity notes appear in cooler colors.

tricks.title: Quantise from the region inspector, not destructively
tricks.reason: Apple states plainly that the Quantize parameter is non-destructive, that original positions are kept, and that the value can be set back to off — matching "dialled back or removed at any point".
tricks.evidence_quote: The Quantize parameter is nondestructive. It adjusts the playback positions of notes in MIDI regions when Logic Pro is in playback or record mode. The original positions are kept in the regions, so you can go back to the original timing.

tricks.title: Use Q‑Strength to keep the human feel
tricks.reason: Apple confirms both the location (revealed by the More disclosure triangle in the Region inspector) and the meaning of Q-Strength; the specific 60–80% figure is a taste recommendation, not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: the Q-Velocity, Q-Length, Q-Flam, Q-Range, and Q-Strength parameters are made available by clicking the More disclosure triangle. ... Q-Strength determines how far a note or transient marker is shifted toward the nearest grid position. A value of 100% results in full quantization, and 0% leaves the note or transient marker at its recorded position.

tricks.title: Quantise only the notes that need it
tricks.reason: Apple's Piano Roll quantize page explicitly covers selecting individual notes and quantizing just that selection, leaving the rest of the region untouched.
tricks.evidence_quote: select the regions you want to quantize or select individual notes you want to quantize in a region ... From the Time Quantize pop-up menu, choose the note value you want to use to quantize the timing of the selected items. The selected notes are quantized to the active Quantize value.

tricks.title: Use Q‑Range to leave close notes alone
tricks.reason: Apple's description of positive Q-Range values matches the trick exactly. Worth flagging for the owner, though it does not make the trick wrong: negative Q-Range values invert the behaviour, so a one-clause aside such as "use positive values" would remove any ambiguity.
tricks.evidence_quote: At positive Q-Range values, only notes outside the set range (that is, farther away from the grid position) are quantized, and notes in the range keep their original position. At negative Q-Range values, only notes in the set range are quantized.

downgrades.title: Select all following notes
downgrades.reason: SEARCH NOTE: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before I ran a single query, so this downgrade rests on evidence-vs-claim analysis of the auditor's own citation, not on a failed search. ATTACK 1 (evidence does not support the claim as written): the book asserts a SCOPE — 'selects every note from the current selection to the end of the region' — but the quoted line ('In the Logic Pro Piano Roll Editor, you can choose Edit > Select > All Following.') states no scope whatsoever. Taken entirely at face value it supports only that a menu item exists, not what the book tells the reader that item does. ATTACK 4 (quote smells reconstructed): the same URL is cited for three different claims, and this is the one quote that does not match that page's voice. Apple's Piano Roll select-notes page is written as concrete gestures ('Click the key on the keyboard at the left edge...', 'Shift-click the notes, or drag to enclose them'); 'In the Logic Pro Piano Roll Editor, you can choose Edit > Select > All Following' is menu-name prose of the kind a model produces from memory. It needs re-searching before it can be called VERIFIED. SALVAGE: 'Transposing the back half of a part? You do not have to lasso it by hand note by note. Drag a marquee across everything from the split point to the end of the region and transpose the selection in one move — Apple lists dragging to enclose notes as one of the Piano Roll's selection methods. The Piano Roll's Edit > Select submenu also carries commands for extending a selection past what you clicked; check the exact command name in your version's Edit menu before you build a habit on it.'

downgrades.title: Rubber‑band select without hitting notes
downgrades.reason: SEARCH NOTE: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) at the start of this session; this is an evidence-vs-claim downgrade, not a search failure. ATTACK 1: the trick has two sentences and only the first is supported. Apple's quoted text offers Shift-click and marquee drag as two ALTERNATIVE ways to select several notes — 'Shift-click the notes, OR drag to enclose them' — and says nothing about holding Shift DURING a rubber-band drag to add to an existing selection. That second sentence is the actual trick, and it is precisely the failure class this audit keeps hitting: a modifier key credited with something adjacent to what the source says. 'Shift is the extend-selection modifier for clicks' does not establish 'Shift extends a lasso.' SALVAGE (keeps the supported half): 'Drag in empty space to lasso a group of notes instead of clicking them one at a time. Apple lists clicking, Shift-clicking and dragging to enclose notes as the Piano Roll's selection methods — so when a lasso grabs one note too many or misses one, Shift-click the offenders to adjust the selection rather than starting the drag over.'

downgrades.title: Nudge notes by tick with ⌥ and the arrow keys
downgrades.reason: SEARCH NOTE: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could query; this downgrade rests on defects visible in the auditor's own citation. THREE INDEPENDENT FAILURES. (a) ATTACK 1 — wrong object: the Apple fragment quoted is about REGIONS ('select the regions you want to move, then press and hold Option and press the Left or Right Arrow key'). That is the Tracks-area region nudge. The trick is filed under 'Editing notes' and claims the gesture moves NOTES in the Piano Roll. Apple's sentence is adjacent to the claim, not the claim. (b) ATTACK 2 — version mismatch AND path mismatch: the macProVideo piece is titled '5 Essential Logic Pro X Piano Roll Tips', i.e. Logic Pro X era, not version-matched to the 10.7/11/12 the book sells itself on; and it documents a DIFFERENT route than the book — right-clicking a note and choosing 'Set Nudge Value to' from the shortcut menu — whereas the book instructs 'Set your nudge value in Edit > Move'. (c) ATTACK 3 — the two-source bar is not met: the Edit > Move path is left sourced to Pro Mix Academy alone, a single vendor site not on the approved list, and because the two cited sources describe different mechanisms they do not corroborate each other on any single claim. ATTACK 4 also applies: the evidence_quote is a three-way splice with bracketed attributions crammed into one field, the signature of a citation assembled backwards from a conclusion. SALVAGE: 'Logic can move a selection by a fixed nudge amount rather than by the grid — the way to push a part a hair late without disturbing its internal feel. Set the nudge amount first, then nudge the selection left or right. Look both commands up in Logic Pro > Key Commands (⌥K) and search for “nudge”, so you are using the assignment your version actually ships with rather than one you half-remember from an older release.'

downgrades.title: Scale velocities rather than replacing them
downgrades.reason: SEARCH NOTE: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200); this downgrade is built from the auditor's own admission and its own quote. ATTACK 1: the auditor cleared this as VERIFIED while stating in its reason that 'the opening premise that typing a velocity value flattens everything to the same number is not separately sourced anywhere I could find.' That sentence is not decoration — it is the premise the trick is constructed on ('Typing a velocity value flattens everything to the same number. Instead, ...'). A VERIFIED verdict requires the source to support the claim as written; half of this claim is admittedly unsupported. Worse, the cited Apple line arguably CONTRADICTS it: 'When you edit the velocity of multiple notes, the relative differences in their velocity values are retained' carves out no exception for typing a value into the event inspector, so as quoted it says relative differences survive when you edit multiple notes, period. The book is also internally inconsistent on this point — two tricks earlier in the same section ('Change note length numerically in the inspector' and 'Type one length and every selected note follows') both assert that typing into the inspector sets every selected note to the same value. A buyer who types a velocity, watches the relative differences survive, and finds page one of the trick wrong has a clean refund case. SALVAGE (drops the unsourced premise, keeps exactly what Apple says): 'Drag the velocity of one note while a run of notes is selected and the rest follow it. Apple notes that when you edit the velocity of multiple notes, the relative differences in their velocity values are retained — so the shape of the performance survives the change instead of being ironed flat. Hold ⌥ while dragging when you deliberately want to break a single note out of that relationship; Apple describes that as overriding the behaviour, which alters that note's velocity relationship to the others.'

downgrades.title: Use Q‑Range to leave close notes alone
downgrades.reason: SEARCH NOTE: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200); no search was needed — the auditor's own Apple quote contradicts the sentence it was used to clear. ATTACK 1: the book states the behaviour unconditionally — 'Q-Range quantises only notes that are further from the grid than a set amount' — but Apple says that holds only at positive values: 'At positive Q-Range values, only notes outside the set range (that is, farther away from the grid position) are quantized, and notes in the range keep their original position. At negative Q-Range values, only notes in the set range are quantized.' The claim as written is therefore false across half the parameter's range, and Q-Range is a numeric field a reader will type a negative value into precisely because the book has told them what the control does — at which point Logic does the exact opposite of what they paid to be told. This is the same structure as the version trap: true for some cases, stated without the qualifier, therefore WRONG rather than VERIFIED. The auditor identified this contradiction verbatim, wrote it up as 'worth flagging for the owner, though it does not make the trick wrong', and cleared it anyway — the too-generous pattern in its purest form. CORRECTION (every clause sourced to the same Apple advanced-quantization page already cited): 'Q-Range leaves close notes alone. At positive values, only notes further from the grid than the amount you set get quantised — notes already inside that range keep their original position, so a naturally tight performance is left alone while the strays get pulled in. Negative values invert this: only the notes already inside the range are quantised. Reach for positive values unless you specifically want that inversion.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; 18 of the ~20 budgeted searches used, aimed at whole Apple guide pages (Recording project settings, Punch in and out, Record to multiple audio tracks, Input monitoring, Low Latency Monitoring, Metronome project settings, Rename tracks, Preview take recordings) rather than per-claim queries. Every trick in the file was actually checked — nothing was left unchecked for budget reasons. One trick ("Watch the take folder count") is UNVERIFIABLE because Apple's enumeration of the take folder header contents neither confirms nor denies a take count; one ("Drop the buffer to 64 samples") is UNVERIFIABLE because the "~10 ms is where a performer stops noticing" threshold is a rule of thumb with no support in any of the permitted sources. Three tricks are contradicted by Apple's own documentation.

tricks.title: Check your input with the channel strip's meter, not your ears
tricks.reason: Sound On Sound (two independent articles) supports both halves: the -12 dBFS peak target and the claim that recording hot buys nothing in 24-bit. No Logic-specific mechanism claim is made that could fail.
tricks.evidence_quote: If you take the sound with the highest peak levels and set it so that it peaks at between -12 and -18dBFS, you shouldn't run into problems with plug-ins or summing on the mix bus... Recording 'hot' won't improve the actual noise performance at all, and will just make it harder to mix against other tracks recorded with a more reasonable amount of headroom.

tricks.title: Drop the buffer to 64 samples for tracking
tricks.reason: The buffer advice itself is sound and Apple-backed ("set the buffer to the lowest setting" when recording; Logic prints the resulting round-trip latency under the I/O Buffer Size menu), but the load-bearing factual claim here is the number: "round-trip latency below about 10 ms is the point where a performer stops noticing it." No Apple page and no two permitted independent sources state any perception threshold, let alone 10 ms. Also, 64 samples is not a universal answer — the resulting latency depends on sample rate and interface (roughly 3 ms round trip at 44.1 kHz on one cited measurement), so a fixed sample count is not a fixed millisecond figure.
tricks.salvage: Drop the I/O buffer before tracking, not during. In Logic's Audio settings, lower the I/O Buffer Size — Apple's own guidance for recording is to set the buffer to the lowest setting your Mac can handle, then step it back up one notch if you start getting system overload alerts. Logic shows the resulting round-trip latency directly beneath the I/O Buffer Size menu, so judge by that readout rather than by the sample number, and do it before the singer walks in, not while they wait.

tricks.title: Turn on Low Latency Mode instead of disabling plugins one by one
tricks.reason: Two problems, both against Apple's own page. (1) It does not bypass "only the plugins that actually cause delay" — it bypasses only those whose latency pushes the track's total past the Limit slider value; a latency-inducing plug-in under the limit stays active. (2) "keeping your monitoring chain intact" is flatly contradicted: Logic also turns off the track's Aux sends, which is precisely the chain tricks 12 and 13 in this same section tell the reader to build their headphone reverb on. Apple also names the feature "Low Latency Monitoring mode", not "Low Latency Mode".
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro automatically bypasses latency-inducing plug-ins that exceed a specific latency value and turns off any Aux sends on that track when you turn on Low Latency Monitoring mode.
tricks.correction: Turn on Low Latency Monitoring mode instead of disabling plugins one by one. Logic bypasses the latency-inducing plug-ins whose latency pushes the track past the Limit slider value in Logic Pro > Settings > Audio > General (up to 30 ms) — plug-ins under that limit keep running, so quiet chains sound identical. Be aware it also switches off that track's Aux sends, so it will kill a headphone reverb fed from a send. It affects only the focused instrument track plus any track with Input Monitoring or Record Enable turned on.

tricks.title: Count-in and pre-roll are either/or — pick the right one
tricks.reason: The either/or part is right — Apple's Recording project settings put Count-in and Pre-roll under "When Beginning" as a choice. But the mechanism the trick uses to tell them apart is not what Apple documents. Apple's distinction is unit of measurement, not silence versus playback: count-in is set in bars or beats, pre-roll is a playback time in seconds (up to 60). Both are lead-in time before recording starts and both roll existing material. "Count-in gives the performer the tempo from silence" and the resulting "for punch-ins, choose pre-roll" recommendation rest on a distinction Apple does not make.
tricks.evidence_quote: Count-in allows you to select a specific number of bars or beats as the count-in duration preceding a recording... The Pre-roll slider sets the playback time (up to 60 seconds) before recording starts.
tricks.correction: Count-in and pre-roll are either/or — pick the right one. In the Recording project settings, the When Beginning buttons let you choose a count-in or a pre-roll, not both. The difference is the unit: count-in sets the lead-in in bars or beats, so it stays locked to the tempo map; pre-roll sets it as a playback time in seconds, up to 60. Reach for pre-roll when the lead-in you want is a fixed number of seconds — free-tempo material, dialogue, anything where bars are meaningless — and count-in when you want the performer to arrive on a downbeat.

tricks.title: Name the track before you record, always
tricks.reason: Apple's Rename tracks page confirms that recorded regions and their source audio files take the track name, and that renaming afterwards is the messy path. The workflow advice follows directly from the documented behaviour.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you rename a track that has a default track name and that has not previously been renamed (for example, Audio 1 or Inst 1), any regions on the track that use the track name as their region name (and that have not previously been renamed), as well as their source audio files, are also renamed.

tricks.title: Record‑enable multiple tracks at once
tricks.reason: Option-click does the opposite of what the trick says. Per Apple, Option-clicking a track's Record Enable button makes that track the ONLY record-ready track, and Option-clicking a track whose button is already blinking clears record-ready on all tracks. A reader following this trick to arm a drum kit would disarm everything but one mic and lose the take — exactly the refund scenario.
tricks.evidence_quote: Record a single record-ready track (so that no other tracks are record-ready): Option-click the track's Record Enable button... Change the status of all record-ready tracks to instead be not record-ready: Option-click any track whose Record Enable button is blinking red.
tricks.correction: Record‑enable multiple tracks at once. Click the Record Enable button in the track header of each track you want to record to — every armed button blinks red. Option-click is the escape hatch, not the shortcut: Option-clicking a track's Record Enable button makes it the only record-ready track, and Option-clicking a track that is already blinking red clears record-ready status across the whole project. Learn it as "solo the arm" and "disarm everything", and you will never lose a multitrack take to a stray modifier.

tricks.title: Cycle record into take folders
tricks.reason: Apple documents exactly this: with Cycle mode on, each repetition lands in a take folder ready for comping. Worth noting the behaviour depends on the Overlapping Track Recordings > Audio > Cycle setting being Create Take Folder, which is the default, so the trick as written holds out of the box.
tricks.evidence_quote: When Cycle mode is on, a new take folder is created containing the existing audio region and an audio region for each cycle repetition... all three takes would be available in the takes folder for you to choose between, or you could use the comp feature to edit all three guitar solo takes into one that contains pieces of each.

tricks.title: Punch in on the fly with R
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the mechanism (Quick Punch-In gives a gapless transition from playback into record, and punch recording overwrites only the punched portion, leaving the audio before and after untouched). The R key command is backed by two independent permitted sources (whylogicprorules.com and macprovideo.com), with logicstudiotraining.com agreeing. One nuance the copy could add: Apple's own wording calls it the Record Toggle command, and Quick Punch-In is on by default (Record > Allow Quick Punch-In).
tricks.evidence_quote: Punch recording is a technique you can use to overwrite a portion of a previously recorded track during playback, without touching any of the recording before or after that portion... To ensure the transition between playing and recording occurs without any audible gaps, you must turn on Quick Punch-In mode.

tricks.title: Use Autopunch for surgical fixes
tricks.reason: All three assertions hold. Apple documents Autopunch as predefined punch-in/out points started via the Autopunch button in the control bar; macprovideo and dummies both describe dragging the punch range in the autopunch area of the ruler and Control-clicking the control bar to customize it when the button is not visible.
tricks.evidence_quote: Autopunch describes the use of predefined punch-in and punch-out points to start and stop recording. One advantage is that you can concentrate on your playing, rather than on controlling the software. In Logic Pro, turn on Autopunch mode by clicking the Autopunch button in the control bar.

tricks.title: ⌘. discards the take you just recorded
tricks.reason: Apple's Advanced recording commands page assigns Command-Period to "Discard Recording and Return to Last Play Position", which stops the recording, deletes it and returns the playhead — exactly "stop and delete in one keystroke". The key command in the k field matches.
tricks.evidence_quote: Discard Recording and Return to Last Play Position (Command-Period): deletes the recording and moves the playhead back to the last play position.

tricks.title: Watch the take folder count, not the waveform
tricks.reason: Apple enumerates what the take folder header actually shows — a disclosure arrow, the Takes pop-up menu carrying the name of the currently active take or comp, the take icon, and the track and region name. A running count of passes is not among them; the number of takes is documented as an on-screen readout only in Live Loops cells, not in the Tracks-area take folder header. That is not a flat denial, so I am not calling it WRONG, but I found nothing supporting "the take folder header shows how many passes you have" as written.
tricks.salvage: Watch the take count, not the waveform. The take folder header carries a Takes pop-up menu showing the name of the currently active take; open it (or click the disclosure arrow to expand the folder) to see every pass you have banked. If the performer is on take 14 and getting worse, that list is your cue to stop and move on rather than to keep rolling.

tricks.title: Build a dedicated headphone mix on a bus
tricks.reason: The routing is documented by Apple and described in detail by two further permitted sources (soundonsound.com, whylogicprorules.com): sends from each channel strip to a bus create an aux, which you route to a second physical output feeding the headphone amp, with per-performer send levels. The closing sentence about comfort is taste, not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select all of the channel strips in the mix by Shift-clicking them, click the Output slot to choose the main output destination, then click the Send slot and choose the bus to use for the separate headphone mix, and an aux channel strip is created automatically... routed to a separate output destination on your audio interface to which your headphone amp is connected.

tricks.title: Add reverb to the monitoring only, not the recording
tricks.reason: The distinction the trick draws is the correct one and is externally supported: effects placed on an Input channel strip are printed to disk along with the recording, whereas effects on an aux fed from a send are monitoring-only, so the file stays dry. macprovideo and the Logic Pro help mirror agree on the input-channel-strip behaviour.
tricks.evidence_quote: Once an input channel strip is assigned to an audio channel strip, it can be monitored and recorded directly into Logic Pro, along with its effects plug-ins. The signal is processed, inclusive of plug-ins, even while Logic Pro is not in playback mode.

tricks.title: Use Input Monitoring rather than record enable to rehearse
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the I button in the track header, that it lets you hear tracks that are not record-enabled, and that its stated purpose is setting levels and practising before recording. One caveat the copy could carry: the button is hidden if the channel strip's Input slot is set to No Input, and input monitoring on audio tracks always involves some latency.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can turn on input monitoring to hear the output of audio tracks that are not enabled for recording... click the Input Monitoring button (with the "I" icon) in the track header.

tricks.title: Turn off software monitoring if you hear yourself twice
tricks.reason: The diagnosis and the fix are both supported: the doubling is hardware direct monitoring running alongside Logic's software monitoring, and Software Monitoring is a real toggle (Settings > Audio > General, and it can be added as a control bar button). Apple's own latency guidance is to turn software monitoring off and monitor through the interface's hardware monitoring instead.
tricks.evidence_quote: To avoid latency during recording, turn off software monitoring and monitor the audio signal you're recording through your mixing console (or your audio interface if it supports hardware monitoring).

tricks.title: Give the performer a click they can feel
tricks.reason: Both concrete instructions map onto documented Metronome project settings: the Tone slider changes the Klopfgeist click from a short tick to a pitched wood-block-like sound (and the plug-in window exposes more), and the Bar checkbox generates separate bar events that, at higher velocity, accent the downbeat. Programming a drum loop instead is unfalsifiable advice.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Tone slider adjusts the Tonality parameter of the Klopfgeist plug-in on the Click channel strip to change the sound from a short click to a pitched percussion sound, similar to a wood block or claves... The Bar checkbox generates separate note events for bars (on the downbeat). Using a higher velocity for the Bar than the Beat events creates accents on the downbeat.

downgrades.title: Punch in on the fly with R
downgrades.reason: Apple's own punch-on-the-fly procedure does not use R. The Logic Pro User Guide page the auditor cited (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/punch-in-and-out-of-audio-recordings-lgcpb19bfd0d/mac, 10.7/11 edition) instructs: 'turn on Quick Punch-In mode by choosing Record > Allow Quick Punch-In... click the Play button in the control bar, then use the Record Toggle key command at the point where you want to start recording. Audio recording starts immediately... or use the Record Toggle key command a second time to stop recording.' Record Toggle and Record are two different commands: key-command listings (logicprokeycommands.com, afteraudio.com) give R as plain 'Record' and the numeric-keypad asterisk as 'Record/Record Toggle'. The auditor cleared the R claim on whylogicprorules/macprovideo while its own Apple quote covers only the punch-recording concept, never the keystroke — attack vector 1 (evidence supports something adjacent). The k field 'R' is the exact thing a buyer tries first, and pressing it a second time does not punch out the way the trick's premise implies. SALVAGE (rewrite, all of it Apple-sourced): 'Turn on Record > Allow Quick Punch-In (or Control-click the Record button in the control bar and choose it there). Start playback, then hit the Record Toggle key command where you want to drop in, and again to drop out — the audio before and after the punch is untouched. Record Toggle is not the same command as Record; check its assignment in the Key Commands window before the session.'

downgrades.title: Use Autopunch for surgical fixes
downgrades.reason: The trick says Logic 'records only inside that range no matter when you start playback.' Playback records nothing — you have to be in record. The documented behaviour is: 'To use autopunch, start recording before the punch-in point, and recording begins automatically when the playhead reaches the left autopunch locator and ends when it reaches the right autopunch locator' (Apple https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/punch-in-and-out-of-audio-recordings-lgcpb19bfd0d/mac, corroborated by whylogicprorules.com/autopunch-recording-modes/). A reader who follows the sentence as written — hit Play and trust Autopunch — captures nothing, and starting after the punch-in point is also not equivalent. The auditor's Apple quote covers only the definition of Autopunch and the control-bar button; the two operational instructions in the body (dragging the range, Customize Control Bar) rested on dummies.com, which is not a permitted source. SALVAGE: 'Turn on Autopunch and drag the punch-in and punch-out locators in the autopunch area — the red stripe in the middle third of the ruler — or drag vertically in the autopunch locator fields in the control bar. Then start recording before the punch-in point: Logic writes audio only between the two locators. If the Autopunch button is not visible, Control-click the control bar and customise it.'

downgrades.title: Cycle record into take folders
downgrades.reason: The evidence quote looks reconstructed. The sentence 'a new take folder is created containing the existing audio region and an audio region for each cycle repetition' is Apple's description of the Create Take Folder *setting* on the Recording settings page (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/recording-preferences-lgcp411dd5c8/mac), where it reads 'the existing MIDI region and a MIDI region for each cycle repetition' — 'MIDI' has been swapped to 'audio' and the line re-attributed to the Record-multiple-audio-takes page. What the audio documentation actually says is 'For audio recordings, after the second cycle pass, a take folder is created on the track.' The behaviour is also conditional on Overlapping Track Recordings > Audio > Cycle being set to Create Take Folder (Logic Pro > Settings > Recording, or Record > Overlapping Audio Recordings > Cycle > Create Take Folder); the auditor made that default load-bearing and cited nothing for it, while the trick states 'Every pass stacks into a take folder' unconditionally. SALVAGE: 'Draw a cycle area and set Record > Overlapping Audio Recordings > Cycle to Create Take Folder. Then let the performer keep going — after the second pass a take folder appears on the track and every pass after that is added to it, ready to be comped. Never stop between takes.'

downgrades.title: Add reverb to the monitoring only, not the recording
downgrades.reason: Version-mismatched single source. The only evidence is a macprovideo article whose own title is 'Using an Input Channel Strip in Logic Pro 9 to Record Audio with Software FX' — Logic 9, for a book covering 10.7/11/12 — and the 'Logic Pro help mirror' the auditor leaned on is skydocu.com, an unofficial Logic Pro X-era copy, not support.apple.com. A follow-up search for the mechanism in current versions returned only forums (logic-users-group, logicprohelp) and a blog (soundswow); no Apple page and no permitted current source states that Input channel strip effects are printed while audio-track inserts are not. The claim is also ambiguous in a way that matters: most readers will read 'the input channel' as the audio track they are recording onto, where inserts are not printed anyway, so the warning is either about a rarely used Mixer object or misleading. SALVAGE (leaning on what is documented — Apple's send-a-mix-to-multiple-destinations page gives 'a separate headphone mix with additional effects' as its stated use case): 'Give the performer reverb without committing to it. Put it on the aux that feeds the headphone mix rather than anywhere in the record path — Apple's example use for that routing is exactly a separate headphone mix with additional effects, so the reverb reaches that output and nothing else.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; I spent 18 of my ~20 allotted calls and checked every trick in section 7 (16 tricks, no group-level \"path\" fields exist in this file, so nothing to check there). WebFetch is blocked in this environment, so all evidence is search-result text that quotes/paraphrases the linked Apple Logic Pro User Guide pages rather than full page reads — quotes below are the returned snippet text, attributed to the page it came from. Two claims stayed genuinely unsettled and are marked UNVERIFIABLE rather than guessed: (a) that Marquee is the *default* Command-click (secondary) tool — sources confirm the Command-click Tool menu exists and sits on the right, and Sound On Sound argues Marquee is the best choice, which cuts against it being a factory default, but nothing states the default either way; (b) the ⇧S assignment for Select Similar Regions — Apple's Select regions page lists ⇧C (Equal Colored), ⇧E (Equal Regions), ⇧M (Muted), ⇧P, ⇧H, but the Similar Regions assignment was truncated in every snippet returned. Note also that the trick \"Esc opens the tool menu\" is a textbook version trap: Esc-based tool switching is Logic 9 behaviour, while Apple's current key-command list gives Show Tool Menu = T.

tricks.title: ⌘T splits every selected region at the playhead
tricks.reason: Apple's Split regions page confirms both the command and the key. The multi-region/multi-track framing follows from the command operating on the selection; the key command itself is named for the playhead position, exactly as the trick describes.
tricks.evidence_quote: The "Split Regions at Playhead" command can be accessed via Edit > Split > Regions at Playhead or by using the key command Command-T, which is labeled as "Split Regions/Events at Playhead Position".

tricks.title: ⌘J joins regions back into one
tricks.reason: Apple's Join regions page confirms the Command-J key command and, specifically, that joining audio creates a new mixdown file that replaces the originals — which is the falsifiable half of the body copy.
tricks.evidence_quote: To join regions in Logic Pro, select the regions, then choose Edit > Bounce or Join > Join. The key command is Command J. ... Audio regions are joined nondestructively, and Logic Pro creates a new file for the joined audio (called a mixdown) that replaces the original regions.

tricks.title: ⌥‑drag copies, ⌥⇧‑drag makes an alias or clone
tricks.reason: Both halves are documented by Apple: Option-drag copies a region, and Option-Shift-drag makes a MIDI alias or an audio clone. The trick's claim that the modifier behaves the same for both region types matches the two guide pages.
tricks.evidence_quote: Option-drag the region to move it to a new position [Cut, copy, and paste regions]. ... Option-Shift-drag the region to the position where you want the alias to start [Create MIDI aliases]. ... Hold down Option-Shift while dragging an audio region [Clone audio regions].

tricks.title: ⌘R repeats the selection once, instantly
tricks.reason: Multiple independent Logic sources confirm Command-R as Repeat Regions/Events (one copy per press) and the separate Repeat Multiple menu item that takes a numeric count, which is exactly what the body copy says.
tricks.evidence_quote: By clicking on a region (or group of regions) and hitting Command+R, you can create a duplicate. For repeating regions multiple times at once, you can choose Edit > Repeat Multiple from the Tracks area local menu bar or use the Repeat Regions Multiple Times key command.

tricks.title: Trim to the playhead from either direction
tricks.reason: The command names given do not exist in Logic. Apple's Resize regions page calls it "Set Region/Event/Marquee Start to Playhead Position" (and the matching End command); Logic's Edit > Trim submenu contains Region Start to Previous Region, Region End to Next Region and Remove Overlaps — no "Trim Region Start to Playhead". A buyer searching Key Commands for the printed name finds nothing.
tricks.evidence_quote: To trim a region start, use the Set Region/Event/Marquee Start to Playhead Position key command. For audio regions, this command also moves the anchor point to the playhead position. ... To lengthen regions, select the regions you want to lengthen, then choose Edit > Trim > Region End to Next Region.
tricks.correction: The commands are “Set Region/Event/Marquee Start to Playhead Position” and the matching End command — search Key Commands (⌥K) for “Playhead Position” and put them on keys. (Note that on audio regions the Start command also moves the region anchor to the playhead.) Related one-shot trims live under Edit > Trim, such as Region End to Next Region. No mouse precision needed.

tricks.title: Use the length fields in the Region inspector
tricks.reason: Apple's Region inspector page confirms all three parameters are present and that values can be typed in numerically rather than dragged — and even recommends typing when you need an exact shared value, which is the point the trick makes.
tricks.evidence_quote: Position shows the region position in bars, beats, division, and ticks, and can be changed by ... editing it numerically ... The playback of regions can be continuously repeated by selecting the Loop checkbox ... to set all selected regions to the same value, you should enter the value numerically rather than by dragging.

tricks.title: Set Snap to Smart and leave it there
tricks.reason: Apple's Snap items to the grid page describes Smart exactly as adaptive, from bars down through finer divisions. One caveat worth noting in a future edit: Apple says it follows the ruler division value as well as the zoom level, not zoom alone — but nothing in the trick is contradicted.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, the "Smart" option in the Snap pop-up menu in the Tracks area allows edit operations to snap to the nearest bar, beat, sub-beat, and so on, depending on the current ruler division value and the zoom level.

tricks.title: Two modifiers, two grades of precision
tricks.reason: Apple's Move regions / Snap pages confirm both grades: Control-drag moves in single-division steps, Control-Shift-drag drops to ticks (or samples when zoomed far in), which is what the trick calls tick-level free movement.
tricks.evidence_quote: Holding down Control while dragging regions moves them in steps of one division. ... when pressing and holding Control and Shift while dragging an item in the Tracks area, the editing grid switches to ticks if editing at lower zoom levels, and to samples at higher zoom levels.

tricks.title: Turn on “Snap Regions to Absolute Value”
tricks.reason: The mechanism described is right, but the framing is contradicted by Apple: Absolute is what Logic already uses by default, so there is nothing to "turn on", and there is no "off" — the opposite setting is a separate menu item, Snap Regions to Relative Value. A reader following this opens the Snap menu and finds it already ticked, with no way to switch it off.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, the Snap function is set to "Snap Regions to Absolute Value." When you move or edit an item, it snaps exactly to the nearest grid position. ... You can also choose "Snap Regions to Relative Value," so that items retain the same relative distance from their original grid positions. For example, when you move a region located at position 2.1.1.16 one beat forward, it snaps to position 2.2.1.16, not 2.2.1.1.
tricks.correction: In the Snap menu. “Snap Regions to Absolute Value” is Logic's default: move or edit an item and it snaps exactly to the nearest grid position, ignoring any offset it had. The opposite is not an off switch but a second menu item, “Snap Regions to Relative Value” — choose that when you are moving a region that sits deliberately off‑grid, so it keeps its distance from the grid (a region at 2.1.1.16 moved one beat forward lands on 2.2.1.16, not 2.2.1.1).

tricks.title: Use Nudge for repeatable movement
tricks.reason: The Move submenu holds the Set Nudge Value to… commands and Option-Left/Option-Right nudge the selection by that value, exactly as written; Apple's Move regions page plus two independent Logic sites agree.
tricks.evidence_quote: To change the nudge value in Logic Pro, right-click a region then select Move > Set Nudge Value to. ... Once you've set a nudge value, press and hold Option and press the Left or Right Arrow key to nudge selected regions.

tricks.title: Esc opens the tool menu, Esc twice returns to the pointer
tricks.reason: Version trap. Esc-opens-the-toolbox (and Esc-Esc for the Pointer) is Logic 9 behaviour. In the versions this book covers, Apple's Tool Menu key-command list gives Show Tool Menu a default assignment of T, and T pressed twice returns to the Pointer. The number-key selection claim could not be confirmed either and should not be restated without checking.
