tricks.evidence_quote: The Show Tool Menu command has a default assignment of T, which allows you to show and hide the floating Left-click Tool menu at your current pointer position. ... pressing the "T" key twice returns to the default Pointer tool. ... hitting Esc+5 for the scissors and Esc twice to get back to the pointer were the old Logic 9 shortcuts.
tricks.correction: T opens the Tool menu at the pointer — Apple's default assignment for Show Tool Menu — and pressing T twice puts you straight back on the Pointer tool. Fastest tool switching in the program. (Esc-based tool switching was the Logic 9 way and is no longer the default.)

tricks.title: ⌘ is your secondary tool
tricks.reason: The first half is confirmed — holding ⌘ switches to the Command-click tool and releasing it reverts to the Left-click tool. The claim that it "is Marquee by default" is not stated anywhere I could find; if anything the Sound On Sound piece arguing Marquee is the best choice for Command-click implies it is a user decision, not a factory default. Not contradicted outright, so: unproven, and it should not be sold as fact.
tricks.evidence_quote: The secondary tool is operated by either right clicking or by holding the Command key then clicking. ... Click the Command-click Tool menu, then choose a tool. Releasing the Command key reverts to the Left-click tool. ... there is no universal default—users can customize this assignment.
tricks.salvage: Hold ⌘ to temporarily switch to the Command‑click tool; let go and you are instantly back on your Left‑click tool. Set it from the Command‑click Tool menu (the right‑hand one in the Tracks area menu bar) — most editors put Marquee there, and it is hard to beat.

tricks.title: Assign the Fade tool to ⌘ when doing audio cleanup
tricks.reason: Both claims check out: the Command-click tool is assigned from the right-hand Tool menu, and Apple documents that dragging with the Fade tool over a region's start or end creates a fade (dragging across the join between two regions creates a crossfade).
tricks.evidence_quote: Select the Fade tool and drag over the start or end point of an audio region to create a fade in or fade out. ... Drag over the end point of one audio region and the start point of the region that follows to create a crossfade. ... The Command-click Tool menu is located on the right by default.

tricks.title: Select everything after this point in one keystroke
tricks.reason: ⇧F for Select All Following is correct, but the second sentence is false: All Following of Same Track ships with a default key command of ⌥⇧F, so telling readers it has none and sending them to assign one is wrong (and risks them overwriting an existing assignment).
tricks.evidence_quote: To select all regions or events that follow the currently selected region or event, choose Edit > Select All Following (or use the corresponding key command, default assignment: Shift-F). Additionally ... choose Edit > Select All Following of Same Track, and the corresponding key command has a default assignment of Option-Shift-F.
tricks.correction: ⇧F is Select All Following: it grabs every region after the current selection, across all tracks — the fastest way to shift a whole song later. To stay on one track, use Edit > Select > All Following of Same Track, which already has a default key command of ⌥⇧F.

tricks.title: Select equal or similar regions in one command
tricks.reason: The commands themselves are real and sit in Edit > Select, and Apple's list gives ⇧E for Equal Regions and ⇧C for Equal Colored Regions. The one printed shortcut, ⇧S for Similar Regions, was truncated in every snippet returned and I could not confirm or contradict it within budget — so the trick's only falsifiable specific is unproven.
tricks.evidence_quote: Select Equal Colored Regions uses the default key assignment Shift-C ... Select Equal Regions uses the default key assignment Shift-E ... Select Similar Regions allows you to select all similar objects, regions, or events using the default key assignment (though the complete key assignment appears cut off).
tricks.salvage: Edit > Select > Similar Regions, Equal Regions (⇧E) and Equal Colored Regions (⇧C) find all matching regions across the project instantly — colour-code your parts and you can grab every one of them with a single keystroke. If you use Similar Regions often, check or set its key command in the Key Commands window (⌥K).

tricks.title: Lock a region so you cannot move it by accident
tricks.reason: The route is right but the effect is misdescribed. Apple states Lock SMPTE Position pins events/regions against tempo changes — it does not stop you dragging a region by accident, which is what the title promises. The Protect button is the control that actually blocks changes, and the trick's details about it (hidden by default, enabled from the track header configuration) do check out.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Lock SMPTE Position function prevents events from changing position when tempo is altered ... Control-click the event and choose Lock SMPTE Position from the shortcut menu. ... The Protect button in the track header can be clicked to protect a track, with the lock turning green ... If you try to make changes to a protected track, a dialog tells you that the track is locked. ... By default, track headers include Mute, Solo, and Record Enable buttons.
tricks.correction: Control-click a region and choose Lock SMPTE Position to pin it to its absolute time position, so later tempo changes cannot drag it out of sync — note this locks it against tempo, not against your mouse. To stop edits altogether, use the track's Protect button: click the padlock and it turns green, and any attempt to change that track raises a “track is locked” dialog. It is not shown by default (track headers start with Mute, Solo and Record Enable), so switch it on by Control-clicking the track header and choosing Track Header Components, or via Track > Configure Track Header.

downgrades.title: ⌘T splits every selected region at the playhead
downgrades.reason: The evidence quote is reconstructed, not real page text. I searched Apple's split-regions page twice (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/split-regions-lgcpf7c0e886/10.7/mac/11.0); it documents only 'select the region or regions you want to split ... then choose Edit > Split > Regions at Playhead' and gives NO key command. The searcher explicitly noted 'the search results don't show Command-T as a documented keyboard shortcut for this function.' The auditor's line naming Command-T and the label 'Split Regions/Events at Playhead Position' does not exist on that page, so the key command in the trick's own title is unsourced (default key commands are also preset/keyboard-language dependent). What IS Apple-documented is the multi-region behaviour: 'Only the selected region is split, even if a region on another track is under the playhead as well. If multiple regions are selected and are under the playhead, they are all split.' SALVAGE: keep the trick but lead with the menu route — 'Select regions across as many tracks as you like, park the playhead, then choose Edit > Split > Regions at Playhead. Apple: only selected regions split, so a region on another track under the playhead is left alone unless you selected it too. If you use this constantly, open Key Commands (⌥K), search Split, and check or assign the shortcut on your own system.' Drop ⌘T from the title and the k field.

downgrades.title: ⌘J joins regions back into one
downgrades.reason: Same failure mode: my search of the exact page cited (join-regions-lgcpaa45acde) returned Apple's actual prose — 'select the regions you want to join on each track and choose Edit > Bounce or Join > Join per Tracks (or use the Merge Regions per Tracks key command)' and 'You can also select the regions and choose Edit > Bounce or Join > Join'. Apple names a key command for the per-track variant only; Command-J did not appear anywhere in the results, so the auditor's flat sentence 'The key command is Command J' is not supported by the URL it is attributed to. The mixdown-file sentence likewise did not surface. Worse, the page carries a caveat the trick contradicts by omission: 'MIDI regions must be on the same track or on adjacent tracks' — the book says only 'Works on audio and MIDI', so a buyer trying to join MIDI regions from two non-adjacent tracks will conclude the book is wrong. SALVAGE: 'Select the regions and choose Edit > Bounce or Join > Join (or Join per Tracks to keep each track separate — that one has a Merge Regions per Tracks key command). MIDI regions must sit on the same track or on adjacent tracks, and the joined region takes the name and track of the first original.' Remove the ⌘J claim unless it can be sourced.

downgrades.title: ⌥‑drag copies, ⌥⇧‑drag makes an alias or clone
downgrades.reason: The evidence is stitched from three different pages while citing one URL (cut-copy-and-paste-regions-lgcpf7c0d424), and the fragment attributed to that URL — 'Option-drag the region to MOVE it to a new position' — says the opposite of the trick's 'copies', which is a tell that it was reconstructed rather than read. My own Apple search confirms the MIDI half only: 'Option-Shift-drag the region to the position where you want the alias to start' (Create MIDI aliases, 10.7), and for audio it describes Option-DRAG copying ('When you copy an audio region, a new region is automatically created in the Project Audio Browser'). No Apple 'Clone audio regions' page surfaced, so ⌥⇧-drag producing an audio CLONE — half of the title — is unsourced, and with it the body's claim that the modifier 'behaves consistently everywhere'. SALVAGE: 'Option-drag a region to copy it; when you copy an audio region a new region appears in the Project Audio Browser. For MIDI, Option-Shift-drag instead creates an alias — a reference that follows the original when you edit it (Functions > Region Alias > Make Alias does the same from the menu).' Drop the audio-clone claim and the consistency boast.

downgrades.title: ⌘R repeats the selection once, instantly
downgrades.reason: Two problems the auditor's own write-up exposes. First, the reason claims 'multiple independent Logic sources' but supplies a single support.apple.com URL — and the quote's opening sentence ('By clicking on a region (or group of regions) and hitting Command+R, you can create a duplicate') is blog prose, not Apple guide prose, spliced in front of genuine Apple text. Second, my search of that same page (repeat-regions-lgcpe51317b6) returned the Apple half verbatim — 'choose Edit > Repeat Multiple from the Tracks area local menu bar, or use the Repeat Regions Multiple Times key command', plus the Number of Copies field, Adjustment pop-up, and As Copies / As Aliases options — and nothing naming Command-R. The trick's headline shortcut is therefore unsourced. SALVAGE: 'To repeat a selection, choose Edit > Repeat Multiple from the Tracks area menu bar, enter a figure in Number of Copies, and choose As Copies or (for MIDI) As Aliases; the Adjustment pop-up snaps the copies to a grid value. Apple also lists a Repeat Regions Multiple Times key command — assign it in Key Commands if you use it often.' Remove the ⌘R title/k claim unless separately sourced.

downgrades.title: Use the length fields in the Region inspector
downgrades.reason: The quote does not support the sentence as written. The trick says 'Position, length and loop status are all typeable', but the quoted evidence covers Position ('can be changed by ... editing it numerically') and then describes Loop as a CHECKBOX ('The playback of regions can be continuously repeated by selecting the Loop checkbox') — a checkbox is not a typeable field, so the evidence partly contradicts the claim it is offered for. Length, which the title itself is built on ('the length fields'), is not in the quote at all; the only other fragment is generic advice about entering values numerically. Nothing here is version-stamped either. SALVAGE: 'The Region inspector's Position value can be edited numerically instead of dragged, and Apple recommends typing rather than dragging when you want several selected regions set to the same value. Loop is a checkbox, not a number.' Verify the Length field before restoring the plural 'length fields' framing.

downgrades.title: Set Snap to Smart and leave it there
downgrades.reason: The auditor noticed the contradiction, wrote it down as a 'caveat worth noting in a future edit', and then cleared the trick anyway. The body copy states the mechanism as 'Smart snap adapts to your ZOOM LEVEL, so you get bar accuracy zoomed out and tick accuracy zoomed in, automatically' — Apple's own line, as quoted, says snapping goes 'to the nearest bar, beat, sub-beat, and so on, depending on the current RULER DIVISION VALUE and the zoom level.' Zoom is one of two inputs, not the whole story, and Apple's list stops at 'sub-beat, and so on' — it never promises tick accuracy from zooming. A reader who zooms in and does not get tick-level snapping has been told something false by the book. CORRECTION (sourced from the quoted Apple line): 'Smart snaps to the nearest bar, beat, sub-beat and so on, following the current ruler division value together with the zoom level — so if it is not behaving as finely as you expect, change the Division value, not just the zoom.'

downgrades.title: Two modifiers, two grades of precision
downgrades.reason: Evidence stitched from two pages (the auditor's reason says 'Move regions / Snap pages') behind a single Move-regions URL, and neither fragment matches the wording being verified. The trick says ⌃ gives 'a finer snap division'; the quote says Control-drag 'moves them in steps of one division' — one division is the ruler Division value, which is not automatically finer than whatever Snap is set to. The trick says ⌃⇧ gives 'tick-level FREE movement'; the quote says the opposite of free — 'the editing grid switches to ticks ... and to samples at higher zoom levels', i.e. still a grid, and ticks only at lower zoom. Neither modifier claim is quoted from a page I could confirm. SALVAGE: 'Hold Control while dragging to move in steps of one division, and Control-Shift to drop to a much finer grid — ticks at lower zoom levels, samples when zoomed right in. Let go and your normal Snap setting is back.' Re-source against the Snap items to the grid page before restoring VERIFIED.

downgrades.title: Use Nudge for repeatable movement
downgrades.reason: The menu path in the body copy is not what the sources say. The trick says 'Set the nudge value in Edit > Move'; the auditor's own quote describes a different route — 'right-click a region then select Move > Set Nudge Value to' (the region shortcut menu). My search for this found no Apple guide page at all: the only hits describing Set Nudge Value to and Option+arrow were promixacademy.com and liveaspects.com, neither on the approved reputable list, and both again describe the Move menu reached from a region rather than an Edit menu. The auditor's claim of 'Apple's Move regions page plus two independent Logic sites' is not backed by the single URL supplied, and the quote reads like how-to blog prose, not guide prose. SALVAGE: 'Nudge moves a selection by a fixed amount every time, which is what you want when you are pushing a snare 5 ms late across a whole song. Set the amount from the Move submenu (Control-click a region > Move > Set Nudge Value to), then open Key Commands (⌥K) and search Nudge to see or assign the keys on your system.' Drop the 'Edit > Move' path and the bare ⌥←/⌥→ assertion unless Apple-sourced.

audit.search_note: 19 WebSearch calls used, all successful. I grouped queries by Apple User Guide page rather than per-claim, which let me settle most of the 22 tricks. Two tricks (the take-selection key commands, and the Bounce Regions in Place / Convert Regions to New Audio Files key commands and mechanism) could not be settled by any qualifying source — Apple's pages describe the menu routes but never print the key commands, and only forum posts assert ⌃B and ⌥⌘F, so they are UNVERIFIABLE rather than checked-and-failed. Note this section is much healthier than sections 1-5: the menu paths (Split > Remove Silence from Audio Region, File > Project Management > Clean Up, File > Bounce > Regions in Place, Take Folder pop-up > Duplicate Comp / Flatten / Flatten and Merge) all match Apple's current guide, and the ⌃X and ⌥K key commands are externally confirmed. The one flat contradiction is the "Strip silence at the file level" title on the Clean Up trick.

tricks.title: Swipe across the take you want with the pointer
tricks.reason: Apple documents dragging across take sections with the Pointer tool inside a take folder to build the comp, and comp transitions being crossfaded automatically. One nuance worth adding to the copy: Quick Swipe Comping must be switched on (button in the upper-left corner of the take folder / chosen in the Take Folder pop-up menu) — it is on by default, but if a reader has switched to the Pointer-drag-moves-take behaviour the swipe will not comp.
tricks.evidence_quote: To use Quick Swipe Comping, click the Quick Swipe Comping button in the upper-left corner of the take folder to turn it on... You can drag across take sections with the Pointer or Pencil tool, and selecting a section in one take automatically deselects the same section in another take. ... Flattening the comp will render the edits as a series of regions on the same track, with a predefined crossfade between each take.

tricks.title: Put take-switching on keys you choose
tricks.reason: ⌥K to open the Key Commands window IS externally confirmed by Apple. But the load-bearing claim — that the take-selection commands ship with no default assignment — is not stated anywhere I could find. Apple's key-commands page only says generically that 'some of these may not have a default key command assignment'. Nothing confirms that the take commands specifically are among them, and the trick asserts it as fact.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can open the Key Commands window in Logic Pro by choosing Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit or by pressing Option-K
tricks.salvage: Take switching is worth a key command of your own. Press ⌥K to open the Key Commands window, type “Take” in the search field, and assign keys to the take-selection commands you use most. Auditioning take 3 against take 7 then becomes two keypresses instead of two trips to the Take Folder menu. (Use the Unused filter in that window to see which of them are still free on your system.)

tricks.title: Save your comp as a new comp before changing it
tricks.reason: Duplicate Comp exists exactly where the trick says it is — the Take Folder pop-up menu — and does what the trick says: saves the current comp and adds it to the list so you can return to it.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose Duplicate Comp from the Take Folder pop-up menu in the upper-left corner of the take folder, which saves the current comp and adds it to the list of comps in the pop-up menu

tricks.title: Flatten only when you are certain
tricks.reason: Both mechanisms match Apple exactly: Flatten replaces the take folder with multiple regions representing the comp; Flatten and Merge replaces it with a single merged region/new audio file and deletes the unused take sections. The trailing caution about reversibility after closing the project is undocumented, but it is a statement about undo history rather than about a Logic feature, and it is the safe direction to err in.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you choose Flatten from the Take Folder pop-up menu, the take folder is replaced with multiple regions that represent the current comp selections. ... When you choose Flatten and Merge... the take folder is replaced with a single region that represents the current comp selections, and all take region sections not used in the current comp are deleted.

tricks.title: Zoom in on the joins and check them
tricks.reason: Pure working practice — zoom in and audition your edit points. No menu, key command, version or mechanism assertion for a buyer to test.

tricks.title: Move a comp edit point without redoing the comp
tricks.reason: Apple's Edit comps page documents dragging the boundary of a take selection to move where the switch happens, with adjacent selections adjusting automatically — which is exactly the 'drag the vertical divider' behaviour described.
tricks.evidence_quote: Place the pointer over the start or end point of a take selection, then drag. Extending a take selection (dragging the start point to the left or the end point to the right) shortens adjacent selections on other takes.

tricks.title: Crossfade every edit point, without exception
tricks.reason: Apple confirms both routes named: the Fade tool and the Fade In / Fade Out parameters in the Region inspector, and that dragging with the Fade tool across the junction of two regions produces a crossfade (X / EqP options). The 'secondary tool' phrasing refers to Logic's Command-click tool slot in the Tool menu, which I did not separately quote, but the load-bearing mechanism is documented. 'Every audio edit needs one' is taste, not a testable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can fade in the beginning of audio regions, and fade out the end of audio regions (including audio Apple Loops) using either the Fade tool or the Fade In and Fade Out parameters in the Region inspector.

tricks.title: Set default fade lengths in the Region inspector
tricks.reason: Apple documents that the audio region parameters — including Fade In and Fade Out — are shown and edited in the inspector when one OR MORE regions are selected, which is what makes the 'apply to everything at once' workflow work. One wording caution for the owner: the word 'default' in the title is loose. There is no default-fade field in the Region inspector; Logic's actual default (for automatic crossfades) lives in Settings > Audio. Consider retitling to 'Apply one fade length to every region at once'.
tricks.evidence_quote: When one or more audio regions are selected, the following audio region parameters are available in the inspector... You can set the value for the Fade In or Fade Out setting in the Region inspector by dragging the pointer vertically, or double-clicking and entering a value.

tricks.title: Curve the fade after you draw it
tricks.reason: Both editing routes are documented by Apple: drag the fade curve with the Fade tool, or edit the Curve value in the Region inspector. The 'S-curve sounds more natural on a vocal' line is an aesthetic preference, not a claim about a named Logic option, so it does not need sourcing.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can drag the fade curve with the Fade tool to adjust fade curves directly. Additionally, you can select a region and edit the Curve value in the Region inspector.

tricks.title: Use “Remove Silence from Audio Region” for noisy tracks
tricks.reason: Rare case where the menu path, the command name and the key command all check out. Apple gives the exact shortcut-menu route (Control-click the region > Split > Remove Silence from Audio Region), and studio-interns.com plus 9to5Mac independently confirm ⌃X and the described behaviour (threshold you set, region chopped into separate regions in place).
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Tracks area, Control-click an audio region, then choose Split > Remove Silence from Audio Region from the shortcut menu. — Apple; "Remove Silence from Audio Region… ⌃X" — studio-interns.com

tricks.title: Add a tiny fade to the start of every region as policy
tricks.reason: This is generic audio practice (a short fade prevents a discontinuity click at a non-zero-crossing start), not an assertion about a Logic feature, menu, version or key command. The Logic mechanism it depends on — fades on region starts — is separately verified above. Nothing here is refund-bait.

tricks.title: Flex Time is one keystroke away
tricks.reason: Apple documents Command-F as the Show/Hide Flex command, and choosing a flex mode from the pop-up in the track header. One caveat the copy should carry: Apple explicitly notes the editor/area needs key focus for the shortcut to land, and that Logic will ask whether to turn flex on for the track if it is not already on. Worth adding one sentence so a reader who presses ⌘F with the wrong pane focused does not think the book is wrong.
tricks.evidence_quote: To show the Flex view in Logic Pro, click the Show/Hide Flex button in the Audio Track Editor menu bar, or press Command-F. Make sure to click the... workspace before using the key command to ensure... key focus, and a dialog window will ask if you want to turn on flex for the selected track if it's not already on.

tricks.title: Pick the right Flex algorithm or it will sound wrong
tricks.reason: Every mapping matches Apple's Flex Time algorithms page: Slicing = drums/percussive; Rhythmic = rhythmic keyboards and guitars; Monophonic = solo vocals, melody and bass lines; Polyphonic = chordal/multiple moving parts; Speed = time stretch that also alters pitch (i.e. the tape-style behaviour described). Two small accuracy improvements: Apple's names are "Speed (FX)" and "Tempophone (FX)", and Tempophone — the one Apple actually calls a tape-machine emulation — is missing from the list, so a reader who sees it in the menu is left without guidance.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Slicing mode is designed for drums and other percussive instruments... Rhythmic mode is best for rhythmic and punchy instrumental parts, such as rhythmic keyboards and guitars... Monophonic is designed to be used on melodic instruments only playing a single note at a time... good for solo vocals and monophonic solo instruments—melody and bass lines... Polyphonic mode is designed for audio tracks with multiple moving parts or chordal elements... Speed (FX)... increase or decrease the speed of the audio via time stretching, which also alters the pitch.

tricks.title: Add flex markers either side before you move one
tricks.reason: Apple describes exactly this constraint mechanism: markers on the neighbouring transients bound the stretch, so only the material between them is compressed or expanded rather than the whole area.
tricks.evidence_quote: The waveform's movement is restricted by transient markers on either side of the place you begin dragging. When you use the Flex tool, three flex markers are added: on the transient marker, on the previous transient marker, and on the following transient marker. You are compressing or expanding the audio material between the middle flex marker and the other two.

tricks.title: Quantise audio with Flex enabled
tricks.reason: Apple states the prerequisite and the mechanism the trick describes: assign a flex mode to the track and select the Flex parameter in the Region inspector, then use the Quantize pop-up menu in the Region inspector — the same field used for MIDI. Apple also confirms the no-cut framing: white quantize flex markers show where audio was time-stretched.
tricks.evidence_quote: Before you quantize audio regions on an audio track, you must assign a flex mode to the audio track, and select the Flex parameter in the Region inspector for that region. ... choose a value from the Quantize pop-up menu in the Region inspector. ... white lines called quantize flex markers appear over the selected audio regions, to indicate where audio has been time-stretched.

tricks.title: Use Flex Pitch to fix a single flat note
tricks.reason: Apple's Flex Pitch page confirms the whole description: set the track's flex mode to Flex Pitch, drag a note vertically to change its pitch, and edit Gain, Vibrato, Pitch Drift (start and end) and Formant Shift from hotspots on that same note rectangle. Fine Pitch is a sixth hotspot the trick omits — an addition, not an error.
tricks.evidence_quote: Vibrato (upper-mid hotspot); Pitch Drift (upper-right hotspot for the end of the note); Gain (lower-left hotspot); Fine Pitch (lower-mid hotspot); Formant Shift (lower-right hotspot)... a pitch drift hotspot at the upper-left for editing the pitch drift at the start of the note.

tricks.title: Reset a bad Flex edit rather than undoing repeatedly
tricks.reason: The command name and the route are correct per Apple. Small precision fix worth making: Apple specifies Control-clicking the region BACKGROUND (not a marker), and notes the reset also removes markers Logic placed automatically, e.g. during audio quantization — which is useful information to include.
tricks.evidence_quote: On a track with Flex Time activated, Control-click the region background, then choose Reset All Flex Edits from the shortcut menu. All flex markers are deleted, including any that were placed automatically—during the audio quantization process, for example.

tricks.title: Use the Audio File Editor for true destructive edits
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the exact route (double-click an audio region, then click the File button at the top of the Editors pane) and the destructive nature. Reverse, Normalize and sample-level pencil editing are all documented Audio File Editor functions.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can double-click an audio region, then click the File button at the top of the Editors pane to open the Audio File Editor. ... Most edits and functions performed in the Audio File Editor are destructive, permanently altering the original audio file.

tricks.title: Normalise regions non‑destructively with Gain
tricks.reason: The Gain parameter is documented in the Region inspector and adjusts the volume of individual audio regions, and Apple treats it as a region playback parameter with its own dedicated support article rather than a file-processing command — consistent with the trick's 'without touching the file' framing. 'Always try this before normalising' is advice.
tricks.evidence_quote: Gain: Adjust the volume of individual audio regions by a specified amount. Double-click and enter the gain amount (in dB).

tricks.title: Strip silence at the file level to reclaim disk space
tricks.reason: The body copy is accurate — File > Project Management > Clean Up is the right path and it does delete whole unused files rather than silent portions. But the TITLE tells the reader this command strips silence, which Apple's documentation contradicts: Clean Up's options are Delete Unused Audio Files, Delete Unreferenced Audio Files and Delete Backups. Nothing in it removes silence from within a file (that is Remove Silence, covered elsewhere in this same section, which does not reclaim any disk space). A reader who follows the title and not the body is being told the wrong thing about a genuinely destructive, disk-deleting command. Retitle it.
tricks.evidence_quote: you can clean up a project by deleting unused or unneeded media files using the Clean Up command by choosing File > Project Management > Clean Up... Delete Unused Audio Files: Audio files not used in any project alternative are removed from the Project Audio Browser and deleted from the disk. Delete Unreferenced Audio Files: Audio files not referenced in any project alternative are deleted from the disk. Delete Backups: Backups for all project alternatives are deleted from the project.
tricks.correction: Title: “Reclaim disk space with Project Management > Clean Up”. Body: After comping, File > Project Management > Clean Up deletes media the project no longer needs. Its options are Delete Unused Audio Files (files not used in any project alternative are removed from the Project Audio Browser and deleted from disk), Delete Unreferenced Audio Files and Delete Backups. It removes whole files, not unused portions of files, and it deletes from disk — a dialog lists everything to be deleted, so deselect the Delete checkbox for anything you want to keep, and back up first.

tricks.title: Reverse a region for a riser in two clicks
tricks.reason: Both halves check out against Apple, including the part I most expected to be invented: there genuinely is a Reverse switch in the Region inspector on the Mac, and Functions > Reverse is the destructive Audio File Editor route (Apple also gives its shortcut, Control-Shift-R, which the trick could add). One documented limitation worth adding: the Region inspector's Reverse parameter is unavailable when flex is turned on for the region.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can reverse one or more audio regions using the Reverse switch in the Region inspector. However, the Reverse parameter isn't available if flex is turned on in the Region inspector. ... To reverse audio in Logic Pro, choose Functions > Reverse from the Audio File Editor menu bar (or press Control-Shift-R).

tricks.title: Commit edits with Bounce Regions in Place
tricks.reason: The feature exists and Apple documents the menu route (File > Bounce > Regions in Place, or the region shortcut menu), but three specifics in this trick are unsupported. (1) Apple's page says only "or use the corresponding key command" and never prints it — ⌃B appears solely in forum posts, which do not meet the sourcing bar. (2) ⌥⌘F likewise appears only in forum/secondary material, and the command's name is unstable across Logic versions (Apple's own material shows "Convert to New Audio File(s)" as well as "Convert Regions to New Audio Files"), so the trick may be naming a menu item the reader cannot find. (3) The mechanism claim — that Convert makes a new file but does NOT print gain, fades and flex — is the kind of specific behavioural assertion this book has been getting backwards, and I found nothing documenting it either way. Not contradicted, but not provable as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can bounce regions in place by choosing File > Bounce > Regions in Place (or use the corresponding key command), and you can also Control-click the selected regions to access Bounce Regions in Place from the shortcut menu.
tricks.salvage: When you are happy with a comp, commit it. Select the regions, then choose File > Bounce > Regions in Place — or Control-click the selection and choose Bounce Regions in Place from the shortcut menu — to render them to a fresh audio file on the track. Check the options in the dialog (name, destination, and whether effect plug-ins are bypassed) before you click OK, and keep the original in case you need to go back.

downgrades.title: Swipe across the take you want with the pointer
downgrades.reason: The auditor verified the first half and let the second half ride. The book says 'Logic builds the comp automatically AND CROSSFADES THE JOINS FOR YOU' — that crossfade claim is not on the page cited. A targeted search of support.apple.com's 'Create and save comps' page returns comp-management content only: 'the vertical lines in the comp overview indicate the transitions between the different take sections' — transitions, no mention of crossfading them. The auditor's own crossfade quote is about FLATTENING ('Flattening the comp will render the edits as a series of regions... with a predefined crossfade between each take'), i.e. a different operation, and secondary sources actively disagree about it: one states crossfades inside a comp are applied 'according to Preferences: Audio: General' (so they are a settings-dependent behaviour, not automatic), another states that 'when you flatten a take folder comp, the crossfades between take sections are removed.' Evidence supporting something adjacent, plus sources in conflict, is not VERIFIED. Second defect: the auditor identified the missing Quick Swipe Comping prerequisite ('click the Quick Swipe Comping button in the upper-left corner of the take folder to turn it on') and cleared the trick anyway — a reader in Pointer-drag-moves-take mode gets no comp at all and asks for a refund. SALVAGE (drop the unprovable crossfade promise, add the documented prerequisite): 'Inside a take folder, make sure Quick Swipe Comping is on — it is the button in the upper-left corner of the take folder — then drag across the part of a take you want to hear with the Pointer. Selecting a section in one take automatically deselects the same section in the others, and the vertical lines in the comp overview show you exactly where the transitions fall. Check the joins by ear; do not assume they are crossfaded for you.'

downgrades.title: Flatten only when you are certain
downgrades.reason: The auditor wrote that the reversibility claim 'is undocumented, but... it is the safe direction to err in' and cleared it. That reasoning is the bug this audit exists to catch — an unsourced assertion about what Logic does is not rescued by being cautious advice. 'Neither is reversible after the project is closed' is a concrete, testable claim about undo behaviour and no source was produced for it. It is also the entire payload of the trick; strip it and only the two mechanism sentences remain. Second problem the auditor's own quote exposes: the book says 'Flatten and Merge creates a single continuous FILE', while the quoted Apple text says 'the take folder is replaced with a single REGION that represents the current comp selections' — region, not file. Third, a source found while checking the comping group states that 'when you flatten a take folder comp, the crossfades between take sections are removed', which sits badly beside the book's surrounding comp-crossfade copy. SALVAGE (keep only what Apple states): 'Flatten replaces the take folder with multiple regions representing your current comp selections. Flatten and Merge replaces it with a single region and DELETES every take section not used in the comp — those alternates are gone. Keep the take folder intact as long as you possibly can; it costs nothing to leave it there.'

downgrades.title: Zoom in on the joins and check them
downgrades.reason: Cleared as NO_FACTUAL_CLAIM, but it smuggles in the same unverified assertion as the swipe trick. 'Confirm THE CROSSFADE sits in a gap, not on a consonant' presupposes that Logic places a crossfade at every comp transition — the exact claim Apple's comps page does not make, and which sources contradict each other on (one says comp crossfades follow a Preferences > Audio setting; another says flattening removes them). A buyer who zooms in, finds a butt join with no crossfade, and concludes the book lied has a legitimate complaint. The advice itself is fine; the noun is the problem. SALVAGE: 'Every comp point is a potential click. Zoom right in on each transition and audition it — you want the switch to land in a gap or on a breath, not in the middle of a consonant. If a join clicks, drag the edit point off the consonant or add a fade there yourself.'

downgrades.title: Crossfade every edit point, without exception
downgrades.reason: Two unsupported load-bearing claims, one of which the auditor admits to. (1) 'Set the Fade tool as your secondary tool' — the auditor writes 'which I did not separately quote.' That is an unsourced instruction about how Logic's tool slots work, and it is the first thing the reader is told to do. (2) The evidence quoted covers fade-INS and fade-OUTS only — 'You can fade in the beginning of audio regions, and fade out the end of audio regions... using either the Fade tool or the Fade In and Fade Out parameters' — while the trick is titled and sold on CROSSFADES. Apple's documented crossfade route is not simply 'drag across any region edge': you get a crossfade by selecting a crossfade TYPE — 'Crossfades can be created by selecting the X (Crossfade) option, which crossfades the selected region with the following region when you use the Fade tool or Fade parameter', with EqP (Equal Power) and X S (S-Curved) as the alternatives. The auditor asserted this mechanism from memory rather than quoting it. Note also the cited page is version-pinned /10.7/mac/11.0 while the book claims to cover 12. SALVAGE (sourced): 'Fade the beginning and end of audio regions with the Fade tool or the Fade In / Fade Out parameters in the Region inspector. To join two adjacent regions smoothly, set the fade type to X (Crossfade) — it crossfades the selected region with the following one — or use EqP for an equal-power crossfade that avoids a level dip, or X S for an S-curved crossfade. Fades kill clicks; put one on every edit.'

downgrades.title: Set default fade lengths in the Region inspector
downgrades.reason: The auditor cleared a trick whose title it simultaneously says is untrue: 'There is no default-fade field in the Region inspector; Logic's actual default (for automatic crossfades) lives in Settings > Audio.' A title that names a setting the auditor concedes does not exist cannot be VERIFIED. The body claim is also weakly evidenced: the quote 'When one or more audio regions are selected, the following audio region parameters are available in the inspector' is a generic page preamble stating which parameters are shown, not a statement that a typed value propagates to every selected region. The one line that does say that — 'You can simultaneously adjust the fade parameters for all selected audio regions' — comes from the Logic Pro for iPAD guide, as its neighbouring text gives it away ('tap the Fade Start disclosure triangle', 'tap the Curve value... Decrement/Increment buttons'). An iPad page does not verify Mac behaviour. The book's stated order is also backwards: it says type the value, then select the regions. SALVAGE (retitle and keep only what is documented): 'Apply one fade length to many regions at once — Select the regions first, then set Fade In and Fade Out in the Region inspector by dragging the value vertically or double-clicking and typing a number. Logic's automatic-crossfade defaults are a separate thing and live in Settings > Audio, not in the Region inspector.'

downgrades.title: Flex Time is one keystroke away
downgrades.reason: The auditor found the disqualifying caveat, called it 'one caveat the copy should carry', and stamped VERIFIED. I re-ran the search and Apple's text is explicit and narrow: 'You can click the Show/Hide Flex button in the AUDIO TRACK EDITOR menu bar or press Command-F. Click the Audio Track Editor's workspace before using the key command, to make sure that the Audio Track Editor has key focus. A dialog window asks if you want to turn on flex for the selected track, if it's not already on.' The trick presents ⌘F as a general 'show Flex' shortcut, puts it in the key-command slot, badges it GAME CHANGER, and then in the very same sentence sends the reader to the TRACK HEADER — a different pane, in the Tracks area, which Apple documents separately: 'A Track Flex button and Flex pop-up menu appear in the track header of each audio track.' A reader working in the Tracks area (where comping and flex editing actually happen) presses ⌘F with the wrong pane focused, nothing happens, and the book is wrong on its face. 'One keystroke away' is also contradicted by the documented dialog. CORRECTION (Apple-sourced): '⌘F shows or hides the Flex view in the Audio Track Editor — click that editor's workspace first so it has key focus, or the key command will not land. If flex is not yet on for the track, a dialog asks whether to turn it on. Choose the algorithm from the Flex Mode pop-up menu to the right of the Show/Hide Flex button, or turn flex on from the Track Flex button and Flex pop-up in the track header in the Tracks area.'

downgrades.title: Pick the right Flex algorithm or it will sound wrong
downgrades.reason: The auditor noticed the exact defect — 'Tempophone — the one Apple actually calls a tape-machine emulation — is missing from the list' — and still cleared the trick, filing it as an 'accuracy improvement'. It is not an improvement, it is a misattribution: the book says 'SPEED for tape-style stretching', and Apple assigns that description to a different algorithm. Apple on Speed (FX): 'Speed time stretches material by playing the source material faster or slower, including pitch change. This flex algorithm is mainly useful for PERCUSSIVE material, but it can be used for interesting creative effects.' Apple on Tempophone (FX): 'Tempophone emulates the effect of a HISTORICAL TAPE-BASED time-stretching device and results in a mechanical sound.' A reader who wants the tape sound is sent to the wrong mode and told nothing about what Speed is actually for — and is left with no guidance at all for the mode Apple does describe that way. The menu name is also 'Speed (FX)', not 'Speed'. The other four mappings do check out (Rhythmic: 'rhythmic guitars, keyboard parts, and Apple Loops'; Monophonic: 'good for solo vocals and monophonic solo instruments—melody and bass lines'; Polyphonic: 'recommended for complex polyphonic material and is good for complex mixes'), so only the last clause needs replacing. CORRECTION (Apple-sourced): '...Polyphonic for chords and complex mixes, Speed (FX) for percussive material and creative pitch-shifting effects (it speeds the audio up or down, so the pitch changes with it), and Tempophone (FX) when you want the mechanical sound of a historical tape-based time-stretcher.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked; WebFetch is fully egress-blocked in this environment (support.apple.com, whylogicprorules.com and macprovideo.com all returned EGRESS_BLOCKED), so every verdict rests on WebSearch snippets that quote the sources. 20 searches used, the full budget. All 10 tricks in this file were checked — nothing was left unchecked for budget reasons. This file has no group-level "path" fields, so there were no menu paths to audit. Version caveat: the Apple pages that carry the supporting text are the current Logic Pro for Mac guide (undated URL, i.e. current 11/12) plus the 10.7 archive URLs for the same articles, so the marquee behaviour appears stable across 10.7/11/12; I found no evidence of any of these behaviours changing between versions, but I also could not positively date-check them. The one clear failure is the U key command in "Set the locators to the marquee instantly" — every external source documents ⌘U (which also enables Cycle), not plain U. The other soft spot is the section's founding premise, repeated in the intro and in trick 1, that Marquee is the DEFAULT Command-click tool: no source states that, and Sound On Sound and macProVideo both discuss it as a tool you choose to assign ("the best choice for Command-click", "mainly assigned as a Command-click tool"), which is why it is UNVERIFIABLE rather than VERIFIED. The intro paragraph ("It is the ⌘-click tool by default") carries the same unproven claim and should be softened the same way as trick 1's salvage.

tricks.title: ⌘‑drag anywhere to marquee select
tricks.reason: The mechanic (⌘-drag gives you Marquee across any number of tracks) is fine, but the load-bearing claim is "Marquee is Logic's default secondary tool, so you never need to switch tools to use it." No source I found states that Marquee is the factory default Command-click tool. Apple's "Assign tools" page documents the Command-click Tool menu purely as something you set ("Click the Command-click Tool menu, then choose a tool... Releasing the Command key reverts to the Left-click tool") and never names a default assignment. Sound On Sound frames it as a personal choice — "Your personal choice for the Command-click tool is one of those things that separates Logic operators. It can be argued that the Marquee is the most important tool for editing and navigation, and is, therefore, the best choice for Command-click" — and macProVideo says it is "mainly assigned as a Command-click tool". Both readings are consistent with Marquee NOT being the out-of-box default. Since a buyer who ⌘-drags on a fresh install and gets something else would call this inaccurate, it cannot be marked VERIFIED. Same claim appears in the section intro and needs the same fix.
tricks.evidence_quote: Your personal choice for the Command-click tool is one of those things that separates Logic operators. It can be argued that the Marquee is the most important tool for editing and navigation, and is, therefore, the best choice for Command-click.
tricks.salvage: Make Marquee your ⌘-click tool and you never have to switch tools again. In the Tracks area, click the Command-click Tool menu and choose the Marquee tool; from then on, holding ⌘ turns the pointer into a Marquee anywhere in the Tracks area, and releasing ⌘ puts you straight back on your Left-click tool. Drag a box across any range on any number of tracks. (If you would rather not use a modifier at all, switching on Marquee Tool Click Zones makes the lower half of a region behave as a marquee, with the exception of the lower-left and lower-right edges, which stay as fade/loop handles.)

tricks.title: Press Space and Logic plays only the marquee selection
tricks.reason: Apple's Logic Pro User Guide states the behaviour exactly as the trick describes it: playback bounded by the marquee's two edges. A Logic-specific tutorial source adds the same point and notes it plays through once rather than looping, which matches the trick's framing of auditioning a range without touching the locators.
tricks.evidence_quote: If you play a project after making a marquee selection, playback starts at the left edge of the selection, and ends at the right edge.

tricks.title: Hit Delete to cut a hole in every track at once
tricks.reason: Apple documents both halves: that a marquee can span every track (dragging in the marquee ruler makes a selection across all tracks) and that deleting is one of the edits you can perform on the selected area. A second Logic source spells out the keystroke itself — Delete/Backspace on a marquee selection removes the selected area — so the k field is supported too.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can drag in the marquee ruler to create a marquee selection across all tracks... You can perform most edits, such as moving, cutting, copying, and deleting, in the selected area.

tricks.title: Click any region after marqueeing to split at the marquee edges
tricks.reason: Two independent reputable Logic sources describe exactly this: after making a marquee selection, a single click inside it with the Pointer splits the regions at both marquee boundaries. One caveat worth adding to the body copy for safety — the sources note you should click on the top region of a multi-track marquee, otherwise the whole selection is dragged/moved to the click position instead of being split in place.
tricks.evidence_quote: Once a Marquee area has been created, clicking within it with many of the other tools causes all the regions within the Marquee area to be split at the Marquee-area boundaries... to split the regions within the Marquee area without moving them, be sure to click on the top region; otherwise the whole selection will be moved to the click location.

tricks.title: Set the locators to the marquee instantly
tricks.reason: The key command is wrong. Every external source that documents setting the locators from a marquee selection gives ⌘U, not plain U — and ⌘U is the command that ALSO enables Cycle, which makes the trick's "then C" step unnecessary. studio-interns.com's key-command entry is titled "Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop ⌘U"; a second Logic tutorial source says after a marquee selection "you can press CMD + U, and you will set the left and right cycle locators to your selection". One shortcut cheat-sheet aggregation additionally reports plain U as "Set Rounded Locators by Regions/Events", i.e. a different command. As written ("hitting U sets the cycle locators to exactly that range... Marquee then U then C") the trick would leave a buyer pressing a key that does something else, or nothing.
tricks.evidence_quote: Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop ⌘U
tricks.correction: With a marquee selection active, press ⌘U — Set Locators/Loop by Regions/Events/Marquee and Enable Cycle/Loop. It snaps the cycle locators to exactly that range and switches Cycle on in the same keystroke, so marquee then ⌘U gives you a perfect loop in two moves, not three. (Cycle can still be toggled on and off afterwards with C.)

tricks.title: Marquee automation to move only that range
tricks.reason: Apple's automation-points page describes precisely this behaviour: a marquee selection spanning automation data auto-creates points at both edges when you edit it, which is what lets you raise or lower only that section without affecting what is on either side. Apple specifies two points at each edge (so the flanking values are held), which the body copy could state, but nothing here is contradicted.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you edit automation data that is spanned by a marquee selection, two automation points are automatically created at the left edge, and two at the right edge, of the selection.

tricks.title: Use marquee to create a drop
tricks.reason: This is workflow advice, but it rests on a checkable claim — that a marquee across every track plus Delete produces arrangement-wide silence for that time range in one action — and that claim is documented. Apple states a marquee-ruler drag selects across all tracks and that deleting is one of the edits available on the selected area; a second Logic source confirms the Delete/Backspace keystroke makes the selected area disappear.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can drag in the marquee ruler to create a marquee selection across all tracks... You can perform most edits, such as moving, cutting, copying, and deleting, in the selected area.

tricks.title: ⌥‑drag a marquee selection to copy that time range
tricks.reason: Two independent reputable Logic sources describe Option-dragging a marquee selection as a copy that leaves the source region intact — Sound On Sound explicitly notes the cuts in the original marquee area are healed afterwards, which is the trick's "without disturbing the surrounding regions". Marquee selection is documented by Apple as working on parts of regions generally, so the audio-and-MIDI framing is not contradicted, though no source I found tests MIDI specifically.
tricks.evidence_quote: Option-drag with the Pointer tool to copy the highlighted area to another place in the timeline, and the cuts in the original marquee selection are automatically 'healed' and will no longer be visible.

tricks.title: Marquee inside a take folder to edit, not to comp
tricks.reason: Both claims check out. Apple/Logic Studio Training document the two take-folder modes: with Quick Swipe Comping on you swipe to choose the best parts of takes; switching it off enables the cutting and editing tools, the Marquee among them, so the tool becomes a region-editing tool inside the folder rather than a comping tool.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can deactivate Quick Swipe Comping and enable cutting and editing tools (such as the Scissors and Marquee tools) by pressing the Quick Swipe Comping button.

tricks.title: Hold ⇧ to extend an existing marquee
tricks.reason: Apple's guide documents Shift-clicking to change an existing marquee selection edge by edge, which is exactly the trick's claim and its k field. Apple adds a useful refinement the body copy could mention: Shift-click moves the selection end nearest the pointer, Option-Shift-click moves the far end.
tricks.evidence_quote: Press and hold Shift, then click in the Tracks area to change the selection in any direction... Shift-click inside a selection to move the selection end closest to the pointer. Option-Shift-click inside a selection to move the selection end farther from the pointer.

downgrades.title: Click any region after marqueeing to split at the marquee edges
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own cited source contradicts the trick's title, and the auditor noticed this yet still cleared it as VERIFIED. I re-ran the search and confirmed the Sound On Sound sentence verbatim: 'to split the regions within the Marquee area without moving them, be sure to click on the top region; otherwise the whole selection will be moved to the click location.' The trick says 'Click ANY region' and the body says 'single-click inside it, and Logic splits the regions at both marquee boundaries automatically.' Per the only evidence on offer, clicking any region other than the top one does NOT split - it DRAGS the entire multi-track selection to wherever the reader clicked. That is a destructive misfire on a trick badged 'GAME CHANGER': a buyer following it literally on a multi-track marquee will move their audio, not cut it, and will reasonably call the book inaccurate. Secondary problem: the source is an undated Sound On Sound Logic column with no version label, so even the corrected behaviour is not confirmed for 10.7/11/12 specifically. CORRECTION (externally sourced, soundonsound.com/techniques/marquee-tool-tips-logic): retitle to 'Click the TOP region after marqueeing to split at the marquee edges' and add to the body: 'On a marquee spanning several tracks, click the topmost region in the selection - clicking a lower one moves the whole selection to the click position instead of splitting it.' With that caveat in the body copy the trick is sound; as written it is not.

downgrades.title: Marquee inside a take folder to edit, not to comp
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote is reconstructed, not real page text. The auditor quotes logicstudiotraining.com as saying 'You can deactivate Quick Swipe Comping and enable cutting and editing tools (such as the Scissors and Marquee tools) by pressing the Quick Swipe Comping button.' I searched that exact page. What it actually describes is toggling via 'the down pointing triangle in the upper right corner of the Take Folder' or the key command Option-Q, and it names the SCISSORS tool - 'Quick Swipe Comping mode must not be active to utilize the capability of cutting take folders with the Scissors tool.' The Marquee, which is the entire claim under test, was not confirmed anywhere in the returned text, and the 'Quick Swipe Comping button' mechanism does not match the page's own description. The quote reads as memory dressed as a citation. Three further failures: (1) the source is a single wiki, not the two independent reputable sources the rules require, and a wiki is the weakest tier; (2) 'Logic Studio' was Apple's Logic 8/9-era bundle (2007-2011), so this is a pre-Logic-Pro-X page being used to verify a claim about 10.7/11/12 - the exact version trap flagged in the brief; (3) the auditor's reason says 'Apple/Logic Studio Training document the two take-folder modes' but no Apple URL was ever cited. The trick also asserts unverified specifics of its own: 'Comping is swiping with the Pointer while Quick Swipe Comping is on' names a tool no cited source names. SALVAGE - keep the toggle, drop the tool list: 'A take folder has two modes. With Quick Swipe Comping on, dragging across takes builds a comp. Switch it off from the menu in the take folder's top-right corner, and the folder stops behaving like a comping surface and starts behaving like a region you can cut and edit. If your edits inside a take folder keep turning into comp swipes, this toggle is why.' That version asserts only the mode toggle and drops the unproven claim that the Marquee specifically becomes available.

downgrades.title: ⌥‑drag a marquee selection to copy that time range
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own reason concedes the case: 'no source I found tests MIDI specifically' - yet the body copy states the trick 'Copies the audio AND MIDI inside the marquee', and it was still cleared VERIFIED. A verdict of VERIFIED requires the source to support the claim exactly as written; half the claim is admittedly unsupported. Additional defects: (1) the reason claims 'Two independent reputable Logic sources' but only one URL and one quote were supplied, and the second was never named - a bare assertion of corroboration is not corroboration; (2) I confirmed the Sound On Sound 'healed' sentence is real at soundonsound.com/techniques/marque-distinction, but I could not establish a publication year for it, and its punning Logic-column style points to a pre-10.7 era, so it is not version-matched to 10.7/11/12; (3) the body promises the copy lands 'without disturbing the surrounding regions', while the quoted source only supports the SOURCE area being healed - it says nothing about what happens to existing regions at the DESTINATION, where a dropped copy will overlap whatever is already there. SALVAGE - keep the sourced half, drop the MIDI claim and the destination over-promise: 'Hold Option and drag a marquee selection with the Pointer to copy that slice of audio elsewhere in the timeline. The cuts left behind in the original marquee area heal automatically, so the source material is left as you found it. Check what is already sitting at the destination before you drop, and audition the result.' That keeps the useful move and asserts only what the source states.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout; support.apple.com is egress-blocked for WebFetch, so all Apple evidence comes from search snippets that quote the guide pages directly. 21 searches used, covering: Show Automation/A key, track vs region automation, Mix > Convert Automation, automation modes (Read/Touch/Latch/Write/Trim/Relative), Mix > Delete Automation, Automation settings pane, Select/copy/move automation, Control-Shift curve drag, marquee boundary points, Command-click tool assignment, Snap Automation, Pencil tool, automation lanes disclosure triangle, plug-in bypass automation, Delete Redundant Automation Points. Genuinely unresolved after searching (marked UNVERIFIABLE, not skipped): (a) whether ⌘-drag is the *default* marquee shortcut — Apple documents the Command-click tool as user-assignable and the tool menus only appear with Complete Features enabled, and a Logic Pro Help thread exists titled "Why am I not getting the marquee tool as a shortcut when I hit Command?"; (b) whether Mix > Show Automation or a disclosure arrow reveals *every* automated parameter (the disclosure-triangle/Option-click behaviour is documented only in the Logic Pro 9 manual and secondary sites, and it is at the lower-left of the track header, not "the bottom of an open automation lane"); (c) whether plug-in bypass is automatable for *every* plug-in (forum-level evidence only, plus reports of slot-specific and 11.2 version bugs); (d) whether a whole-project "delete all automation" command exists — Apple's Delete automation page lists only the three "…on Selected Track" variants in every snippet returned. One further caveat not counted as a verdict: Apple's Delete automation page never lists "Delete Redundant Automation Points" under Mix > Delete Automation; the command's existence is confirmed only as a key command (⌃⌫) via studio-interns.com, so the menu path in that trick may also be wrong.

tricks.title: Know the difference between Track and Region automation
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the A key opens automation view and confirms both mechanisms exactly as described (track automation stays fixed to the timeline, region automation travels with the region). Caveat worth a copy tweak: Apple's wording for the switch is the automation controls in the track header; the Apple page does not literally say "dropdown", that wording is supported only by secondary sources (skydocu mirror of Logic Pro Help, dummies.com).
tricks.evidence_quote: With track automation, if you re-record, move, or copy regions (either to another point on the same track or to another track entirely) the automation data remains tied to the initial point on the track in which it was created. However, with region automation … if you move or copy the region (either to another point on the same track, or to another track) the automation remains with the region. [and, from the Show automation curves page:] choose Mix > Show Automation (or press A)

tricks.title: Use Region automation for anything that belongs to the part
tricks.reason: Apple's track-vs-region page states exactly this behavioural difference, and specifically recommends region automation for instrument parameters — which is what a filter sweep inside a synth riff is.
tricks.evidence_quote: with region automation … if you move or copy the region (either to another point on the same track, or to another track) the automation remains with the region. Region automation is particularly useful when you are automating instrument parameters.

tricks.title: Convert between the two without redrawing
tricks.reason: The menu path and the exact command name are confirmed, and the reverse command exists too (four commands total: Convert Visible/All Track Automation to Region Automation, and Convert Visible/All Region Automation to Track Automation). FLAG for the owner: the trailing sentence "Nothing is lost either way" is not stated by any source found and is the one clause a buyer could argue with — recommend softening it to "the curves are carried over rather than redrawn".
tricks.evidence_quote: "Convert Visible Track Automation to Region Automation" is a command found in the Mix > Convert Automation submenu that converts displayed track automation to region automation … "Convert Visible Region Automation to Track Automation" … "Convert All Track Automation to Region Automation" … "Convert All Region Automation to Track Automation"

tricks.title: Press A to toggle automation view
tricks.reason: Apple's Show automation curves page gives the A key command explicitly alongside the menu route, for the 10.7 guide and the current (11.x/12) guide alike.
tricks.evidence_quote: To show automation in Logic Pro, you can choose Mix > Show Automation (or press A).

tricks.title: Use Latch mode for almost everything
tricks.reason: All four mode descriptions match Apple's own definitions: Latch holds the new value after release, Touch returns to existing automation, Write erases, Read plays back only. "Latch is the right default" is opinion and not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: Read: Plays back all automation that exists on the track … You can't change the value … Touch: … After the fader or knob is released, the parameter follows existing automation on the track. Latch: Works like Touch mode, but after the fader or knob is released, the new parameter value replaces existing automation on the track.

tricks.title: Never leave a track in Write mode
tricks.reason: Apple documents exactly the destructive behaviour claimed, including erasure when you touch nothing at all. The "destroyed more mixes than any other setting" line is rhetoric, not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Write mode, existing track automation data is erased as the playhead passes it. If you move any of the Mixer's controls, this movement is recorded; if you don't, existing data is simply deleted as the playhead passes it.

tricks.title: Draw automation with the Pencil tool for precision
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Pencil tool as the tool for drawing series of automation points (with curved/stepped variants governed by the Automation settings). The comparative claim ("faster and more accurate than performing it") is taste, and the mechanism it rests on is confirmed.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can use the Pencil Tool to draw multiple automation points on an automation curve. With Logic Pro in automation mode, click-drag or Option-click-drag the Pencil Tool across the automation curve.

tricks.title: Delete an automation point without dragging it
tricks.reason: All three methods named in the trick appear verbatim in Apple's Delete automation page: double-click, select then Delete, and the Eraser tool.
tricks.evidence_quote: With Logic Pro in automation mode, you can double-click the automation point, select the automation point then press Delete, or drag across the automation point with the Eraser tool.

tricks.title: Curve any line by dragging its middle with ⌃⇧
tricks.reason: The modifier in the k field matches Apple exactly (Control-Shift drag with the Pointer tool on the curve between two points), and it holds for the 10.7 and current guides.
tricks.evidence_quote: Hold down Control-Shift while dragging an automation curve with the Pointer tool. An automation curve between two automation points represents continuously changing parameter values.

tricks.title: Trim automation up or down as a group
tricks.reason: Two problems against Apple's own text. (1) There is no standalone "Trim mode" to sit in — Apple states Trim "works in combination with Touch and Latch automation modes", so the reader following this will look for a mode that does nothing on its own. (2) Apple restricts Trim to Volume, Pan and Send levels, and describes it as offsetting by the amount you move the control as you pass over the automation — not as shifting "the entire existing automation curve" in one gesture, which is what the 1 dB vocal example implies.
tricks.evidence_quote: Trim: Offsets the value of the existing automation (Volume, Pan, Send levels) by adjusting it up or down by the amount you move the fader or control. Works in combination with Touch and Latch automation modes.
tricks.correction: Trim is not a mode on its own — you switch it on in combination with Touch or Latch. Once it is on, moving the fader offsets the existing automation up or down by the amount you move, keeping the shape of the curve, and it applies to Volume, Pan and Send levels. Run the section you want to lift with Trim Latch engaged to push a whole automated vocal up by a decibel.

tricks.title: Use Relative mode to layer a second pass
tricks.reason: Apple describes Relative exactly as an added secondary curve that offsets the existing primary curve, i.e. the original moves survive. Worth knowing (not contradicted by the trick): Apple scopes it to Volume, Pan and Send levels, and it combines with Touch, Latch and Write.
tricks.evidence_quote: Relative: Adds a secondary automation curve that offsets the existing primary curve for the selected parameter (Volume, Pan, Send levels). Works in combination with Touch, Latch, and Write automation modes.

tricks.title: Marquee a range then drag the line to change only that section
tricks.reason: The body copy is confirmed — Apple states that editing automation spanned by a marquee selection auto-creates points at both edges, so the change cannot bleed outwards. What I could NOT confirm is the k field, "⌘ + drag": Apple documents the Command-click tool as something you assign yourself ("click the Command-click Tool menu, then choose a tool"), the Command-click/Right-click Tool menus only appear when Complete Features is enabled in Preferences > Advanced, and a Logic Pro Help thread exists titled "Why am I not getting the marquee tool as a shortcut when I hit Command?". No source found says Marquee is the factory default for Command-click, so the shortcut as printed will fail for some buyers.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you edit automation data that is spanned by a marquee selection, two automation points are automatically created at the left edge, and two at the right edge, of the selection.
tricks.salvage: Select the Marquee tool and drag across the bars you want to change, then drag the automation line inside that selection. Logic creates two automation points at each edge of the marquee automatically, so the change is boxed in and does not bleed into the surrounding bars. If you have assigned Marquee as your Command-click tool (Logic Pro > Preferences > Advanced must have the full feature set enabled for that menu to appear), you can hold Command to grab it without switching tools.

tricks.title: Show every automated parameter at once
tricks.reason: Two unsupported specifics. Apple documents Mix > Show Automation only as showing automation curves (the same thing A does) — nothing found says it reveals every parameter containing data. And the disclosure control that opens extra lanes is at the lower left of the track header, not "at the bottom of an open automation lane"; a single click opens one further lane, and it is Option-click that opens many lanes for already-recorded parameters. That behaviour is documented in the Logic Pro 9 manual and repeated on dummies.com and LogicProGEM, but I found no current-guide (10.7/11/12) Apple confirmation, so the version status is unproven.
tricks.evidence_quote: To display additional automation lanes, click the disclosure triangle to the lower left of a track name, which opens a separate automation sub-lane, below the track … Option-click the (closed) triangle to open up to 30 automation subtracks, which will display existing (already recorded) automation data.
tricks.salvage: Press A to show automation, then click the small disclosure triangle at the lower left of the track header to open an extra automation lane underneath the track. Repeat it to stack more lanes, and pick the parameter for each lane from the automation parameter pop-up menu in its header — that way you can see several written parameters side by side instead of flipping between them.

tricks.title: Copy automation between tracks
tricks.reason: Apple's procedure explicitly has you move the playhead to the insertion point first, and states the paste lands at the playhead position — not at the same timeline position it was copied from. A buyer following the trick as written will get the automation dropped wherever the playhead happens to be.
tricks.evidence_quote: Drag across the region with the Marquee tool. Choose Edit > Copy from the Tracks area menu bar. Select the track you want to copy the automation data to, then move the playhead to the insertion point. Choose Edit > Paste from the Tracks area menu bar. The region selection, along with its automation, is copied to the target track at the playhead position.
tricks.correction: Drag across the range with the Marquee tool and choose Edit > Copy. Select the destination track, move the playhead to the point where you want the data to start, then choose Edit > Paste — the automation lands at the playhead, so park the playhead deliberately (or set it from the original selection first) if you want the copy to sit at the same bar.

tricks.title: Delete all automation on a track in one command
tricks.reason: The named command is confirmed verbatim — Mix > Delete Automation > Delete All Automation on Selected Track. But the second sentence is not: every snippet of Apple's Delete automation page lists only three commands, all scoped to the selected track (Delete Visible / Delete All / Delete Orphaned Automation on Selected Track). No whole-project equivalent turned up in the current guide, so "Also available for the whole project" is an unsupported claim a buyer can check in ten seconds.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, you can choose options from Mix > Delete Automation: Delete Visible Automation on Selected Track removes automation for the active automation parameter; Delete All Automation on Selected Track removes all automation from the selected track; and Delete Orphaned Automation on Selected Track removes all orphaned automation from the selected track.
tricks.salvage: Mix > Delete Automation > Delete All Automation on Selected Track wipes every parameter on that track in one move. The same submenu also holds Delete Visible Automation on Selected Track, which clears only the parameter currently displayed, and Delete Orphaned Automation on Selected Track for data left behind by plug-ins you have removed.

tricks.title: Automation follows regions if you tell it to
tricks.reason: The setting name, its location in the Automation settings pane, and all three pop-up values (Never / Always / Ask) are confirmed, as is the described behaviour of dragging a region taking its automation along.
tricks.evidence_quote: The "Move Track Automation with Regions" pop-up menu determines what happens to automation data when you move regions … Never: Doesn't move automation when you move regions. Always: Always moves automation when you move regions. Ask: A dialog prompts you to move the automation data—or leave it where it is—whenever you move a region.

tricks.title: Thin dense automation after recording a controller pass
tricks.reason: The command exists, but not as the trick describes it. Delete Redundant Automation Points is global — it removes redundant points on all regions and all tracks — so "Select the range, then …" is misleading: the selection does not scope it, and a reader will unknowingly rewrite automation across the whole project. Separately, Apple's Delete automation page does not list this command under Mix > Delete Automation at all (it lists only the three Selected Track commands); the command is documented as a key command, ⌃⌫.
tricks.evidence_quote: Delete Redundant Automation Points ⌃⌫ … removes all redundant automation points on all regions and tracks.
tricks.correction: Recording modwheel or a fader creates thousands of points. Delete Redundant Automation Points (key command Control-Delete) strips the points that do not change the shape of the curve — but note it is a global command: it acts on all regions and all tracks, not just the range you have selected. To thin one passage only, select the points in that range with the Marquee or Pointer tool and press Delete, then redraw.

tricks.title: Snap automation to the grid when it needs to be rhythmic
tricks.reason: Automation does not simply obey the same Snap setting as regions. Apple documents a separate Snap Automation submenu inside the Snap pop-up with its own value, set independently in the Tracks area and the Piano Roll Editor. A reader who sets the region Snap value expecting automation to follow will not get the behaviour promised.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose Snap Automation from the Snap pop-up menu and select a value from the submenu, after which automation edits snap to the value chosen in the Snap Automation submenu … it can be set independently in the Tracks area and the Piano Roll Editor
tricks.correction: Automation snaps to its own grid value, set separately from regions: open the Snap pop-up menu in the Tracks area, choose Snap Automation, and pick a value from the submenu. Automation edits then snap to that value, and you can set it independently in the Tracks area and the Piano Roll Editor — so your filter stabs land on the beat without changing how regions snap.

tricks.title: Automate plugin bypass for effect changes
tricks.reason: No Apple guide page found that states plug-in bypass is an automatable parameter, let alone that it is available for every plug-in. Support for the practice is forum-level only (Logic Pro Help, Logic Users Group), and the same searches surfaced counter-reports — a Gearspace thread "Can't automate plugin bypass on 6th plugin slot" and an Apple Community thread about bypass automation breaking in Logic Pro 11.2 (reportedly fixed in 11.2.1). The universal "Every plugin's bypass state is automatable" is exactly the kind of absolute a buyer can disprove with one plug-in.
tricks.evidence_quote: select the lane for "insert bypass," which is one of the parameters for an effect and works the same way as any other parameter
tricks.salvage: Insert bypass usually appears in the track's automation parameter pop-up menu alongside the plug-in's own parameters, so you can switch an effect in and out on the timeline. Automating a delay in and out this way is cleaner than riding its mix knob. Check the parameter list for the slot in question before you commit to the approach — bypass is not exposed identically for every plug-in and every insert slot.

tricks.title: Automate send levels rather than plugin mix knobs
tricks.reason: Pure workflow preference. The only underlying assertions — that a send has a fader on the mixer and its own automation lane — are generic and not the sort of specific, checkable claim a buyer would dispute. Nothing here asserts a menu path, key command, version or mechanism.
