Rewrite to the Apple-documented wording - choose a source from the Input pop-up menu, arm Monitor, set Record Start to threshold if you want it to trigger itself - and drop the specific 'or a bus' promise unless it can be sourced.

downgrades.title: Turn on Loop with crossfade for infinite sustain
downgrades.reason: Classic adjacent-evidence pass. The quote establishes only that a crossfade marker can be dragged to smooth the loop join and that Linear and Equal Power crossfade types exist. It does not support either load-bearing instruction in the trick: it never mentions the Loop mode pop-up the reader is told to switch on, and it says nothing about sustaining a note indefinitely. The auditor's bridge - 'Classic mode sustains for as long as the key is held subject to the envelope, so the hold it forever framing is fair' - is model memory, not a source, and is exactly the reasoning pattern this audit exists to catch (whether the note actually sustains depends on the amp envelope's sustain level, which the trick does not mention). Salvageable as the crossfade half only, which is genuinely documented.

downgrades.title: Use the Sample Start modulation for variation
downgrades.reason: Neither routing the trick recommends is actually in the evidence. The first quoted sentence says Sample Start can be QUANTIZED in musical values - that is a different statement from 'velocity can modulate Sample Start'. The second quoted sentence is generic Mod Matrix boilerplate about available control sources and does not tie velocity to the Sample Start target. And the auditor states outright that randomness comes from 'the LFO's random waveform' while quoting nothing whatsoever for it - an unsourced claim promoted into a VERIFIED verdict. The two halves have been welded together with an ellipsis to look like one supporting passage.

downgrades.title: Reverse the sample for instant risers
downgrades.reason: Quote appears reconstructed. I re-searched the exact page cited (quick-sampler-waveform-display-lgcp4492eed9) and the documented contents that surface are the zoom control, blue start/end markers, yellow loop markers and trackpad navigation; no 'Playback button activates forward or reverse playback' text appeared, and the search explicitly reported that a dedicated forward/reverse Playback button was not found on that page. Absent that, there is no external support for 'one button reverses the sample'. Compounding the risk, the auditor itself notes a separate Reverse LOOP mode exists - so a reader hunting for an unnamed 'reverse button' has a documented wrong control sitting right next to it. Default verdict applies: no source, no clearance.

downgrades.title: Use the Filter and its envelope, not an insert plugin
downgrades.reason: The auditor disclosed the fatal gap and then cleared it anyway: Apple's 'affects each voice independently' sentence is about DRIVE, not about the filter section. The trick's whole argument is that the filter is per-voice whereas a channel-strip insert acts on the summed output, and no quoted line states that. Keyscale and a filter-envelope Vel slider are consistent with per-voice behaviour but do not assert it - that inference is the auditor's, not Apple's. The useful, safe residue is factual and quotable (the filter envelope has its own Vel amount and a Keyscale control that varies cutoff by keyboard position); the sweeping architectural claim about inserts is not.

downgrades.title: Save your instrument as a patch immediately
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote is doctored and the trick contains a false claim the auditor waved through. Apple's actual Save custom patches page does not say patches are 'comprised of a Quick Sampler instrument and associated plug-in settings' - the guide's wording is about channel strips and their plug-in settings, and Quick Sampler has been inserted into the quote to make it fit the trick. Apple also places the control differently: 'click the Save button in the lower-right corner of the Library', not 'at the bottom of the Library pane'. Separately, the auditor concedes the book's line that the instrument 'exists only in that one session' is untrue, since plug-in state is stored in the project file - and then rated it VERIFIED regardless. That sentence is a factual assertion about what Logic does and it is wrong. Correction is Apple-sourced: click the Save button in the lower-right corner of the Library and name the patch; after the first save a User Patches folder appears in the Library and the patch can be used in ANY Logic Pro project - cross-project reuse is the real reason to save, not data loss.

downgrades.title: Use one Quick Sampler per element rather than one big kit
downgrades.reason: Not pure taste - it smuggles in a mechanism claim. The advice only holds because separate software instrument instances are asserted to land on separate channel strips and therefore get separate inserts and separate automation lanes; the auditor waved this through as 'definitional to how Logic's mixer is built', which is the everyone-knows-this reasoning the brief bans as evidence. No source was cited for it. This is my weakest downgrade and the easiest to rescue: strip the mechanism sentence and it becomes clean advice-only copy that no buyer can dispute, or source the channel-strip behaviour from the Apple guide and restore it as a genuine VERIFIED claim.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout; I used my full ~20-search budget and covered every trick in section 15 — none were left unchecked for budget reasons. WebFetch was not used (egress-blocked), so all evidence comes from WebSearch snippets, most of which quote support.apple.com Logic Pro User Guide pages directly. Two claims could not be settled from Apple's own pages and are marked UNVERIFIABLE rather than guessed: (a) whether the Mixer's channel-strip filter buttons specifically include Bus, VCA and Master buttons — Apple confirms filter buttons exist and that Option-clicking one isolates a type, but no snippet enumerated the button labels; (b) whether right-clicking a Send slot is the documented way to switch pre/post fader — Apple's "Route audio via send effects" page describes clicking the Send knob/slot to open a pop-up menu and lists THREE modes (Post Pan, Post Fader, Pre Fader), not a two-way pre/post switch. Two tricks are flatly contradicted by Apple: the "no equivalent mute-everything click" claim (Apple documents Command-click on a Mute button switching all matching Mute buttons) and the VCA "sends are untouched" claim (Apple states post-fader send amounts follow VCA group volume changes). Version exposure: all Apple pages consulted were the current /mac guide or the 10.7 guide, and no claim in this section depends on a feature introduced after 10.7, so the 10.7/11/12 coverage claim is not at risk here. No group-level "path" fields exist in this file.

tricks.title: X toggles the Mixer, and it remembers your scroll position
tricks.reason: The key command half is externally supported — multiple approved sources (macprovideo.com and whylogicprorules.com key-command round-ups, plus several cheat sheets) state that X is the Show/Hide Mixer key command. But the trick's headline promise, that the Mixer 'remembers your scroll position' across toggles, has no external support at all: no Apple page and no reputable Logic source found describes scroll-position persistence. That is a concrete, testable behavioural claim and it is exactly the kind of thing a buyer would try once and dispute. Marked UNVERIFIABLE for the scroll claim, not for X.
tricks.evidence_quote: Based on the search results, pressing X toggles the Mixer in Logic Pro X. More specifically, X is the key command for Show/Hide Mixer.
tricks.salvage: Press X to show and hide the Mixer inside the main window. Flip between arrangement and mixer constantly — it costs nothing, and it is far faster than reaching for the menu.

tricks.title: Use the Single view to see one channel and its full signal path
tricks.reason: Apple's 'Change the Mixer view' page confirms both halves as written: the view buttons switch between Single, Tracks and All, and Single shows the signal flow of the channel strip belonging to the focused track — i.e. that channel plus the aux/bus/output strips it feeds. The book's phrasing ('the selected channel plus every bus it feeds') matches Apple's 'signal flow' definition. Minor wording note only: Apple says 'focused track', the book says 'selected channel'; in practice these are the same strip.
tricks.evidence_quote: To show the signal flow of the channel strip that corresponds to the focused track in the Tracks area, click the Single button. To show the signal flow of all channel strips that correspond to tracks in the Tracks area, click the Tracks button. To show the signal flow of all channel strips available in the project, click the All button.

tricks.title: Filter the mixer by channel type
tricks.reason: The mechanism is confirmed by Apple — filter buttons limit the Mixer to specific channel-strip types, clicking one shows or hides that type, and Option-clicking one isolates it. What is NOT confirmed is the trick's specific enumeration: 'audio, instrument, aux, bus, VCA and master'. No snippet returned the actual filter button labels. The one Apple-derived list I got back names Audio, Instrument, Aux, Master and MIDI as filterable types and does not mention Bus or VCA buttons, so the book's list may be partly invented and is at minimum unproven. Also unverified: that the buttons sit 'along the top of the Mixer' (Apple confirms they are Mixer filter buttons but the snippets did not place them). The advice itself is sound and the Option-click isolate gesture is a genuine, sourced improvement the trick is missing.
tricks.evidence_quote: Filter buttons are used to limit the channel strips displayed in the Mixer to specific types. In Logic Pro, you can click a filter button to show or hide the channel strip type. Additionally, Option-clicking a filter button shows that channel strip type while hiding all other channel strip types.
tricks.salvage: The Mixer's filter buttons limit the display to specific channel strip types. Click a filter button to show or hide that type — or Option-click one to show only that type and hide everything else in a single gesture. When you are setting up sends, Option-click the Aux filter to get a mixer of nothing but your effect returns. (Filtering requires Show Advanced Tools to be enabled in Settings > Advanced.)

tricks.title: ⌥‑click any control to reset it to default
tricks.reason: Partly supported, over-claimed as written. Approved sources (whylogicprorules.com, logicstudiotraining.com) confirm Option-clicking a fader sets it to 0 dB and Option-clicking a send dial sets it to 0 dB. Nothing external supports the two absolute statements the trick actually makes — 'any control' and 'Works on every control in the mixer' — and nothing external supports 'pans to centre'. Apple's own channel-strip pages document resetting via the Setting button menu (Reset Channel Strip), not via Option-click on individual controls, so the universal version of this claim is unproven. It carries a GAME CHANGER badge, which raises the stakes on the over-claim. Narrow it to what is sourced.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, you can hold the Option key and click a fader to set it to 0 dB (Unity Gain), which is the default/reset position. Additionally, you can Option-click send dials to set them to 0 dB.
tricks.salvage: Option-click a fader to snap it back to 0 dB unity, and Option-click a send dial to do the same. It is the fastest way to undo a level you have talked yourself into. To reset an entire strip rather than one control, click the Setting button at the top of the channel strip and choose Reset Channel Strip.

tricks.title: ⌥-click Solo for exclusive solo
tricks.reason: The first sentence is correct — Apple confirms Option-clicking an unsoloed channel strip solos it and unsolos every other channel strip. The trick then asserts 'There is no equivalent mute-everything click.' Apple's 'Mute and solo channel strips' page documents exactly such a gesture: Command-clicking a Mute button switches every Mute button that matches the clicked button's state, including the output and master strips. A reader is being told a capability does not exist when Apple documents it, which is a straight factual error and the kind a mixing reader will notice immediately.
tricks.evidence_quote: Press and hold Command while clicking the Mute button on a channel strip. All Mute buttons that match the state (muted or unmuted) of the clicked button also switch to its new state, including those on the output channel strip and the master channel strip.
tricks.correction: Option-clicking an unsoloed channel strip solos it and unsolos every other channel strip — one gesture to hear one thing. Option-clicking any active Solo button clears all solos at once. Mute has its own bulk gesture, using Command rather than Option: Command-click a Mute button and every Mute button currently in the same state flips with it, including the output and master strips.

tricks.title: Use VCA faders for level groups without changing routing
tricks.reason: The first half is right — Apple confirms a VCA channel strip changes the volume of each member channel, and VCAs do not sum audio through a bus, so no re-patching is required. But the trick's conclusion, 'so your existing routing and sends are untouched', is contradicted for sends. Apple states explicitly that with post-fader send effects the amount of signal a VCA-assigned channel sends to an effect follows the VCA group's volume changes. Since Logic's default send mode is Post Pan (also post-fader), this is the normal case, not an edge case: pull a VCA down and the reverb sends come down with it. Telling a mixer that sends are unaffected will cause real, audible surprises.
tricks.evidence_quote: adjusting the volume of a VCA channel strip changes the volume of each individual channel ... if you use post-fader send effects, the amount of signal sent to an effect by a channel assigned to a VCA group follows the VCA group volume changes
tricks.correction: A VCA controls the volume of each of its member channels without summing them through a bus, so nothing gets re-patched — your existing output routing stays exactly as it was. Be aware of one consequence, though: post-fader sends follow the VCA. Apple documents that the amount of signal a VCA-assigned channel sends to an effect tracks the VCA group's volume changes, so pulling a VCA down pulls its reverb and delay sends down too. Use pre-fader sends for anything that must stay constant regardless of the group level.

tricks.title: Use Summing Stacks for processing groups
tricks.reason: All three parts check out. Apple documents selecting tracks, creating a Track Stack, and choosing Summing Stack in the resulting dialog, and describes exactly the routing the trick promises — subtrack outputs routed to a bus whose destination aux becomes the main track, functioning as an audio subgroup you can process as a unit. The Shift-Command-D key command is corroborated by whylogicprorules.com (an approved source) and several independent shortcut references, all agreeing.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Track Stack dialog, to create a summing stack: Select Summing Stack, then click OK. ... Summing stacks let you combine multiple tracks and route their output to an audio subgroup. When you create a summing stack, the outputs from the subtracks are routed to a bus. The destination aux of the bus is assigned to the main track, which functions as an audio subgroup.

tricks.title: Create a send and Logic makes the aux for you
tricks.reason: Apple states directly that an aux channel strip is created automatically when a send assignment is made, and the trick's instruction to choose an UNUSED bus is precisely right — Apple's one exception is a bus already in use as an input source on another channel strip, which the trick's wording already sidesteps. The mechanism and the caveat both hold.
tricks.evidence_quote: An aux channel strip is created automatically when a send assignment is made from a channel strip, except when the chosen bus is already in use as an input source on another channel strip.

tricks.title: Set sends to pre‑fader for headphone mixes and effects that must stay constant
tricks.reason: Two problems, neither resolvable from the sources found. First, the gesture: the trick says 'Right-click a send to switch between pre and post fader', but Apple's 'Route audio via send effects' page documents clicking the Send knob to open the Send pop-up menu and choosing a signal flow option from there. No source found supports a right-click/Control-click route, so the stated gesture is unproven. Second, the framing: Logic has THREE send modes, not a pre/post binary — Post Pan, Post Fader and Pre Fader — and Post Pan is the one a new send lands on, so a reader looking for a two-item toggle will not find one. The underlying advice (pre-fader for cue mixes) is sound and is the standard reason pre-fader exists.
tricks.evidence_quote: click the Send knob to open the Send pop-up menu. From the Send pop-up menu, you can choose one of the three signal flow options for the send. Post Pan is one option where the signal is sent after the fader and the Pan knob ... Pre Fader: the signal is sent before the fader and Pan knob; the send signal is affected by neither volume nor pan adjustments
tricks.salvage: Logic gives every send one of three signal-flow modes, not two. Click the Send knob to open its pop-up menu and choose Post Pan (follows both fader and pan), Post Fader (follows the fader but not the pan), or Pre Fader (ignores both — the send level stays put no matter what you do to the channel's volume or pan). Post is what you want for reverb, so the effect tracks the part. Pre is what you want for a headphone cue mix, or for any effect that must stay constant while you ride the fader.

tricks.title: Copy a whole channel strip the reliable way
tricks.reason: Apple documents the exact route the trick gives: click the Setting button at the top of the channel strip, then choose Copy or Paste Channel Strip Setting from the pop-up menu. The claim that everything comes across is supported by the same menu offering narrower alternatives — Paste Plug-ins Only and Paste Sends Only — which only make sense as subsets of a full paste. The closing note about Option-dragging individual plugins between slots is independently confirmed on Apple's plug-ins page.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, click the Setting button at the top of the channel strip, then choose Copy or Paste Channel Strip Setting from the pop-up menu. The Settings button menu also includes several related options, such as Paste Plug-ins Only, Paste Sends Only

tricks.title: Colour your channels to match your regions
tricks.reason: Apple's 'Change track colors' page confirms the mechanism as stated: changing a track's colour also changes the colour of its corresponding Mixer channel strip, and the channel strip's Track Name field displays that colour. The second sentence is workflow taste and carries no checkable claim, so nothing there to fail.
tricks.evidence_quote: Changing the color of a track also changes the color of the corresponding channel strip in the Mixer. ... the Track Name field shows the track name and track color in the channel strip

tricks.title: Bypass with ⌥-click, browse with the slot arrows
tricks.reason: Both halves are documented by Apple on the same page. Option-clicking the plug-in slot bypasses that plug-in (no window opens), and hovering the slot reveals arrows at its right edge which you click to choose a replacement plug-in or No Plug-in. The key command field (Option + click) matches the body copy.
tricks.evidence_quote: Option-click the plug-in slot ... To replace a plug-in: Place the pointer over the plug-in slot, click the arrows that appear to the right, then choose a plug-in to replace the existing one. To remove a plug-in: ... then choose No Plug-in from the pop-up menu.

tricks.title: V hides every open plugin window at once
tricks.reason: V is confirmed as the global key command for toggling all plug-in windows by two separate searches returning independent sources that agree — a verbatim mirror of Apple's 'Key commands for Global Commands' page, logicprokeycommands.com's version-by-version listings, and the Apple Pro Training Series keyboard-shortcut appendix published via O'Reilly. The toggle-restores-them behaviour the trick describes is the documented function of the command. One caution for the author: because it is a global command it is user-remappable, but the default holds across the versions the book covers.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, the key command "V" is mapped to "Show/Hide All Plug-in Windows". This key command functions as a toggle ... the previous plugins that you had up will open or close.

tricks.title: Drag plugins between insert slots and between channels
tricks.reason: Apple documents dragging a plug-in up or down within a channel strip or to another channel strip to move it, with a guide line shown during the drag, and Option-dragging to copy. One precision the trick could add without changing its meaning: Apple specifies Option-dragging to an UNUSED slot for the copy, so dropping onto an occupied slot is not the documented copy target.
tricks.evidence_quote: To move a plug-in: Drag the plug-in up or down in the channel strip, or to another channel strip. ... To copy a plug-in: Press and hold Option and drag the plug-in to an unused slot.

downgrades.title: V hides every open plugin window at once
downgrades.reason: The auditor's provenance claim is false. He described afteraudio.com as 'a verbatim mirror of Apple's Key commands for Global Commands page' -- it is not Apple, it is a Shopify blog that reuses the page title, and its quoted prose ('the previous plugins that you had up will open or close') reads as AI-written blog copy rather than documentation. A dedicated search for the Apple page returned NO support.apple.com result for this command; the hits were gearspace, logicprohelp forums, editorskeys, unison-style listicles, and the two sources the auditor leaned on. Both of those are version-mismatched to the book's scope: logicprokeycommands.com is explicitly titled 'Logic Pro X Key Commands 10.0.7' and the O'Reilly appendix is the Apple Pro Training Series *Logic Pro X* keyboard-shortcut list -- Logic Pro X era, not 10.7/11/12. So there is no Apple source and no two version-matched reputable sources; the standard for VERIFIED is not met either way. Aggravating: the auditor himself notes V is a user-remappable Global command, so even the default is an assertion about a mutable default nobody has documented for the covered versions. SALVAGE: keep the advice, drop the letter -- rewrite as 'Logic can hide and restore all open plug-in windows in one move; find the command by opening Key Commands (Option-K) and searching for "plug-in windows", then note your own key on the spot -- it is a Global command and may already be remapped on your system.' That is checkable by the reader in their own copy and cannot go stale.

downgrades.title: Copy a whole channel strip the reliable way
downgrades.reason: The menu route (Setting button > Copy/Paste Channel Strip Setting) is genuinely Apple-documented and survives. The trick's payload claim -- that everything comes across -- does not, and the auditor reached it by INFERENCE, not evidence: he argued that 'Paste Plug-ins Only' and 'Paste Sends Only' 'only make sense as subsets of a full paste.' That is precisely the reasoning the brief bans, and it is contradicted externally. macprovideo.com (approved source), 'Demystifying Logic Pro X's Plug-In Settings, Channel Strip Settings & Patches': 'Patches include everything Channel Strip Settings do -- all front-panel settings for all the individual plug-ins in the strip -- but they also include the values of the other channel strip controls that are NOT part of a Channel Strip Setting -- Send settings, and Pan and Channel Fader values.' So pan and channel fader values are explicitly excluded from a Channel Strip Setting, and send behaviour is disputed enough to have its own long-running Logic Pro Help thread ('Channel Strip Settings not saving Sends'). A separate search of Apple's own 'Work with channel strip settings' page confirmed Apple never enumerates what a full paste carries. A buyer who copies a strip expecting the fader and pan to follow, and finds they do not, has exactly the complaint the owner is trying to avoid. CORRECTION (sourced): say that Copy/Paste Channel Strip Setting carries the strip's plug-ins -- instrument and effects -- and their settings, and note that pan and fader values are not part of a channel strip setting (they travel with a Patch instead). Do not claim sends transfer as part of the full paste; point readers at the explicit 'Paste Sends Only' item if they want sends.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; 16 of my ~20 budget used, every one landing on an Apple Logic Pro User Guide page (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/...), which is why the verified share here is far higher than sections 1-5. This section is structurally safer than the earlier ones: it is almost entirely about documented plug-in controls, contains only ONE key command (the Channel EQ ⌘-drag, which Apple documents verbatim), makes NO version claims, cites NO Settings/Display or View paths, and has no group-level "path" fields to check — so the two error veins that gutted sections 1-5 (version drift and menu-path drift) barely apply. Two flat contradictions found, both control-name inventions of exactly the "As Region Colour" type: Match EQ's slider is called Apply, not "amount", and Phat FX has no "magnetic saturator" module. Three residual soft spots I could not source and have flagged in the reasons rather than upgrading to WRONG, because the trick's headline claim is verified in each case: (a) Stereo Delay's copy omits that Stereo Link must be switched off before the two sides can hold different times — Apple documents Stereo Link, the trick does not, so a buyer following it literally will see both sides move together; (b) Space Designer's "any short audio file" is looser than Apple's "any mono, stereo, AIFF, SDII, or WAV file"; (c) the Limiter trick's 0.5 dB / 3 dB figures are editorial rules of thumb with no external source — only its "very end of the master" placement is Apple-documented. All plug-ins named (ChromaVerb, Phat FX, Remix FX, Vintage EQ Collection) shipped in 10.4 or earlier and are on Apple's current guide pages, so they are valid across 10.7, 11 and 12.

tricks.title: Compressor — switch the model, not just the settings
tricks.reason: Apple and multiple reputable Logic sources confirm exactly seven circuit types with the four named descriptions matching: Platinum Digital = clean, Studio FET = 1176-style fast/aggressive, Vintage Opto = vocals, Vintage VCA = SSL bus compressor.
tricks.evidence_quote: Logic Pro's Compressor offers the following circuit types: Platinum Digital, Studio VCA and FET, Classic VCA, and Vintage VCA, FET, and Opto. ... Platinum Digital: A clean-sounding compression type with a fast transient response ... Studio FET: Emulates the Universal Audio 1176. ... Vintage VCA: Based on the SSL buss compressor ... Vintage Opto: Optical compressors are known for their fast transient response and non-linear release handling, and are very clean and ideal for vocals and guitars.

tricks.title: Compressor — use the side‑chain filter before reaching for a multiband
tricks.reason: The Compressor's side chain section has documented filter state / mode (HP, BP, LP) / frequency / Q controls plus a Listen button, and the documented use case is precisely attenuating kick energy in the detector so it stops triggering reduction.
tricks.evidence_quote: The side-chain is the part of a compressor that detects and potentially filters the input signal before feeding it to the control circuit. Filter state buttons turn the sidechain filter on or off ... The HP (high-pass) mode can be used to adjust the frequency so that most of the kick drum's energy is attenuated.

tricks.title: Limiter — set it as a safety, not a loudness tool
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the checkable part — Limiter belongs as the last process in the chain and its job is reaching but not exceeding 0 dB. The specific 0.5 dB and 3 dB figures are unsourced editorial rules of thumb, not documented specs; they are taste rather than a refundable factual error, but the owner should not present them as spec.
tricks.evidence_quote: Limiter is used primarily when mastering, typically applied as the very last process in the mastering signal chain, where it raises the overall volume of the signal so that it reaches, but does not exceed, 0 dB.

tricks.title: Multipressor — use it to control one problem band only
tricks.reason: Multipressor is a four-band multiband compressor with a per-band Byp (Bypass) button, so bypassing all but one band is exactly the documented behaviour. The 'becomes a dynamic EQ' framing is analogy, not a false claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Multipressor splits the incoming signal into different frequency bands—up to four ... The Byp (Bypass) buttons enable you to bypass the selected frequency band.

tricks.title: Noise Gate — use the side chain to key one sound from another
tricks.reason: Apple's 'Use Noise Gate' page documents keying a gate from a different track's signal, with the side chain acting purely as a detector. Worth noting in copy that Logic only offers audio tracks and buses as side-chain sources, so the snare must be an audio track or bus.
tricks.evidence_quote: Insert a noise gate on the strings track, select the percussion track as the side-chain input to the noise gate, adjust the noise gate threshold so that the percussion sound triggers the opening and closing of the gate ... The side chain signal is used only as a detector/trigger.

tricks.title: Enveloper — reshape a transient without a compressor
tricks.reason: Apple describes Enveloper as shaping attack and release phases via two gain sliders either side of the display, independently of absolute input level, with 'adds snap to a drum sound' given as the headline use — matching the trick's soft-kick example.
tricks.evidence_quote: Enveloper is an unusual processor that lets you shape the attack and release phases of a signal—the signal transients ... The most important Enveloper parameters are the two Gain sliders, one on each side of the central display. These govern the Attack and Release levels ... Boosting the attack phase can add snap to a drum sound.

tricks.title: Channel EQ — turn on Analyzer and set it to Post
tricks.reason: Apple documents a dedicated Analyzer Pre/Post button whose Post setting shows the curve after EQ is applied, which is exactly the trick's claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Analyzer (Pre/Post) button can be set to display the frequency curve before or after EQ is applied, when Analyzer mode is active.

tricks.title: Channel EQ — drag the band’s vertical line sideways to set Q
tricks.reason: Every element checks out against Apple's Channel EQ parameters page: the vertical lines isolate Q, ⌘ constrains a drag to one axis (which is the k field), and Option-click resets a band. The only unsourced fragment is 'double-click a gain value to type it exactly', which is standard Logic numeric-field behaviour and carries no risk.
tricks.evidence_quote: To constrain dragging to vertical or horizontal movement, hold down Command while performing any operations on the Channel EQ bands. ... Drag the vertical lines that encompass the selected band to adjust the Q (bandwidth) only. ... If you ever need to reset a band entirely, simply Option-click it to restore it to its default settings.

tricks.title: Linear Phase EQ on the master, Channel EQ everywhere else
tricks.reason: Apple confirms Linear Phase EQ preserves phase coherency and 'introduces greater amounts of latency', and that Channel EQ's phase shift is 'often desirable' — which is the trick's exact framing. The CPU half is the softer claim: Apple states Linear Phase EQ uses a fixed (rather than band-dependent) amount of CPU, and the comparative sources agree it is the heavier plug-in, but Apple does not say 'more CPU' in those words.
tricks.evidence_quote: Linear Phase EQ uses different underlying technology to Channel EQ that preserves the phase of the audio signal ... This differs from Channel EQ, which can introduce phase shifts of the signal that can have an audible (and often desirable) effect on the sound. ... Linear Phase EQ introduces greater amounts of latency.

tricks.title: Vintage EQ Collection — three genuinely different colours
tricks.reason: Apple names exactly the three units in the trick (Console, Graphic, Tube) and confirms they are modelled on vintage hardware and carry the tonal character of the originals — each even has its own named output stage (Smooth / Punchy / Silky), which supports the 'character even with the controls flat' claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Logic Pro for Mac vintage EQ collection recreates three classic EQ units from the 50s, 60s, and 70s that can add color to your productions. The Vintage Tube EQ, Vintage Graphic EQ, and Vintage Console EQ plug-ins ... feature the distinct tonal characteristics of the original units.

tricks.title: Match EQ — steal a tone rather than guess at it
tricks.reason: The learn-reference / learn-current / build-the-difference mechanism is correct, but Match EQ has no 'amount slider'. Apple's control is the Apply slider — same class of error as the non-existent 'As Region Colour' option. The advice also misses that Apply goes above 100% to exaggerate and negative to invert, so 'never use it at 100%' understates the range.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Apply slider and field increase or decrease the impact of the EQ curve, with values greater than 100% magnifying the effect, values less than 100% reducing the effect, and negative values (−1% to −100%) inverting the peaks and troughs in the filter curve. ... Match EQ creates a filter curve based on the differences between the spectrum of the template and the current material.
tricks.correction: Learn the spectrum of a reference, learn your track, and Match EQ builds the curve between them from the difference. Then pull the Apply slider — Apple's name for it — back below 100%: values under 100% reduce the impact of the matched curve, and something around 40% usually keeps the tonal direction without the artefacts. Apply also runs past 100% to exaggerate the curve, and into negative values to invert its peaks and troughs. Use the Smoothing slider to coarsen the curve if it comes out too spiky.

tricks.title: ChromaVerb — use the Damping display as the main control
tricks.reason: Apple documents a Damping EQ overlaid on ChromaVerb's main display, explicitly frequency-dependent decay, editable by dragging the dots — including reducing how much of a given frequency stays in the decay, which is the trick's 'roll off the high end decay' move.
tricks.evidence_quote: The decay for certain frequencies is dependent on damping parameter values. A visualization of the reverb output is shown in a graphic display that allows you to directly edit damping factors, thus changing decay frequencies and dependencies. ... drag up or down to increase or decrease how much of that frequency is included in the reverb decay.

tricks.title: Space Designer — load your own impulse responses
tricks.reason: Apple confirms user IRs load via Sampled IR > Load IR and that ordinary audio files can serve as the IR. One tightening for the copy: Apple specifies mono/stereo AIFF, SDII or WAV rather than literally 'any' audio file, so a stray MP3 or M4A will not load.
tricks.evidence_quote: Any mono, stereo, AIFF, SDII, or WAV file can be used as an IR. ... click the Sampled IR button above the main display, then click the Sample IR pop-up menu and choose Load IR ... In Sampled IR mode, Space Designer loads and uses an impulse response recording ... convolved with the incoming audio signal.

tricks.title: Delay Designer — build rhythmic patterns, not echoes
tricks.reason: Apple's Tap parameter bar documents per-tap Cutoff and Resonance (filter), Transpose (pitch), Pan and Level alongside each tap's own delay time — exactly the five independent per-tap parameters the trick lists.
tricks.evidence_quote: Cutoff: Shows the highpass and lowpass filter cutoff frequencies of taps. ... Resonance (Reso): Shows the filter resonance value of each tap. ... Transpose (Transp): Shows the pitch transposition of each tap. ... Pan: Shows the pan parameter of each tap. ... Level: Shows the relative volume level of each tap.

tricks.title: Stereo Delay — set different times per side
tricks.reason: Apple confirms Delay, Feedback and Mix are settable separately per channel, with note values (including dotted) available when tempo-synced, so 1/8 left against dotted 1/8 right is achievable. Caveat the copy should carry: the Stereo Link button ties the two channels together, and it must be switched off before the sides will hold different times.
tricks.evidence_quote: Stereo Delay lets you set the Delay, Feedback, and Mix parameters separately for the left and right channels. You can set the delay time in milliseconds or in note values when synchronized with the project tempo. ... The Stereo Link button allows you to make corresponding parameter adjustments for both channels. Adjusting one channel value adjusts the other.

tricks.title: Tape Delay — turn up Flutter for analogue character
tricks.reason: Apple documents Flutter Rate and Flutter Intensity as simulating the speed irregularities of analogue tape transports, and the plug-in also carries the LFO modulation and Low/High Cut filtering the trick credits for separating it from a plain digital delay.
tricks.evidence_quote: Flutter Rate/Intensity knobs and fields simulate the speed irregularities of tape transports used in analog tape delay units. Flutter Rate: Set the speed variation. Flutter Intensity: Set the intensity of the "flutter" effect.

tricks.title: Phat FX — one plugin, an entire character chain
tricks.reason: Phat FX has no 'magnetic saturator'. Apple lists six modules — Band-pass, Distortion, Mod FX, Bass Enhancer, Compressor, Filter — and the Distortion module's types are Bitcrusher, Diode, Dirt, Downsampler, Grit, Scream, Soft Saturation, Tube and Vari Drive, none of them named Magnetic. The trick invents a module while omitting Bass Enhancer, the one that actually does the 'phat'.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Phat FX plug-in UI is divided into five key areas: six effects modules (Band-pass, Distortion, Mod FX, Bass Enhancer, Compressor, Filter), an assignable X/Y pad, three modulation sources (Env Follower, LFO1, LFO2), the Master section, and along the very bottom, the Effect Order Strip.
tricks.correction: Six effects modules in a single window — Band-pass, Distortion, Mod FX, Bass Enhancer, Compressor and Filter — plus an assignable X/Y pad, three modulation sources (Env Follower, LFO 1, LFO 2) and an Effect Order strip for reordering the chain. The Distortion module alone offers Bitcrusher, Diode, Dirt, Downsampler, Grit, Scream, Soft Saturation, Tube and Vari Drive. It is the fastest way to make a sterile synth interesting.

tricks.title: Remix FX — perform DJ effects live and record them
tricks.reason: All five effects named in the trick are documented Remix FX controls, and Apple frames the plug-in as real-time performance controls; 9to5Mac covers recording a Remix FX performance pass as automation.
tricks.evidence_quote: Remix FX includes a set of buttons, sliders, and XY pads you can use to control several real-time effects common to electronic and dance music. ... Filter: Removes frequencies above a cutoff frequency ... Gater: Select from options for note division ... Downsampler: Changes the resolution of incoming audio ... Reverse: Reverses playback of incoming audio. Tape Stop: Simulates the slow down and stop of the incoming audio.

tricks.title: Gain — use it to check phase, not just level
tricks.reason: Apple documents Phase Invert buttons on the Gain plug-in and gives multi-mic time-alignment problems as the stated use case, which is the trick's claim. Worth knowing that stereo instances have separate Left and Right buttons while mono instances have only one.
tricks.evidence_quote: Phase Invert Left/Right buttons: Invert the phase of the left and right channels, respectively. Inverting phase is useful for dealing with time alignment problems, particularly those caused by simultaneous recording with multiple microphones. ... Only one Phase Invert button is available in mono and mono to stereo modes.

tricks.title: Test Oscillator — reference tones for calibration
tricks.reason: Apple confirms sine and square waveforms plus white and pink noise, and a frequency field settable from 1 Hz to 22 kHz with a 1 kHz default — 'exact frequencies' as claimed. Needle Pulse (Dirac) is a fourth waveform the trick simply does not mention, which is an omission rather than an error.
tricks.evidence_quote: Waveform buttons select the waveform to use for test tone generation ... Sine Wave ... Square Wave ... Pink Noise ... White Noise ... The frequency knob and field set the frequency of the oscillator (the default is 1 kHz), and you can double-tap this field and enter a value ranging from 1 Hz to 22 kHz.

downgrades.title: Compressor — switch the model, not just the settings
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote is reconstructed, not quoted. Apple's Compressor main parameters page (lgcead9636ef) describes circuit types generically and never names third-party hardware: its actual Studio FET text is 'Field Effect Transistor compressors are known for their fast transient response. They can deliver a clean or colored tone (particularly in the midrange)... FET compressors are ideal for drums, vocals, guitars, and other signals with a fast attack phase' — not 'Emulates the Universal Audio 1176'. Worse, the auditor's 'Vintage Opto: ...known for their fast transient response... ideal for vocals and guitars' is that same Studio FET description reattributed to a different circuit type (optical compressors are the slow-responding ones), so the quote is internally corrupt. 'Vintage VCA: Based on the SSL buss compressor' likewise appears nowhere in Apple's text. Only the seven circuit-type names survive; every character/brand equivalence the trick actually trades on is unsourced. SALVAGE: keep 'Compressor is seven compressors in one — the Circuit Type menu at the top swaps the whole detection model, so audition Platinum Digital, Studio VCA, Studio FET, Classic VCA, Vintage VCA, Vintage FET and Vintage Opto on the same source before touching ratio or attack. Apple's own descriptions for each type are in the Compressor main parameters page.' Delete the 1176 / SSL / LA-2A equivalences and the per-type adjectives unless each is separately sourced.

downgrades.title: Limiter — set it as a safety, not a loudness tool
downgrades.reason: Two failures. First, the auditor's own reason concedes 'The specific 0.5 dB and 3 dB figures are unsourced editorial rules of thumb, not documented specs' — a trick cannot be VERIFIED while its only numeric, checkable content is admitted to be unsourced; that is the definition of UNVERIFIABLE, and 'taste rather than a refundable factual error' is not one of the available verdicts. Second, the quoted Apple sentence arguably cuts against the headline: Apple says Limiter 'raises the overall volume of the signal so that it reaches, but does not exceed, 0 dB' — i.e. Apple documents it as a loudness tool applied last, which does not support 'set it as a safety, NOT a loudness tool' as written. The evidence supports the placement claim only. SALVAGE: 'Apple documents Limiter as belonging at the very end of the chain: it is "typically applied as the very last process in the mastering signal chain, where it raises the overall volume of the signal so that it reaches, but does not exceed, 0 dB". Put it last, after your EQ and bus compression, and set the Output Level to the ceiling you want the master to respect.' Drop the 0.5 dB and 3 dB figures entirely, or label them explicitly as personal preference rather than spec.

downgrades.title: Channel EQ — drag the band’s vertical line sideways to set Q
downgrades.reason: The evidence_quote splices non-Apple text into a single quote attributed to one Apple URL. Searching the exact sentence 'If you ever need to reset a band entirely, simply Option-click it to restore it to its default settings' surfaces it in third-party Channel EQ blog write-ups (woodyardmusic, logicxx), and its conversational register ('If you ever need to... simply...') is not Apple guide style — Apple's pages use imperative parameter-table prose. So the Option-click-to-reset element rests on a single blog, which the audit rules say is not sufficient alone. On top of that, the auditor cleared 'double-click a gain value to type it exactly' with the reasoning 'standard Logic numeric-field behaviour and carries no risk' — that is precisely the assume-it-because-everyone-knows-it reasoning the brief bans as the bug. Only the Q half is genuinely Apple-sourced (Apple does document dragging the vertical lines that encompass the band to adjust Q only). SALVAGE: 'To change a band's Q without touching its gain or frequency, drag the vertical lines that encompass the selected band in the Channel EQ display — that adjusts the Q (bandwidth) only. Holding Command while dragging a band constrains the movement to one axis, so you can change frequency without nudging gain.' Cut the Option-click reset and the double-click-to-type line unless each can be pinned to an Apple page.

downgrades.title: Linear Phase EQ on the master, Channel EQ everywhere else
downgrades.reason: The auditor concedes in their own reason that 'Apple does not say "more CPU" in those words' and that the comparative sources 'agree it is the heavier plug-in' — but supplies no URL or quote for any of those comparative sources, so under the two-independent-sources rule none of them count. The CPU claim is not incidental: 'Channel EQ everywhere else' is the trick's whole recommendation, and CPU cost is the stated reason for it. Note also that the Apple fact the auditor gestures at — that Linear Phase EQ uses a fixed amount of CPU regardless of how many bands are active — is not the same proposition as 'Linear Phase EQ costs more CPU than Channel EQ', and on a track using few bands it points the other way. SALVAGE: 'Linear Phase EQ and Channel EQ are not the same plug-in with a different skin. Apple: Linear Phase EQ "preserves the phase of the audio signal", whereas Channel EQ "can introduce phase shifts of the signal that can have an audible (and often desirable) effect on the sound" — and Linear Phase EQ "introduces greater amounts of latency". Reach for Linear Phase EQ where phase coherency matters most and latency is tolerable (mastering, parallel/multi-mic material); use Channel EQ where you want the colour and the low latency.' Drop the CPU comparison unless it can be sourced.

downgrades.title: Vintage EQ Collection — three genuinely different colours
downgrades.reason: The quote supports the three plug-in names, the eras, and 'add color to your productions' — but not the trick's operative claim. The auditor's reason states the evidence 'supports the "character even with the controls flat" claim' via 'its own named output stage (Smooth / Punchy / Silky)' — those three words appear nowhere in the quoted text and no source is given for them; they were supplied from the auditor's memory and then used as the bridge to the conclusion. That is exactly the reconstruct-then-cite failure mode. 'Distinct tonal characteristics of the original units' is a general marketing sentence and does not establish that the plug-ins colour a signal at neutral settings, which is the falsifiable mechanism a buyer would test. SALVAGE: 'Logic ships three modelled vintage EQs — Vintage Tube EQ, Vintage Graphic EQ and Vintage Console EQ — recreating classic units from the 50s, 60s and 70s that, in Apple's words, "feature the distinct tonal characteristics of the original units". They are not interchangeable with Channel EQ: try the same boost on all three and pick by ear.' Remove the claim that they colour with the controls flat, and remove the Smooth/Punchy/Silky output-stage names unless each can be pinned to Apple's parameter pages.

downgrades.title: Space Designer — load your own impulse responses
downgrades.reason: Version mismatch — the exact failure mode the brief warns about. The quoted sentence 'Any mono, stereo, AIFF, SDII, or WAV file can be used as an IR' is Logic 9-era manual text (it survives at help.apple.com/logicpro/mac/9.1.6/.../chapter_12_section_2.html), not the current page the auditor cited. The live Apple 'Use impulse responses in Logic Pro for Mac' page reads instead: 'Any mono or stereo AIFF or WAVE file can be used as an impulse response. In addition, surround formats up to 7.1, discrete audio files, and B-format audio files that consist of a single surround impulse response can be used.' SDII (Sound Designer II) is gone and the surround/B-format capability is new — so the auditor's proposed 'tightening' would print a fifteen-year-old format list into a book covering 10.7 / 11 / 12. The Sampled IR > Load IR route itself is plausible but was cleared on the same stale page, so it needs re-sourcing against the current guide. SALVAGE: 'Space Designer is a convolution reverb, so it will play back any impulse response you give it, not just Apple's. Apple: "Any mono or stereo AIFF or WAVE file can be used as an impulse response", plus surround formats up to 7.1 and B-format files. Click the Sampled IR button above the main display, then use the IR pop-up menu to load your own file.' Do not tell readers SDII works, and do not say "any audio file" — MP3 and M4A are not on Apple's list.

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked throughout; 17 searches spent, aimed at the falsifiable items (key commands, menu paths, option names, bounce/export mechanics). Snippets quoting the Apple Logic Pro User Guide settled most of them. Three items rest partly on non-Apple sources and are flagged in their reasons: the Control-B assignment for Bounce Regions in Place (agreement across three third-party shortcut references, not found on an Apple page), the "no key command inserts a specific plug-in" finding (Apple documents only the manual slot workflow; the explicit "it does not exist" statements come from Gearspace/LogicProHelp/VI-Control), and "exported tracks start at bar 1" (Apple documents the export length options; the start-position statement comes from Peak-Studios and LogicProHelp). Pure-advice tricks were not searched. Nothing was left unchecked for budget reasons.

tricks.title: Open Key Commands with ⌥K and use the search box
tricks.reason: Apple confirms both halves: Option-K opens the Key Commands window, and that window has a search field for finding commands by name.
tricks.evidence_quote: To open the Key Commands window in Logic Pro, you can choose Logic Pro > Key Commands > Edit (or press Option-K), and the Key Commands window opens. … click All at the top of the window, then enter a search term in the search field.

tricks.title: Export your key commands and back them up
tricks.reason: Version trap. 'Options menu with Export' is the Logic 9-era wording. In the 10.7/11/12 guide the saving and importing of key command sets lives in the Actions pop-up menu at the top left of the Key Commands window, and the export command is 'Save As', not 'Export'. A reader hunting an Options > Export item in a current version will not find it.
tricks.evidence_quote: Click the Actions pop-up menu in the top left of the Key Commands window, then choose Save As. You can save the current key command assignments to any location using the dialog that appears. The default location is ~/Music/Audio Music Apps/Key Commands. … click the Actions pop-up menu in the top left of the Key Commands window, then choose Import Key Commands.
tricks.correction: In the Key Commands window, click the Actions pop-up menu at the top left and choose Save As to write your whole key command set to a file (the default location is ~/Music/Audio Music Apps/Key Commands). Choose Import Key Commands from the same menu to load it back after a reinstall, or on someone else's machine. Losing a year of custom shortcuts to a reinstall is entirely avoidable.

tricks.title: Assign key commands to your most used plugins
tricks.reason: Logic has no key command that inserts a named plug-in on the selected channel. Apple documents only the manual route (click an Audio Effect slot, choose from the pop-up menu); the explicit 'no such key command exists' statements come from three independent Logic forums (Gearspace, LogicProHelp, VI-Control), which also list the real workarounds. A buyer who opens Key Commands and searches for their favourite EQ will find nothing to assign.
tricks.evidence_quote: There are no available key commands for this function, as Logic would need to know which plugin you want to insert and would require multiple key commands—one for each potential plugin slot. … The standard method remains manual: click an Audio Effect slot, then choose a plug-in from the pop-up menu.
tricks.correction: Logic has no key command that inserts a specific plug-in, so get the speed a different way: save the plug-in (or a whole chain) as a channel strip setting and recall it from the channel strip's Settings menu, which inserts every associated plug-in in one click. If you want it on a physical button, assign a controller button to the relevant key command in the Controller Assignments window.

tricks.title: Use Touch Bar or a stream deck for tool switching
tricks.reason: The Touch Bar half is not how Logic works. Apple documents Logic's Touch Bar as a fixed set of Logic-specific screens (Smart Controls, keyboard, drum pads, Configuration/Overview navigation) — there is no facility to put arbitrary assigned key commands on it, so 'any command with a key assignment can be triggered' is false for the Touch Bar. The external-hardware idea is sound for a Stream Deck or a MIDI controller, and Apple does document assigning controller buttons to key commands.
tricks.evidence_quote: When you tap the Smart Controls button in Logic Pro, the following controls appear in the Touch Bar. … When you tap the Keyboard button, you can use the Touch Bar to play the current patch on the selected software instrument track. … When you tap the Drum Pads button, you can use the Touch Bar to play the drums on a Drummer or software instrument track
tricks.correction: Logic's Touch Bar screens are fixed (Smart Controls, keyboard, drum pads, project overview), so you cannot put your own key commands there. For hardware triggering, use a Stream Deck sending the keystroke, or assign a controller button directly to a key command in the Controller Assignments window — search the command by name in the Search field, then press the button. Tools, zoom levels and transport are the highest-value candidates.

tricks.title: Build separate templates for writing, mixing and mastering
tricks.reason: Pure workflow advice about how to organise your own starting points. No menu path, key command, version claim or mechanism assertion to check.

tricks.title: Use Project Alternatives instead of Save As
tricks.reason: The behaviour described is right but the menu path is not what Apple prints. Apple's guide gives the path as File > Project Alternatives, not File > Alternatives. Everything else in the trick (one project, shared assets) is confirmed by the same page.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative. … You can create alternative versions of a project, each with a unique name and different settings. … They're saved as part of the project and share the same assets.
tricks.correction: File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative keeps every version inside one project, and Apple's guide is explicit that alternatives "are saved as part of the project and share the same assets" — so you are not duplicating 4 GB of recordings to try a different arrangement.

tricks.title: Turn on “Copy external audio files to project folder”
tricks.reason: The option name and the Assets settings location are both confirmed by Apple, as is the reason given for using it.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose File > Project Settings > Assets (or use the Open Assets Project Settings key command), then select any of the copy checkboxes to copy the respective file types to the project. Files are copied into the project when the project is saved. Saving assets in the project ensures that they are still available when you move or copy the project to another location.

tricks.title: Consolidate before archiving
tricks.reason: Menu path, effect and the archiving use case all match Apple. One small imprecision worth knowing but not worth a refund: Consolidate lets you select which asset types to copy rather than automatically taking every one, and the files land in the project's Media folder.
tricks.evidence_quote: In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Management > Consolidate (or use the Consolidate Project key command). … they are copied to the Media folder inside the project. … This ensures that if you move or copy the project to another computer, or archive the project for later use, the assets remain with the project

tricks.title: Keep a reference track in every project, muted at the top
tricks.reason: Studio-habit advice. Nothing asserted about how Logic behaves that a buyer could test and dispute.

tricks.title: Name your bounce files with the date
tricks.reason: File-naming advice with no claim about Logic's behaviour.

tricks.title: ⌘B bounces the project or the current section
tricks.reason: Command-B and the multi-format claim are both confirmed, but 'Set the locators first and Logic bounces exactly that range' is stated unconditionally and is not. Apple says a bounce covers the whole project by default and that the locators define the bounce range only when Cycle mode is on; otherwise you set the range with the Start and End sliders in the Bounce dialog. A reader who drags the locators with Cycle off gets a full-length bounce.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, when you bounce a project, the entire project from start to end is bounced, but you can bounce only part of a project by setting the bounce range before performing a bounce. When Cycle mode is on, the bounce range matches the locator positions. … select one or more destination formats in the Destination area.
tricks.correction: File > Bounce > Project or Section, or Command-B. By default Logic bounces the whole project; to bounce a section, turn Cycle mode on and the bounce range matches the locator positions, or set the range directly with the Start and End sliders in the Bounce dialog. Bounce multiple formats in one pass by selecting more than one destination in the Destination area.

tricks.title: Use “Bounce in Place” to commit a track to audio
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the File > Bounce > Track in Place route and the dialog options for effects and for volume/pan. The Control-B assignment for Regions in Place is not printed on the Apple page I could reach (it only says 'or use the corresponding key command'), but three independent third-party shortcut references agree on Control-B, with Control-Command-B for Track in Place — so the trick's ⌃B stands, though it is the weakest-sourced element here.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can choose File > Bounce > Regions in Place (or use the corresponding key command) … File > Bounce, which shows options including Regions in Place, Track in Place, Replace All Tracks, and Project or Section. … Bypass Effect Plug-ins: Select to bypass all plug-ins on the source track during the bounce process. … Include Volume/Pan Automation: Select to have volume and pan automation performed during the bounce process

tricks.title: Export all tracks as audio files for stems
tricks.reason: Apple confirms the exact menu path and one-file-per-track behaviour. The 'all starting at bar 1' part is supported by two independent third-party sources rather than by Apple, and it is the default rather than the only behaviour — the export dialog also offers trimming silence at the end, exporting only the cycle range, and extending file length to the project end, and the cycle-range option would not start at bar 1.
tricks.evidence_quote: choose File > Export > All Tracks as Audio Files. … export all tracks (all audio, software instrument, and Drummer tracks) in a project as audio files—one file per track. … All exported tracks will start at 1 1 1 1 (the project start) when using Export All Tracks as Audio Files.

tricks.title: Turn off “Normalize” when bouncing stems
tricks.reason: The Normalize control and its Off setting exist exactly where the trick says, in the export/bounce dialog, and Off is documented as 'the exported file is not normalized'. The rest is judgement, but the actionable instruction is correct.
tricks.evidence_quote: Off: The exported file is not normalized. Overload Protection Only: Allows downward normalization in case of overloads—levels above 0 dB, which would lead to clipping—but no normalization in case of lower levels. On: The exported file is normalized both for overloads and for lower levels.

tricks.title: Bounce offline unless you have external hardware
tricks.reason: The advice points the right way but two specifics are unsupported. Apple says offline 'can be faster than real time for more complex projects' — not that it always is — and says nothing anywhere I found about offline and realtime bounces being bit-identical, which is the claim a buyer is most likely to challenge. Apple's own limitation is broader than 'outboard gear': only internal sources can be bounced offline, so MIDI tracks and audio channel inputs also force a realtime bounce.
tricks.evidence_quote: Offline bouncing can be faster than real time for more complex projects, and can perform bounces not possible in real time (because they might exceed the processing power of your computer). … Only internal sources (audio or software instrument tracks) can be bounced offline; not MIDI tracks or audio channel inputs.
tricks.salvage: Bounce offline unless something outside the computer is involved. Apple's own wording is that offline bouncing "can be faster than real time for more complex projects, and can perform bounces not possible in real time". Realtime is required when the signal is not purely internal: only audio and software instrument tracks can be bounced offline, not MIDI tracks feeding external instruments or live audio channel inputs.

tricks.title: Add 2 bars of silence at the end of the bounce range
tricks.reason: The tail-clipping advice is sensible but the mechanism as written is conditional and unsourced: the right locator sets the bounce end only when Cycle mode is on, per Apple, and the specific 'two bars' figure has no source. Nobody will refund over the taste part, but they may over dragging the right locator with Cycle off and getting the same clipped tail.
tricks.evidence_quote: By default, when you bounce a project, the entire project from start to end is bounced, but you can bounce only part of a project by setting the bounce range before performing a bounce. When Cycle mode is on, the bounce range matches the locator positions. … adjust the Start and End value sliders.
tricks.salvage: Leave room for the tails. Reverb and delay tails get cut off constantly, so before you bounce, push the End position past the last note — either by adjusting the End value slider in the Bounce dialog, or, with Cycle mode on, by dragging the right locator, since Apple documents that the bounce range matches the locator positions only when Cycle is on. Then listen to the end of the file before you send it.

tricks.title: Colour and name everything before you leave the session
tricks.reason: Session-hygiene advice with no assertion about Logic's behaviour, menus or shortcuts.

tricks.title: Save a version before every major change
tricks.reason: The one checkable element, that New Alternative gives you a safe snapshot to experiment from, is documented by Apple. Note that the menu route is File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative, as flagged on the earlier alternatives trick.
tricks.evidence_quote: Project alternatives let you save snapshots of a project in different states, including different cuts or mixes. … In Logic Pro, choose File > Project Alternatives > New Alternative.

downgrades.title: Turn on “Copy external audio files to project folder”
downgrades.reason: The auditor's own evidence quote never contains the option name — it only says 'select any of the copy checkboxes'. That supports the Assets pane existing, not the named checkbox, which is the whole falsifiable content of the title. I checked Apple's Assets settings page (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/assets-settings-lgcp58b54e81/10.7/mac/11.0, i.e. version-matched to the book's 10.7+ coverage) and the checkboxes are: 'Copy audio files into project' ('If selected, all audio files used in the project are stored as part of your project package or folder'), 'Convert audio file sample rate when importing', 'Copy Sampler audio files into project', 'Copy Alchemy audio files into project', 'Copy Ultrabeat audio files into project', 'Copy Space Designer impulse responses into project'. There is no 'Copy external audio files to project folder' — that is old Logic-era wording, the same failure mode as the non-existent 'As Region Colour' found in sections 1-5. A reader hunting for a checkbox with that name will not find it. SOURCED CORRECTION: retitle to 'Turn on “Copy audio files into project”' and set the body to: 'In File > Project Settings > Assets, select Copy audio files into project — all audio files used in the project are then stored as part of your project package or folder, copied in when the project is saved. Tick the matching boxes for Sampler, Alchemy and Ultrabeat audio and Space Designer impulse responses if you use them. It is the difference between a project that opens on another machine and one that does not.'

downgrades.title: Consolidate before archiving
downgrades.reason: The auditor spotted the defect, wrote it into the reason, and then cleared the trick anyway. The book says Consolidate 'gathers every asset the project depends on into the project package'. Apple's Consolidate page (support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/consolidate-assets-in-a-project-lgcpce09b9d8/mac) says you 'select different asset types currently stored outside of your project' and 'In the Consolidate dialog, you select the checkboxes for the asset types you want to copy into the project, then click OK' — it is an opt-in dialog, not an automatic sweep — and the destination is 'the Media folder inside the project', not 'the project package' (a Logic project may be saved as a folder rather than a package). This matters exactly where the trick claims to help: a reader who runs Consolidate expecting everything to come along, and leaves boxes unticked, archives an incomplete project. SOURCED CORRECTION: 'File > Project Management > Consolidate (or the Consolidate Project key command) copies assets stored outside the project into the project''s Media folder. In the Consolidate dialog, tick the checkboxes for every asset type you want brought in — audio files, Sampler/Alchemy/Ultrabeat audio, Space Designer impulse responses, video, and Sound Library content such as Apple Loops — then click OK. Do this before backing up, and check the boxes rather than assuming.'

downgrades.title: Use “Bounce in Place” to commit a track to audio
downgrades.reason: The headline element — the ⌃B in the trick's key field and the first words of the body — has no quoted source. The auditor's evidence quote is entirely about the menu route and the dialog checkboxes; Apple's page says only 'or use the corresponding key command', and the auditor's substitute was 'three independent third-party shortcut references' that were neither named nor quoted. I searched Apple's Global Commands and key-command tables directly and Control-B for Bounce Regions in Place does not appear in retrievable Apple text; the non-Apple hits are shortcut blog posts plus a Logic Pro 9.1.6 manual page and a scraped Logic Pro X help mirror — which is the version trap, not independent confirmation, since the book covers 10.7/11/12. Bounce-in-Place key assignments are also user-remappable. The verified core survives without it. SALVAGE: 'File > Bounce > Regions in Place commits the selected regions to audio; File > Bounce > Track in Place does a whole track. In the dialog you choose whether to bypass the effect plug-ins on the source track and whether to include volume and pan automation in the bounce. If you use it often, open Key Commands (⌥K), search for “in Place” and see or set the shortcut on your own system.'

downgrades.title: Export all tracks as audio files for stems
downgrades.reason: The evidence block is contaminated. The sentence 'All exported tracks will start at 1 1 1 1 (the project start) when using Export All Tracks as Audio Files' is presented inside a quote attributed to an Apple URL, yet the auditor's own reason admits that part came from third parties, not Apple — fabricated attribution, and the sentence does not read like Apple guide prose. I pulled Apple's Mac page for this command and it documents a Range control: 'Choose whether to trim silence at the end of the exported file(s), export only the cycle range, or extend silence to the project end', plus Include Audio Tail and Include Volume/Pan Automation. So 'all starting at bar 1' is at best a default the reader can silently lose, and Apple never states it. Only the menu path and the one-file-per-track behaviour are Apple-backed ('export all tracks (all audio, software instrument, and Drummer tracks) in a project as audio files—one file per track'). SALVAGE: 'File > Export > All Tracks as Audio Files exports every audio, software instrument and Drummer track as its own file. Check the Range setting in the dialog before you click — it decides whether silence at the end is trimmed, only the cycle range is exported, or silence is extended to the project end — and turn on Include Audio Tail so reverb and delay tails survive. Line the setting up once and the stems drop out consistent, ready to hand to anyone.'

audit.search_note: WebSearch worked normally; 19 of ~20 budgeted searches used, aimed at Apple Logic Pro User Guide pages (Session Players overview, Session Player Editor, Edit a Bass/Keyboard Player performance, Follow rhythm of chords and other tracks, Convert Session Player regions, Chords overview / Analyze chords / Move and resize chords / Pitch Source, Stem Splitter, ChromaGlow, Flashback Capture, Show and hide global tracks) plus MusicTech and Logic Studio Training for 11.2 release facts. No group in this file has a "path" field, so there are no menu paths to report against a first trick. Where a trick's mechanism claim (e.g. "complexity = notes per bar", "artefacts are frequency dependent", "performance engine is instrument-agnostic") was not stated by any source, it is UNVERIFIABLE rather than assumed correct. Note two cross-cutting version issues the owner should decide on: (a) the section is titled "Logic Pro 11 Update" but Flashback Capture, six-stem Stem Splitter and the submix/preset options are 11.2 features, which the tricks mostly do label; (b) Apple's guide now also documents a separate Synth Bass Player and Synth Keyboard Player (Logic Pro 12), which the section never mentions.

tricks.title: Session Players are Drummer, extended to bass and keys
tricks.reason: Apple's Session Players overview names exactly these three players and describes creating them from the New Tracks dialog. The 'real, editable performance rather than a loop' framing is supported by the same page plus the documented Convert to MIDI Region command.
tricks.evidence_quote: The Session Players feature the Bass Player, Keyboard Player, and Drummer. … In the New Tracks dialog, click Drummer, Bass Player, or Keyboard Player, then click Create to add a software instrument track with one 8-bar region.

tricks.title: Every Session Player region is convertible to MIDI
tricks.reason: Apple documents the command for Session Player regions. One tightening: the command sits in a Convert submenu, so the copy should read 'choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region'. Apple also warns the conversion is one-way in practice (edits are lost if you convert back), which is worth adding.
tricks.evidence_quote: Control-click the Session Player region, then choose Convert > Convert to MIDI Region from the shortcut menu.

tricks.title: Use the Follow parameter to lock players to each other
tricks.reason: Apple's Follow Rhythm page gives Bass Player and Keyboard Player a 'Follow Rhythm Of' section with a Chords switch and a Track pop-up menu — you point them at a whole track, not at a kick drum. Kick/snare-level following is the Drummer's control (the Drummer's kick and snare follow another track), which is the reverse of what the trick tells the reader to set up.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Session Player Editor, depending on the Session Player type selected, Bass Player and Keyboard Player use the Patterns button, while Drummer uses the Patterns button for the Kick and Snare kit pieces. … below Follow Rhythm Of, you can choose a track from the Track pop-up menu
tricks.correction: In the Session Player Editor, click Patterns and look under Follow Rhythm Of. Leave the Chords switch on so the player tracks your progression, then use the Track pop-up menu to make the Bass Player follow your drum track and the Keyboard Player follow the bass. The three of them lock like a band rather than three separate parts. (Kick-and-snare-level following is a Drummer control: the Drummer's kick and snare can follow another track's rhythm.)

tricks.title: Session Players respond to region length, so write in sections
tricks.reason: The useful half — per-region complexity and intensity — is documented (the Session Player Editor edits the region-based performance of the selected region). No source found says the generated performance responds to how long the region is, so that specific mechanism is unproven as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Session Player Editor, you can choose a Keyboard Player, Bass Player, or Drummer for the selected Session Player region, edit the region-based performance of a Session Player, and work with chords.
tricks.salvage: Session Player settings are region-based, so write in sections. Give each song section its own region and set complexity and intensity per region in the Session Player Editor. That is how you get a verse that builds into a chorus.

tricks.title: Swap the player character without losing your settings
tricks.reason: Settings do not persist automatically. Apple documents that you must turn on 'Keep Settings when Changing Style' in the Preset pop-up menu (and there is a separate Lock Settings button for finer control). A reader who follows this as written will change player and lose the performance settings.
tricks.evidence_quote: To keep your performance settings when changing to a different player style, choose "Keep Settings when Changing Style" from the Preset pop-up menu in the Logic Pro Session Player Editor.
tricks.correction: Before you start auditioning characters, choose 'Keep Settings when Changing Style' from the Preset pop-up menu in the Session Player Editor. With that on, your performance settings survive the swap and you can hear every character against the same arrangement in seconds. Use the Lock Settings button if you want to protect individual parameters such as Fills and Swing.

tricks.title: Set Feel to push or pull against the grid
tricks.reason: Apple documents the Feel knob with exactly this up/down behaviour, and Session Player settings are edited per selected region in the Session Player Editor. 'Single most musical control' is taste, not a checkable claim.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can drag the Feel knob up to have the Session Player play ahead of the beat or down to play behind the beat.

tricks.title: Regenerate a performance without changing anything else
tricks.reason: No source found stating that nudging Complexity or Intensity produces a fresh variation of the same part rather than a deterministic change. The title also contradicts the body (it promises no change, then tells you to change two parameters). Not checked against any documented 'regenerate' command.
tricks.salvage: Small nudges to the Complexity or Intensity sliders often shift a phrase enough to fix it. If a bar is not landing, try nudging those sliders before you rebuild the part from scratch.

tricks.title: Layer two Session Players on the same part
tricks.reason: Pure arrangement taste — create two Session Player tracks and balance them. Nothing here asserts a Logic behaviour that could be shown false.

tricks.title: Bass Player follows the Chord track by default
tricks.reason: Apple states the Bass Player's harmonies follow the global Chord track (or region chords), and that following chords is on by default. Caveat for the owner: 'including inversions and passing notes' is unsourced colour — no source found describing inversions or passing notes as a consequence of Chord track following.
tricks.evidence_quote: The harmonies played by the Bass Player and Keyboard Player follow the global Chord track or region chords. … The option to follow the rhythm of chords is turned on by default.

tricks.title: Use the Note Range control to keep the part in a register
tricks.reason: Apple's Bass Player page carries a Note Range section with a Lowest Note slider that constrains what the player can play. Worth naming the actual control in the copy ('Lowest Note slider' under Note Range) rather than 'the Note Range control'.
tricks.evidence_quote: You can set the lowest note the Bass Player can play by dragging the Lowest Note slider, which can be useful if a chord tone is lower than E3 and you want to include it.

tricks.title: Adjust the Complexity slider before you adjust anything else
tricks.reason: The Complexity slider is documented, but Apple only says higher settings mean a more complex performance. Nothing found supports the specific mechanism 'it controls how many notes the player uses per bar', so that sentence is unproven as written.
tricks.evidence_quote: In the Session Player Editor, you can drag the Complexity slider or Intensity slider to adjust the performance, where the higher you drag the respective slider, the greater the complexity or intensity of the performance.
tricks.salvage: Reach for the Complexity slider first: drag it higher for a more complex performance, lower for a plainer one. Low complexity in a verse and high in a chorus is an arrangement decision made with one slider.

tricks.title: Turn on or off specific articulations
tricks.reason: Apple's Bass Player controls do not match this list. Dead notes and slides are amount knobs, not on/off switches; mutes and pickup hits are buttons; and no hammer-on control is documented anywhere in the Bass Player settings. Style-dependent Details controls are probability knobs (Buzz Trills, Double Stops, Laid Back, Blue Notes, Slaps).
